title: David Ellison says AI could be the ‘biggest creative unlock in modern history’
title_en: David Ellison says AI could be the ‘biggest creative unlock in modern history’
author: The Verge AI
article_content:
Posts from this topic will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Paramount Skydance’s CEO compared AI to CGI, but said it ‘will never be a replacement’ for artists.﻿

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

During Paramount Skydance’s latest earnings call, CEO David Ellison said “it’s hard to imagine” AI won’t have a bigger impact on the film industry than CGI. In response to a question about the company’s outlook for AI, Ellison said:

“I think when you zoom out and look at production, AI really has the potential to be the biggest creative unlock in modern history. The last time we saw anything close to this was really the, you know, advent of CGI and digital composites in the early 90s. That technology gave birth to amazing stories like Jurassic Park and Terminator 2, and it’s hard to imagine that AI is not going to have a more significant impact than that. And I personally believe that’s going to be an incredible unlock on creativity.”

Ellison gave Terminator as an example, describing how it cost $4 million to make, but “if you wanted to make that picture today, shot for shot, it’s $60 to 70 million.” He went on to suggest AI might be able to help with that: “We think these tools will help unlock more original storytelling by being able to make the budgets more digestible to be able to take that amount of risk.”

Ellison said AI will “significantly” reshape Paramount Skydance’s business, saying the company has been developing its own AI tools. As a result of those tools, Ellison claims, “content will be easier to produce, projects across the organization will speed up, and how we work will transform.” He emphasized that “all of this makes the value of premium IP and live events more valuable, not less.”

Ellison also noted that “in a world of AI slop, we think there will always be a premium for truly hand-crafted storytelling.” He added, “We also continue to believe that artificial intelligence is a tool for artists and will never be a replacement for them.”

派拉蒙 Skydance 的首席执行官将人工智能与 CGI 进行了比较，但表示它“永远不会取代”艺术家。

该作者的帖子将添加到您的每日电子邮件摘要和主页源中。

在派拉蒙 Skydance 最新的财报电话会议上，首席执行官戴维·埃里森 (David Ellison) 表示，“很难想象”人工智能对电影业的影响不会比 CGI 更大。在回答有关公司人工智能前景的问题时，埃里森表示：

“我认为，当你放眼观察制作时，人工智能确实有潜力成为现代历史上最大的创意解锁。我们上一次看到类似的东西实际上是 90 年代初 CGI 和数字复合材料的出现。这项技术催生了《侏罗纪公园》和《终结者 2》等精彩故事，很难想象人工智能不会产生比这更重大的影响。我个人相信，这将是创造力的一个令人难以置信的解锁。”

埃里森以《终结者》为例，描述了它的制作成本为 400 万美元，但“如果你今天想拍那部电影，一个镜头一个镜头，就需要 60 到 7000 万美元。”他接着建议人工智能可能会对此有所帮助：“我们认为这些工具将有助于解锁更多原创故事，让预算更容易消化，从而能够承担如此大的风险。”

埃里森表示，人工智能将“显着”重塑派拉蒙 Skydance 的业务，并表示该公司一直在开发自己的人工智能工具。埃里森声称，由于使用了这些工具，“内容将更容易制作，整个组织的项目将加快，我们的工作方式将发生转变。”他强调，“所有这些都让优质IP和现场活动的价值变得更有价值，而不是更少。”

埃里森还指出，“在人工智能的世界里，我们认为真正手工制作的故事讲述永远都会有溢价。”他补充道，“我们也仍然相信人工智能是艺术家的工具，永远不会取代他们。”

title: Jensen Huang’s Troubles Leave the AI Industry Reeling
title_en: Jensen Huang’s Troubles Leave the AI Industry Reeling
author: Wired AI
article_content:
Over the last few days, Huang’s status as an AI titan has come under scrutiny amid an admission that he had an affair with Alice Huang, an executive at a Singapore-based company whom US intelligence services concluded was a Chinese intelligence asset.

Nvidia’s board of directors said that the company would launch an investigation into the incident. Huang, the company said, “fully supports the review and has committed to cooperating with it.” Huang earned $36 million last year, owned about 3.5 percent of Nvidia as of March, according to a corporate filing—which also noted that Huang is an at-will employee who can be let go anytime without severance.

How exactly the investigation shakes out, and what it means for Huang’s future at the company, remains to be seen. But the incident at least puts his position at risk, and raises questions about how the industry will respond.

“He’s the person who decides who gets the chips and who doesn't,” says David Yoffie, a professor at Harvard Business School who tracks the chip industry.

Nvidia, which Huang cofounded in 1993, controls 90 percent of the market for chips used in training frontier AI models. With those chips in short supply, Huang has the power to determine which areas of AI get a boost next. Nvidia has also bankrolled much of the AI buildout, investing billions in the very companies buying its chips, such as OpenAI and Anthropic. When Elon Musk wants to build a new data center, Yoffie says, he can put in a call to Huang.

Internally, Huang closely manages even small details at Nvidia, responds to emails from any one of its roughly 60,000 staffers, and raises his voice to get points across, according to current and former employees. He’s a regular on cable TV and at tech conferences, where he’s been trying to deflate concerns about an AI market bubble and boost the positioning of his company.

But Nvidia has no other executive anywhere close to Huang’s prominence, and no apparent potential successor. “We have no idea who would replace him,” Yoffie says. “You put someone new into that position, if you're a customer, who knows what that's going to mean.”

Ryan Fedasiuk, a senior fellow at the think tank Foundation for American Innovation, says that Huang has played such an important role—and become so close to the president—that he has become load-bearing for the entire US AI industry.

“On the one hand, Huang is irreplaceable. He built Nvidia into the juggernaut it is today, and he was the visionary behind the GPU, which has sustained the intelligence revolution,” Fedasiuk says. But he says that the company, which is indispensable to the AI industry, has to come first.

“He has to be replaceable as the CEO of the world's largest company, at $4 trillion in capex.”

Nvidia shares fell more than 4 percent on Monday, even as broader stock market indices rose.

The board’s investigation will most likely focus on whether Huang violated any company policies, Yoffie says. But the FBI could also investigate whether laws were broken, and Congress may decide to look into whether Huang’s affair influenced the US government’s policy on selling chips to China.

Nvidia didn’t immediately respond to WIRED’s request for comment.

The scandal also raises serious questions about whether China may have gained sensitive information about US AI companies and the government’s strategy on China, Fedasiuk says.

Huang’s affair appears especially damning given how outspoken he has been in recent years against calls for more aggressive technology export controls on China. His credibility on the topic could be permanently in doubt.

Both the first Trump administration and the Biden administration imposed export controls designed to limit China’s access to Nvidia’s chips, as well as technology required to mint advanced semiconductors. In his second term, however, Trump loosened these controls, giving China access to older generations of Nvidia chips; it was better to make China reliant on US technology, the argument went.

Sam Bresnick, a research fellow at Georgetown University’s Center for Security and Emerging Technology, says the Huang scandal is likely to accelerate efforts to crack down on chip exports.

“There was going to be more of an impetus to control what chips are getting sent to China anyway,” he says. “I expect there to be more scrutiny on what's going on, what's getting sent to China. I think there's also going to be more scrutiny from the Commerce Department.”

title_zh: 黄仁勋卷入间谍绯闻，董事会介入调查
summary_zh: 英伟达CEO黄仁勋被曝与新加坡某公司高管存在不正当关系，该女子被指涉及情报背景，英伟达董事会已启动调查
article_content_zh:
过去几天，黄的人工智能巨头地位受到密切关注，因为他承认与一家新加坡公司高管爱丽丝·黄(Alice Huang)有染，美国情报部门断定该公司是中国情报资产。

英伟达董事会表示，公司将对这一事件展开调查。该公司表示，黄先生“完全支持此次审查，并承诺与其合作。”根据一份公司文件显示，黄去年赚了 3600 万美元，截至 3 月份，他持有 Nvidia 约 3.5% 的股份，文件还指出，黄是一名随意员工，可以随时被解雇，且无需支付遣散费。

调查究竟如何进行，以及这对黄在公司的未来意味着什么，还有待观察。但这一事件至少让他的地位面临风险，并引发了业界将如何应对的疑问。

“他是决定谁获得芯片、谁不获得芯片的人，”追踪芯片行业的哈佛商学院教授戴维·约菲 (David Yoffie) 表示。

黄仁勋于 1993 年与他人共同创立的 Nvidia 控制着用于训练前沿人工智能模型的芯片市场的 90%。由于这些芯片供应短缺，黄仁勋有能力决定人工智能的哪些领域接下来会得到推动。英伟达还为人工智能建设提供了大部分资金，向购买其芯片的公司投资了数十亿美元，例如 OpenAI 和 Anthropic。尤菲说，当埃隆·马斯克想要建立一个新的数据中心时，他可以给黄打电话。

据现任和前任员工称，在内部，黄在 Nvidia 密切管理着哪怕是很小的细节，回复大约 60,000 名员工中任何一位的电子邮件，并提高声音表达观点。他是有线电视和科技会议的常客，他一直在努力消除人们对人工智能市场泡沫的担忧，并提升公司的定位。

但英伟达没有其他高管能与黄的地位相提并论，也没有明显的潜在继任者。 “我们不知道谁会取代他，”约菲说。 “如果你是客户，你让一个新人担任这个职位，谁知道这意味着什么。”

美国创新基金会智库高级研究员瑞安·费达西克 (Ryan Fedasiuk) 表示，黄仁勋发挥了如此重要的作用，并且与总统关系如此密切，以至于他已经成为整个美国人工智能行业的负担。

“一方面，黄仁勋是不可替代的。他将 Nvidia 打造成今天的巨头，他是 GPU 背后的远见卓识者，推动了智能革命，”Fedasiuk 说道。但他表示，人工智能行业不可或缺的公司必须是第一位的。

“作为全球最大公司（资本支出达 4 万亿美元）的首席执行官，他必须被替换。”

尽管股市整体指数上涨，但英伟达股价周一仍下跌逾 4%。

约菲表示，董事会的调查很可能会集中在黄是否违反任何公司政策上。但联邦调查局也可能调查是否违反法律，国会可能决定调查黄的事件是否影响了美国政府向中国出售芯片的政策。

英伟达没有立即回应《连线》杂志的置评请求。

费达修克表示，这一丑闻还引发了严重的问题，即中国是否可能获得了有关美国人工智能公司以及政府对华战略的敏感信息。

ai_analysis.briefing_zh: 英伟达CEO黄仁勋被曝与新加坡某公司高管Alice Huang存在婚外情，美国情报机构认定该女子为中国情报资产。目前英伟达董事会已启动全面调查，黄仁勋承诺配合，鉴于其在该公司处于可被随时解雇的雇用协议下，此次丑闻使其CEO职位面临前所未有的存续风险。

title: Here’s what Trump said he knew about Jensen Huang
title_en: Here’s what Trump said he knew about Jensen Huang
author: The Verge AI
article_content:
Posts from this topic will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

In a White House press conference, President Trump was vague about when learned of Jensen Huang’s affair.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

President Trump held a White House press briefing earlier today and responded to several questions about his knowledge of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s affair with an alleged Chinese spy. Huang said this weekend that he had been “​​unfaithful” to his wife, and the company has opened an investigation into Huang.

Recent articles from The New York Times indicated that Trump had been aware of a relationship between Huang and Alice Huang, the suspected spy, before information about it became public. In October, The New York Times reported that Trump had been briefed “roughly a year ago” on intelligence that Huang and the alleged spy, Alice Huang, had developed a close relationship, but he didn’t do anything with the information. Yesterday, the NYT reported that Secretary of State Marco Rubio helped draft a memo to Trump officials about the relationship before Trump visited China in May.

In the press conference, Trump wasn’t specific about when he learned of the affair. But Trump said Huang told him today that he had “no idea” the person was a spy.

Here are Trump’s responses to questions about Jensen Huang from his press briefing today. You can watch a replay of the press conference on MS Now’s YouTube channel.

When were you first informed that there was an issue with Jensen Huang and the affair? What was presented to you at the time?

I would say that when I heard about it, first of all, I was amazed because I view him as a very high-quality person. I’ve known him a long time. It’s the largest, by value, the largest or one of the largest companies in the world. He did that with a chip. When you think about it, you’ve got a chip that’s 10 years advanced, can’t be… the Blackwell can’t even be copied. He’s an amazing guy.

I just hope there’s no problem. If there is a problem, we’ll let you know about it. But I hope there’s no problem. I believe he’s suffering greatly. I read his statement. And I believe he’s suffering greatly. Moreso because of his family. His wife who he loves and his family. But he is definitely suffering.

Just to follow up on the, “When were you first told of these potential issues with Mr. Huang?” You didn’t answer that question.

Well I’ve been hearing about it, and I’ve been reading a little bit about it over a period of time. But, not too long ago.

We’ll look into it. I know the FBI’s looking into it in terms of something else. I think that he’ll be in good shape.

Are you going to bring up the case of Jensen Huang with President Xi when you visit with him next week?

No, I don’t think so. Maybe, I’m sure, President Xi will ask me about it. I just know Jensen very well. I just think he’s a very honorable man. He built a great company. American company. I think he’s a very honorable guy. I feel very confident that he’ll be in good shape.

Sticking with Jensen Huang, when you went to China earlier this year in May, did you know about these alleged ties to the spy then?

No, I didn’t hear about it then. But a lot of people have heard about it. And Jensen totally denies that. I asked him today, because I did speak to him today just to see if he’s feeling alright, how are you doing… and I asked him about that. He said he had absolutely no idea that the person in question was a spy. I asked him that question, did you have any idea that she was a spy? He said, I had no idea that she was a spy. And I really believe him.

I want to put a finer point on when exactly you were made aware of the intelligence around Jensen Huang.

Oh, I’d have to check. But this has been going on…

But there are reports that Secretary Rubio put an intelligence memo out last year. Did you read that memo?

I’d certainly check with the intelligence people. It could have been mentioned. Certainly it didn’t make much of an impact on me.

在白宫新闻发布会上，特朗普总统对于何时得知黄仁勋的恋情含糊其辞。

该作者的帖子将添加到您的每日电子邮件摘要和主页源中。

特朗普总统今天早些时候举行了白宫新闻发布会，并回答了有关他对英伟达首席执行官黄仁勋与一名涉嫌中国间谍的恋情的了解的几个问题。黄本周末表示，他对妻子“不忠”，公司已对黄展开调查。

《纽约时报》最近的文章指出，特朗普在相关信息公开之前就已经意识到黄与涉嫌间谍的爱丽丝·黄之间的关系。 10 月，《纽约时报》报道称，特朗普“大约一年前”就已获悉黄与所谓间谍爱丽丝·黄 (Alice Huang) 建立了密切关系的情报，但他没有对这些信息采取任何行动。昨天，《纽约时报》报道称，在特朗普五月访华之前，国务卿马可·卢比奥帮助起草了一份给特朗普官员的关于中美关系的备忘录。

在新闻发布会上，特朗普没有具体说明他是何时得知这一事件的。但特朗普表示，黄今天告诉他，他“不知道”这个人是间谍。

以下是特朗普在今天的新闻发布会上对有关黄仁勋问题的回应。您可以在 MS Now 的 YouTube 频道上观看新闻发布会的重播。

你什么时候第一次得知黄仁勋和这件事存在问题？当时向您呈现了什么？

我想说，当我听说这件事时，首先我很惊讶，因为我认为他是一个非常高素质的人。我认识他很久了。按价值计算，它是世界上最大的公司或最大的公司之一。他用芯片做到了这一点。当你想一想，你拥有的芯片已经先进了 10 年，不可能……Blackwell 甚至无法复制。他是一个了不起的人。

我只是希望没有问题。如果出现问题，我们会通知您。但我希望没有问题。我相信他正在承受很大的痛苦。我读了他的声明。我相信他正在承受巨大的痛苦。更何况是因为他的家庭。他所爱的妻子和他的家人。但他肯定是在受苦。

只是跟进，“你什么时候第一次被告知与黄先生的这些潜在问题？”你没有回答这个问题。

嗯，我一直听说过它，并且一段时间以来我一直在阅读一些有关它的内容。但是，不久前。

我们会调查一下。我知道联邦调查局正在从其他方面调查此事。我认为他会保持良好的状态。

下周你会见习主席时，是否会向他提及黄仁勋案？

title: A report by short seller Culper Research from May is resurfacing because it had flagged Jensen Huang's relationship with Alice Huang as "uncomfortably close" (Sarah Perez/TechCrunch)
title_en: A report by short seller Culper Research from May is resurfacing because it had flagged Jensen Huang's relationship with Alice Huang as "uncomfortably close" (Sarah Perez/TechCrunch)
author: TechCrunch
article_content:
Six months before the Nvidia spy scandal emerged, the New York-based short seller firm Culper Research had already raised questions about Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s unusually close relationship with Alice Huang, an executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based company that buys Nvidia chips. She is now suspected to be a Chinese spy.

The Nvidia CEO admitted to an extramarital affair over the weekend, and the company has now opened a formal investigation into his relationship with Alice Huang (who shares his last name but is not related). U.S. intelligence officials believe she was recruited by the Chinese government to collect intelligence on Jensen Huang and influence his position regarding U.S. export controls on advanced AI chips.

Culper’s May 13 report is resurfacing because it picked up on the connection between Jensen Huang and Alice Huang while investigating Megaspeed’s ties to Nvidia.

NEW: We are short Nvidia $NVDA. We believe Nvidia has a significant China problem. Please see our full report and disclosures now available on our website, link in bio. pic.twitter.com/oTaJyL7S2R

In particular, the report called the relationship between the two executives “uncomfortably close,” noting that the Nvidia CEO was spotted partying and socializing with Alice Huang on multiple occasions. The report even claimed that some Nvidia employees wondered whether they had a “special relationship.”

Culper Research also theorized the China business that Nvidia lost to export controls had been rerouted through Southeast Asia, and that Megaspeed, a major chip buyer in the region, was secretly financed by Chinese tech giant Alibaba through shell companies. It pointed to financial records that showed Megaspeed’s total liabilities and equity had grown from $33 million at the end of 2023 to around $3 billion by the end of 2024, much of it in the form of refundable deposits from an unidentified source.

Financial Times reported Monday that documents show Alibaba lent money to Megaspeed through subsidiaries.

Culper is a short seller, so it stood to financially benefit from making these allegations, and those about possible illegal chip diversion have not been independently verified. Its report is available on the web and was posted to X back in May.

title_zh: 黄仁勋卷入间谍丑闻引发轩然大波
summary_zh: 英伟达CEO黄仁勋承认婚外情并接受调查，其交往对象被指为试图刺探芯片出口管制的外国间谍
article_content_zh:
在英伟达间谍丑闻曝光的六个月前，总部位于纽约的卖空公司 Culper Research 就已经对英伟达首席执行官黄仁勋与购买英伟达芯片的新加坡公司 Megaspeed 的高管 Alice Huang 之间异常密切的关系提出了质疑。她现在被怀疑是中国间谍。

这位英伟达首席执行官周末承认了婚外情，该公司现已对他与爱丽丝·黄（Alice Huang）（与他姓氏相同，但没有亲属关系）的关系展开正式调查。美国情报官员认为，她被中国政府招募来收集有关黄仁勋的情报，并影响他在美国先进人工智能芯片出口管制方面的立场。

Culper 5 月 13 日的报告重新浮出水面，因为它在调查 Megaspeed 与 Nvidia 的关系时发现了 Jensen Huang 和 Alice Huang 之间的联系。

新消息：我们做空 Nvidia $NVDA。我们认为英伟达存在严重的中国问题。请参阅我们网站上的完整报告和披露信息（简历中的链接）。 pic.twitter.com/oTaJyL7S2R

该报告特别指出，两位高管之间的关系“极其密切”，并指出英伟达首席执行官多次被发现与爱丽丝·黄 (Alice Huang) 参加派对和社交活动。该报道甚至声称，一些英伟达员工怀疑他们是否存在“特殊关系”。

Culper Research 还推测，英伟达因出口管制而失去的中国业务已改道至东南亚，而该地区的主要芯片买家 Megaspeed 则由中国科技巨头阿里巴巴通过空壳公司秘密资助。它指出，财务记录显示，Megaspeed 的总负债和股本已从 2023 年底的 3300 万美元增长到 2024 年底的约 30 亿美元，其中大部分是以来源不明的可退还存款的形式出现的。

英国《金融时报》周一报道称，文件显示阿里巴巴通过子公司向 Megaspeed 借钱。

卡尔珀是卖空者，因此它可以从提出这些指控中获得经济利益，而有关可能的非法芯片转移的指控尚未得到独立证实。其报告可在网上获取，并于 5 月份发布到 X。

当您通过我们文章中的链接购买时，我们可能会赚取少量佣金。这并不影响我们的编辑独立性。

title: Everything we know so far about the Nvidia spy scandal targeting CEO Jensen Huang
title_en: Everything we know so far about the Nvidia spy scandal targeting CEO Jensen Huang
author: The Verge AI
article_content:
The leather-jacketed CEO of Nvidia, Jensen Huang, has acknowledged an affair with Megaspeed exec Alice Huang, spurring an investigation by his company and intense discussions worldwide. Recent reporting noted that since last year, US intelligence reports had identified Alice Huang (no relation) as not only the exec for an AI compute company renting access to Nvidia GPUs, but also a spy for China’s Ministry of State Security.

In recent years, Nvidia has become a key part of the Trump administration’s AI push, a central figure in negotiations over potential Chinese access to cutting-edge AI hardware, and a company that has used its now $4 trillion-plus market cap to finance other AI companies, including the “neoclouds” like Coreweave who have been some of its biggest customers.  So far, Nvidia and Jensen Huang have said that they have “no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised,” but that hasn’t settled things as the investigation continues.

title: Apple is now offering additional AI access via one-time $50 "intelligence usage packs" when monthly usage caps are met, starting in its Creator Studio apps (Ryan Christoffel/9to5Mac)
title_en: Apple is now offering additional AI access via one-time $50 "intelligence usage packs" when monthly usage caps are met, starting in its Creator Studio apps (Ryan Christoffel/9to5Mac)
author: 9to5Mac
article_content:
Apple has said it will eventually charge for expanded usage of select AI features. Now the first ‘intelligence usage packs’ have arrived tied to Apple Creator Studio apps. Here are the details.

And now, Apple has officially launched its first take on charging for AI features via the new Logic Pro update—with more coming soon.

With Logic Pro’s latest update, if you select Logic Pro from the menu bar, then ‘Intelligence Features’ and ‘Show Usage,’ there’s an option to ‘Buy More Usage.’

The only option is a $49.99 one-time purchase of an ‘intelligence usage pack.’

Right now the only app that lets you buy additional AI usage is Logic Pro, but when the rest of the already-announced Apple Creator Studio updates debut this month, usage packs are expected to be available in Final Cut Pro, Pixelmator Pro, and the iWork suite as well.

For now, these usage packs are limited to Creator Studio apps. But we’ll likely see a similar model arrive for expanded access to other server-based AI features like Siri AI, Image Playground, Photos editing tools, and more in the future.

Full terms and conditions for AI usage packs are available here.

Have you used any of the new AI features in Apple Creator Studio? How are they working for you? Let us know in the comments.

You must be logged in to post a comment.

Ryan got his start in journalism as an Editor at MacStories, where he worked for four years covering Apple news, writing app reviews, and more. For two years he co-hosted the Adapt podcast on Relay FM, which focused entirely on the iPad. As a result, it should come as no surprise that his favorite Apple device is the iPad Pro.

title: Jensen Huang's affair shines a spotlight on Nvidia's weak board and opaque succession planning at what has become the world's most important company (Semafor)
title_en: Jensen Huang's affair shines a spotlight on Nvidia's weak board and opaque succession planning at what has become the world's most important company (Semafor)
author: Semafor
article_content:
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s spy scandal shines a spotlight on thin corporate governance and opaque succession planning at what has become the world’s most important company.

Huang’s chances of remaining as CEO, after admitting to an affair with a woman suspected of spying for Chinese intelligence services, are now in the hands of a board of directors that lacks the experience and stature typically found at companies of Nvidia’s size and importance. They have allowed Huang to run the company with no obvious successor and a leadership structure with little precedent in corporate America, in which he has more than 50 direct reports.

Top of mind, too, is what Nvidia would be without Huang, its CEO since he co-founded the company in 1993. He has nearly single-handedly turned Nvidia from a niche maker of graphics chips for video games into the centerpiece of the world’s AI boom — and, depending on the day, its most valuable company.

“It appears [Huang] did mislead the public,” said Gary Gensler, the former chair of the Securities & Exchange Commission under the Biden administration, referencing earlier denials by Huang and the company that his dealings were “all completely normal and not unusual.”

“It’s really a question of is that material, and today’s stock drop will suggest to a court it was material,” Gensler said. Nvidia’s shares were down 5% in afternoon trading, slicing more than $200 billion from its market value. When asked if the SEC was going to investigate, an agency spokesperson declined to comment.

For its part, Nvidia’s board has said it still has confidence in Huang.

The average Nvidia board member has been there almost 15 years — nearly twice as long as the average S&P 500 director. Nvidia’s lead director is a 77-year-old former law-firm executive. None of the board members are current or former S&P 500 CEOs or have national-security experience. (Meta and Microsoft each have four big-company CEOs on their boards.) Huang and two other directors have been on the board since the company’s founding 33 years ago.

“The board composition suggests this is… a CEO exercising effective control over the board instead of vice versa,” said Jill Fisch, a professor at The University of Pennsylvania’s Carey Law School, adding that long tenure on a board can reduce directors’ independence and breed complacency.

At the same time, she said, Nvidia exemplifies how limited boards’ ability to check executives’ power can be when their CEO is known as an industry visionary: “How do you say no to someone with this track record of success?”

Nvidia has never publicly signaled a succession plan for Huang, both of whose adult children work for the company. It also lacks a clear No. 2, with no president or chief operating officer. The word “succession” appears nowhere in its most recent annual report to shareholders, versus 25 times for Microsoft and 16 for Alphabet.

The Nvidia board has for years enabled Huang’s unusual management style, in which he has more than 50 direct reports. It’s a nearly unheard-of management structure that is meant to enable Nvidia to operate at what Huang has called the “speed of light,” but leaves the company without an obvious internal replacement for Huang, should the board’s investigation unearth facts that make it untenable for him to remain CEO.

It also sets up a talent drain: If Huang is ultimately fired and replaced with an insider, “you’re going to have 59 people who will all think ‘it should have been me,’” said Jason Schloetzer, a professor at Georgetown University who co-authors an annual report on CEO succession planning. “A horse race with 60 horses has no good solution.”

That will likely force directors to look outside, with a short list of CEOs from seasoned chipmakers such as AMD’s Lisa Su or Broadcom’s Hock Tan.

Huang’s case has implications beyond those raised by “the usual sex scandal in the corporate boardroom,” said John C. Coffee Jr, a Columbia Law School professor and veteran corporate governance expert. “Other companies have fired the CEO [for infidelity] but those companies probably didn’t have quite as important a figure as CEO,” he said. “It’s possible he was at most negligent,” Coffee said, “but negligence doesn’t require that you shoot yourself in the foot by firing a well regarded CEO.”

The company’s investigation, and likely congressional hearings, will help determine whether Huang did anything during the course of his extramarital relationship to compromise company secrets or US national security in an industry of intense significance to the geopolitical competition between the US and China. The board said on Sunday it had “no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised,” and President Donald Trump expressed confidence in Huang.

The company will also face questions about an earlier investigation it said it conducted into the allegations. Any suggestion that Huang misled the board, or that the company knowingly misled investors about a material issue could expose it to even more shareholder litigation. Enforcement action is another risk, though Gensler said “I think this administration does things differently. The President has already spoken on the matter.”

article_content_zh:
英伟达首席执行官黄仁勋的间谍丑闻凸显了这家全球最重要公司薄弱的公司治理和不透明的继任计划。

在承认与一名涉嫌为中国情报部门从事间谍活动的女性有染后，黄仁勋继续担任首席执行官的机会现在掌握在董事会手中，而董事会缺乏英伟达这样规模和重要性的公司通常具备的经验和地位。他们允许黄在没有明显继任者的情况下管理公司，其领导结构在美国企业界几乎没有先例，黄在美国企业界有超过 50 名直接下属。

人们最关心的问题还包括，如果黄仁勋自 1993 年与他人共同创立了公司以来，如果没有黄仁勋，英伟达将会是什么样子。他几乎凭借一己之力，将英伟达从视频游戏图形芯片的利基制造商转变为世界人工智能热潮的核心，并且根据具体情况，成为该公司最有价值的公司。

拜登政府时期的美国证券交易委员会前主席加里·詹斯勒（Gary Gensler）表示：“看来（黄）确实误导了公众。”他提到黄和该公司早些时候否认他的交易“完全正常，并不罕见”。

“这确实是一个重要的问题，今天的股价下跌将向法庭表明这是重要的，”詹斯勒说。下午交易中，英伟达股价下跌 5%，市值缩水逾 2000 亿美元。当被问及 SEC 是否会进行调查时，该机构发言人拒绝发表评论。

英伟达董事会表示，仍然对黄仁勋充满信心。

Nvidia 董事会成员的平均任职时间接近 15 年，几乎是标准普尔 500 强董事平均任职时间的两倍。 Nvidia 的首席董事是一位 77 岁的前律师事务所高管。董事会成员均不是现任或前任标准普尔 500 强公司首席执行官，也没有国家安全经验。 （Meta 和微软的董事会各有四位大公司首席执行官。）自 33 年前公司成立以来，黄仁勋和另外两名董事一直是董事会成员。

宾夕法尼亚大学凯里法学院教授吉尔·费什 (Jill Fisch) 表示：“董事会的构成表明，这是……首席执行官对董事会行使有效控制，而不是反过来。”她补充说，在董事会任职时间过长会降低董事的独立性并滋生自满情绪。

与此同时，她说，英伟达的例子表明，当首席执行官被誉为行业远见卓识时，董事会检查高管权力的能力是多么有限：“你如何对拥有如此成功记录的人说不？”

英伟达从未公开表示过黄的继任计划，黄的两个成年子女都在该公司工作。它还缺乏明确的第二名，没有总裁或首席运营官。 “继任”一词在其最近向股东提交的年度报告中没有出现，而微软则出现了 25 次，Alphabet 则出现了 16 次。

多年来，Nvidia 董事会一直支持黄的不同寻常的管理风格，他有 50 多名直接下属。这是一种几乎闻所未闻的管理结构，旨在使英伟达能够以黄仁勋所说的“光速”运营，但如果董事会的调查发现黄仁勋无法继续担任首席执行官，那么公司内部将没有明显的替代者。

它还会造成人才外流：如果黄最终被解雇并由内部人士取代，“将会有 59 个人都认为‘应该是我’，”乔治城大学教授贾森·施洛泽 (Jason Schloetzer) 说，他是 CEO 继任计划年度报告的合著者。 “一场60匹马的赛马没有什么好的解决办法。”

这可能会迫使董事们将目光投向外部，其中包括AMD的Lisa Su或Broadcom的Hock Tan等经验丰富的芯片制造商的首席执行官名单。

哥伦比亚法学院教授、资深公司治理专家小约翰·C·科菲 (John C. Coffee Jr) 表示，黄的案件的影响超出了“公司董事会中常见的性丑闻”所引发的影响。 “其他公司因不忠而解雇了首席执行官，但这些公司可能没有像首席执行官那么重要的人物，”他说。 “他最多可能是疏忽大意，”咖啡说，“但疏忽并不意味着你解雇了一位备受尊敬的首席执行官，搬起石头砸自己的脚。”

title: Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 cement Anthropic's AI lead just before its IPO
title_en: Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 cement Anthropic's AI lead just before its IPO
author: THE DECODER
article_content:
Anthropic's Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 reclaim the AI performance lead shortly before the company's IPO, in some cases by a wide margin. Opus 5.5 remains Anthropic's recommended model for everyday use.

Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 share the same model foundation but, just like their predecessors, differ in access. Fable includes safeguards that block risky tasks in cybersecurity and biology and is available to all users. Mythos removes certain of these restrictions and is open only to organizations that apply through Anthropic's Verification Programs for Cybersecurity or Life Sciences.

Pricing is $8 per million input tokens and $40 per million output tokens. On paper, at least, that's a cut from the predecessors, which cost $10 and $50. What users actually pay depends on token consumption, which varies with tasks, settings, and software environments. Anthropic positions the new models for the most demanding technical work and continues to recommend Claude Opus 5.5 for everyday use.

The models produce output up to 30 percent faster than Fable 5.1 and Mythos 5.1, Anthropic says. An optional fast mode for select organizations speeds up token output by up to a factor of 2.5 but costs twice as much and is available only on certain platforms, including Claude Code, the Claude Platform, Google Cloud, and Microsoft Foundry.

Artificial Analysis’s benchmarks put Fable 5.2 clearly ahead of its rivals. On the current Index v5 at the highest compute tier, it takes first place with 65 points, five ahead of Gemini 4 Carbon (60, High tier), which Google still hasn't released, six ahead of Claude Opus 5.5 (59, Max tier), and a striking 15 ahead of Claude Fable 5.1, which came out only in early September.

Fable 5.2 scores best in five of nine individual tests, according to Artificial Analysis. It hits 80 percent on HLE-Diamond, a test with expert-level academic questions, 73 percent on Terminal-Bench-Science, which tests whether an AI agent can independently run scientific workflows in a terminal, and 49 percent on FrontierCode 2.0, which evaluates whether an agent can deliver useful code changes in real open-source projects.

Fable 5.2 is weaker in agentic knowledge work and terminal-based coding. It reaches 1,785 Elo on AA-Briefcase, a benchmark for multi-step knowledge work tasks, just behind Claude Sonnet 5.5 (1,813) and within the confidence interval of Opus 5.5 (1,800). On Terminal-Bench 4.0, which measures multi-step terminal tasks in areas like software development and security, it scores 60 percent, tied with Opus 5.5. Kimi K3.1 Pro (67 percent), Gemini 4 Carbon (65 percent), and Sonnet 5.5 (64 percent) rank higher here.

Peak quality comes at a price, though. Per-task costs at the highest tier average $26.50, about 2.6 times as much as Opus 5.5 ($10) and roughly double Fable 5.1 ($12.99). Fable 5.2 still scores 62 points on the Intelligence Index at the lower High and Xhigh tiers, ahead of every other model at any tier according to Artificial Analysis, while consuming far fewer tokens: 98,000 output tokens per task compared to 173,000 for Opus 5.5 at the Max tier.

The new models also set records in cybersecurity, which is seeing intense debate right now. Mythos 5.2 finds more vulnerabilities than earlier models and is better at reproducing and fixing them, Anthropic says. Fable, the publicly available variant, blocks most security-related tasks as a result, including penetration tests and exploit code generation. Opus 4.8 responds to blocked cybersecurity requests instead, and Opus 5 responds to blocked biology requests.

Anthropic uses an internal test called CVE Rediscovery to check how many published vulnerabilities from the CVE database (Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures, a system for cataloging known software flaws) a model can independently find when given the project's state before the fix.

Mythos 5.2 found 10.2 percent more vulnerabilities than Opus 5.5 and 14.4 percent more than Mythos 5.1 in the October 2026 run with 1,829 CVEs, Anthropic says. It led at every compute tier. One security firm reported that one in six confirmed bugs Mythos 5.2 found had been missed by all other frontier models tested, according to Anthropic.

Anthropic says it deliberately held the model back during training from improving at capabilities that could most directly accelerate AI development, so-called RSI, which is widely discussed as a risk right now. Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 perform roughly on par with Opus 5.5 in areas like optimizing compute kernels for accelerator chips and improving large language model architectures, the company says.

Related capabilities like agentic coding, hardware development, and traditional AI research, including interpretability research, aren't affected, according to Anthropic. Claude now writes over 90 percent of the changes merged into Anthropic's core codebase, under human guidance, the company says. Anthropic also claims the model programmed an operating system from scratch in an internal test.

The example likely to draw the most attention comes once again from mathematics. About 1,000 Fable 5.2 agents fully formalized the proof of Fermat's Last Theorem, translating it into the Lean programming language so a computer can verify it step by step, Anthropic says.

Fermat's Last Theorem states that the familiar equation a² + b² = c² has no whole-number solutions for powers higher than squares. Nobody could prove this for centuries until Andrew Wiles presented a proof over a hundred pages long in 1995. Its machine verification has now been completed for the first time. It took 30 hours.

An earlier, unpublished research version of Claude needed 11 days for the same task and relied on a purpose-built environment and guidance from a human researcher. The Fable 5.2 agents started with brief instructions, organized their collaboration on their own, and used no mathematical references, Anthropic says. The only progress metric was a list of intermediate lemmas. The model used one-third of the action tokens of the first attempt and produced a proof seven times shorter.

Anthropic ran Opus 5.5 in the same setup with 1,000 agents for comparison. Opus managed just 26 percent of the formalization in 18 hours and made barely any progress after that through hour 30.

title_zh: Claude Fable 5.2 和 Mythos 5.2 在 Anthropic 首次公开募股前巩固了其人工智能领先地位
summary_zh: Anthropic推出Claude Fable 5.2及Mythos 5.2模型，通过提升运行速度与降低API报价，试图在IPO前巩固性能领先地位
article_content_zh:
Anthropic 的 Claude Fable 5.2 和 Mythos 5.2 在该公司 IPO 前不久重新夺回了人工智能性能领先地位，在某些情况下还大幅领先。 Opus 5.5 仍然是 Anthropic 推荐的日常使用型号。

Claude Fable 5.2 和 Claude Mythos 5.2 具有相同的模型基础，但就像它们的前辈一样，访问权限有所不同。 Fable 包含阻止网络安全和生物学中的危险任务的保护措施，并且可供所有用户使用。 Mythos 消除了其中某些限制，并且仅向通过 Anthropic 网络安全或生命科学验证计划申请的组织开放。

定价为每百万输入代币 8 美元，每百万输出代币 40 美元。至少在纸面上，这比前代产品的成本有所降低，前代产品的成本为 10 美元和 50 美元。用户实际支付的费用取决于代币消耗，而代币消耗因任务、设置和软件环境而异。 Anthropic 将新型号定位于最苛刻的技术工作，并继续推荐 Claude Opus 5.5 适合日常使用。

Anthropic 表示，这些模型的输出速度比 Fable 5.1 和 Mythos 5.1 快 30%。针对特定组织的可选快速模式可将代币输出速度提高高达 2.5 倍，但成本是其两倍，并且仅在某些平台上可用，包括 Claude Code、Claude Platform、Google Cloud 和 Microsoft Foundry。

Artificial Analysis 的基准测试显示《神鬼寓言 5.2》明显领先于其竞争对手。在当前最高计算层的 Index v5 上，它以 65 分排名第一，比 Google 尚未发布的 Gemini 4 Carbon（60，高级）领先 5 分，领先 Claude Opus 5.5（59，最高层）6 分，比 9 月初才发布的 Claude Fable 5.1 领先 15 分。

根据人工分析，《神鬼寓言 5.2》在九项单独测试中的五项中得分最高。在 HLE-Diamond（一项包含专家级学术问题的测试）上，它的得分为 80%；在 Terminal-Bench-Science（测试 AI 代理是否可以在终端中独立运行科学工作流程）上，得分为 73%；在 FrontierCode 2.0（评估代理是否可以在真正的开源项目中提供有用的代码更改）上，得分为 49%。

《神鬼寓言 5.2》在代理知识工作和基于终端的编码方面较弱。它在 AA-Briefcase（多步骤知识工作任务的基准）上达到 1,785 Elo，仅落后于 Claude Sonnet 5.5 (1,813)，并且处于 Opus 5.5 (1,800) 的置信区间内。 Terminal-Bench 4.0 衡量软件开发和安全等领域的多步骤终端任务，其得分为 60%，与 Opus 5.5 持平。 Kimi K3.1 Pro（67%）、Gemini 4 Carbon（65%）和Sonnet 5.5（64%）在这里排名更高。

不过，顶级品质是有代价的。最高级别的每任务平均成本为 26.50 美元，大约是 Opus 5.5（10 美元）的 2.6 倍，大约是 Fable 5.1（12.99 美元）的两倍。根据人工分析，《神鬼寓言 5.2》在较低的 High 和 Xhigh 级别的智力指数上仍得分 62 分，领先于任何级别的所有其他模型，同时消耗的令牌少得多：每个任务的输出令牌为 98,000 个，而 Opus 5.5 在 Max 级别的输出令牌为 173,000 个。

新模型还在网络安全方面创下了记录，目前网络安全领域引发了激烈的争论。 Anthropic 表示，Mythos 5.2 比早期模型发现了更多漏洞，并且能够更好地重现和修复这些漏洞。 Fable 是公开可用的变体，因此会阻止大多数与安全相关的任务，包括渗透测试和漏洞利用代码生成。 Opus 4.8 响应被阻止的网络安全请求，Opus 5 响应被阻止的生物学请求。

Anthropic 使用名为 CVE Rediscovery 的内部测试来检查在给定修复前的项目状态时，模型可以从 CVE 数据库（常见漏洞和暴露，用于对已知软件缺陷进行编目的系统）中独立找到多少已发布的漏洞。

Anthropic 表示，在 2026 年 10 月的运行中，Mythos 5.2 发现的漏洞比 Opus 5.5 多 10.2%，比 Mythos 5.1 多 14.4%，共发现 1,829 个 CVE。它在每个计算层都处于领先地位。据 Anthropic 称，一家安全公司报告称，Mythos 5.2 发现的六分之一的已确认错误已被所有其他测试的前沿模型遗漏。

Anthropic 表示，它在训练过程中故意阻止模型提高最能直接加速人工智能开发的能力，即所谓的 RSI，目前人们广泛将其视为一种风险。该公司表示，Fable 5.2 和 Mythos 5.2 在优化加速器芯片的计算内核和改进大型语言模型架构等领域的表现与 Opus 5.5 大致相当。

Anthropic 表示，代理编码、硬件开发和传统人工智能研究（包括可解释性研究）等相关功能不会受到影响。该公司表示，现在超过 90% 的更改都是由 Claude 在人工指导下编写并合并到 Anthropic 的核心代码库中的。 Anthropic 还声称该模型在内部测试中从头开始编写了操作系统。

最引起关注的例子再次来自数学。 Anthropic 表示，大约 1,000 个 Fable 5.2 智能体完全形式化了费马大定理的证明，将其翻译成精益编程语言，以便计算机可以逐步验证它。

title: Meta launches Muse Ember, a small AI model built for the repetitive work agents actually do
title_en: Meta launches Muse Ember, a small AI model built for the repetitive work agents actually do
author: THE DECODER
article_content:
Meta has introduced Muse Ember, its smallest and most efficient AI model to date. It's designed for the routine tasks AI agents handle all day: calling tools, handling small coding tasks, routing requests, extracting data, and processing long documents. Meta says Muse Ember delivers more intelligence per dollar at every reasoning level than Claude Haiku 5.5 or GPT-6 Luna. It costs about $0.14 per task in the Artificial Analysis test, while the larger Muse Spark 1.3 costs $2.39 for a nearly identical score of 36 versus 37. Muse Ember leads in most of Meta's own tests, but Haiku outperforms it on real coding tasks in FrontierCode 2.0-AA, scoring 34.9 percent to Muse Ember's 27.2 percent.

The model handles text, images, audio, and video and can process up to one million tokens at once. It's available now through the Meta Model API and Muse Code at $0.10 per million input tokens and $0.50 per million output tokens.

title: Vulnerability that lets hackers SSH into Linux devices is under active exploitation
title_en: Vulnerability that lets hackers SSH into Linux devices is under active exploitation
author: Ars Technica
article_content:
Hackers are actively exploiting a recently discovered critical vulnerability that allows them to log in to privileged accounts on many Linux systems, multiple researchers are reporting.

The vulnerability, tracked under the name *sshole, arises from the interaction between OpenSSH and a code library known as musl. Linux systems that use both of these packages and meet certain other requirements can be hacked to give unauthenticated access to high-privilege accounts in a matter of seconds. *sshole became publicly known last Thursday and quickly stoked concerns it could lead to widespread compromise of Linux machines. Four days later, the prediction shows signs of becoming real.

Security firm Greynoise said Monday that honeypots it maintains in Southeast Asia have come under attack by a group it’s tracking as GT10. The group conducted “mature intrusions" into the systems, which Greynoise uses to detect attempted or successful attacks in real time. Greynoise subsequently gained access to a GT10 server that revealed potential other victims and some of the tools used in the campaign. title: The backlash about data centers might really just be about electricity
title_en: The backlash about data centers might really just be about electricity
author: MIT Tech Review
article_content:
As voters went to the polls across the US last week, I was in Ashburn, Virginia, part of what’s known as Data Center Alley—the world’s largest data center hub. It’s also where the backlash now sweeping the country arguably first began taking shape.

Driving through it is surreal. Concrete monolithic buildings loom along every major road, with names like Skybox and CloudHQ.

It’s accepted wisdom in Big Tech that the war against data centers must be about something bigger than just data centers themselves. Two days after the midterms, OpenAI’s chief global affairs officer, Chris Lehane, wrote that data centers “have become a proxy for public unease about affordability, corporate power, and people losing control over their futures.” It’s a culture war, in other words.

But spending a few days in Data Center Alley left me wondering if it’s really the proxy that Lehane describes. I came away convinced that the data center backlash is more about electricity than Big Tech admits. The industry can improve its image, but it can’t escape the physical consequences of its enormous appetite for electricity.

Here’s why. There are two ways to power the sort of data center that AI companies want: connecting to the grid, or generating electricity onsite. In Virginia’s Loudoun County, where data centers are ubiquitous but have been built at a steadier pace than the breakneck expansion now underway elsewhere in the country, most are connected to the existing grid.

One facility I went inside, operated by Equinix, has massive diesel generators onsite for backup but gets its power from the local utility, Dominion Energy. Much of Dominion’s electricity is generated by natural gas (which is cleaner than coal or oil, but worse than renewables).

The average data center operating in this part of Virginia today has a power capacity of 54 megawatts. That’s more than the power draw of the Denver International Airport.

Elena Schlossberg, a prominent activist against data centers in Virginia, told me she’s “always banging my head against the wall” when the industry paints the fight as a culture war. “It was always about power,” she says—that is, electricity.

Some Virginia protesters appear more animated by a broader anti-tech populism than Schlossberg, to be fair. But it’s the particular consequences of drawing so much power from the grid that have done the most to shape how the backlash has played out.

Recent protests have led to new rules from the state that data centers must pay fully for the cost of new transmission lines to the grid and make sure they’re not spread among everyone else. Data center developers told me they’re preparing for new rules that would cut them off from grid power during peak demand. Schlossberg also worries about the downstream effects of a strained grid—for example, that data centers will run more diesel generators or that Dominion Energy will expand fossil fuel inputs rather than renewables to meet demand.

The overwhelming majority of AI data centers being built elsewhere in the country are not designed this way. The scale desired is so massive that companies are setting up in rural areas where there is virtually no grid infrastructure to connect to. Building there means bringing your own power (so-called “behind the meter” power), in the form of natural-gas-powered turbines. Companies also build diesel generators for backup. Anthropic, for example, has reportedly agreed to pay $3.4 billion for gas turbines in what’s described as the largest power generation purchase by an AI company.

Even if grids were nearby, they’d be unlikely to serve the amount of power demanded. The smallest data centers attractive for AI training are 300 megawatts. It’s a lot of power for one industrial site, but not unprecedented: One data center developer told me he’s eyeing a former steel mill already equipped to draw that much electricity from the grid.

But the ideal facilities are more like 6,000 megawatts. That’s the estimated draw of the city of Chicago, which is powered by more than 20 power plants within the city alone (and dozens farther out).

The notion of data center companies’ bringing their own power might seem attractive at first, because they wouldn’t be straining the grid. But generating electricity at this scale inevitably affects surrounding communities, and when public utilities build infrastructure of this magnitude, communities have traditionally expected a say in where it goes. Now, private companies are undertaking projects on a similar scale.

Natural-gas turbines of any scale release air pollutants. When diesel generators are used, it’s even worse. And in the unprecedented rush to get these facilities operating, companies have become horrible neighbors (recall that Elon Musk violated air quality laws when he set up dozens of turbines to power a data center in Memphis, according to the Environmental Protection Agency).

Big Tech’s tendency to chalk the backlash up to a culture war obfuscates one simple fact: There’s only so pleasant you can make a small city of computers to live around. Sure, companies can pursue better deals that raise tax revenues, hire local workers, and get more community involvement, as the protests are leading them to do. But if a small town is asked to welcome a Walt Disney World, an international airport, a steel plant, and the power plants to run them all, should we be surprised by its trepidation?

Again, that’s not to say this is the sole reason for opposition to data centers. Fears of job losses, existential risks, and concentrated corporate power all fuel the backlash, as does misinformation (most facilities use far less water than many people think). Nor is consuming enormous amounts of electricity inherently bad: Many of the advances that have improved modern life have required just that.

But as one developer recently told me, industry insiders see their ambitions as constrained less by public opposition than by a lack of electricity. That should tell us something.

So what happens next? It’s possible that newly elected politicians’ actual stances on data centers won’t be as negative as the ones they campaigned on. But what seems true regardless is that if new data centers need their own power generated onsite, they’ll go where there are the fewest people able to resist them. That might mean the Permian Basin, where a network of natural-gas lines can be easy for developers to connect to and populations are sparse. Companies might also try their chances abroad; Google, in fact, announced the day after the elections that it will spend $15 billion on data center projects in Malaysia.

But there’s one place where Big Tech may find virtually no limits at all, as Elon Musk posted just hours after the midterms results came rolling in: “Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now.”

article_content_zh:
上周，当美国各地的选民前往投票站时，我正在弗吉尼亚州阿什本，那里是世界上最大的数据中心枢纽——数据中心巷的一部分。可以说，现在席卷全国的强烈反对情绪也正是从这里开始形成的。

开车穿过它是超现实的。每条主要道路上都矗立着混凝土整体建筑，其名称包括 Skybox 和 CloudHQ。

大型科技公司普遍认为，针对数据中心的战争必须涉及比数据中心本身更大的事情。中期选举两天后，OpenAI 首席全球事务官 Chris Lehane 写道，数据中心“已经成为公众对负担能力、企业权力以及人们失去对未来的控制感到不安的代表。”换句话说，这是一场文化战争。

但在数据中心巷待了几天后，我想知道这是否真的是 Lehane 描述的代理。我确信数据中心的强烈反对更多地与电力有关，而不是大型科技公司所承认的。该行业可以改善其形象，但无法摆脱对电力的巨大需求所带来的物理后果。

原因如下。人工智能公司想要的数据中心有两种供电方式：连接到电网或现场发电。在弗吉尼亚州的劳登县，数据中心无处不在，但其建设速度比该国其他地方目前正在进行的高速扩张更为稳定，大多数数据中心都连接到现有电网。

我走进的一处设施由 Equinix 运营，现场配有大型柴油发电机作为备用，但其电力来自当地公用事业公司 Dominion Energy。多米尼恩的大部分电力由天然气发电（天然气比煤炭或石油更清洁，但比可再生能源差）。

目前，弗吉尼亚州该地区运营的数据中心的平均电力容量为 54 兆瓦。这比丹佛国际机场的耗电量还要多。

弗吉尼亚州著名的反对数据中心活动人士埃琳娜·施洛斯伯格 (Elena Schlossberg) 告诉我，当业界将这场斗争描绘成一场文化战争时，她“总是用头撞墙”。 “这总是与电力有关，”她说——也就是说，电力。

公平地说，一些弗吉尼亚州的抗议者似乎对更广泛的反科技民粹主义比施洛斯伯格更感兴趣。但正是从电网汲取如此多电力所产生的特殊后果，才最有力地塑造了强烈反对的结果。

最近的抗议活动导致该州出台了新规定，即数据中心必须全额支付通往电网的新输电线路的成本，并确保它们不会蔓延到其他地方。数据中心开发商告诉我，他们正在准备新的规则，这些规则将在高峰需求期间切断他们的电网供电。施洛斯伯格还担心电网紧张的下游影响，例如，数据中心将运行更多柴油发电机，或者多米尼恩能源公司将扩大化石燃料投入而不是可再生能源以满足需求。

该国其他地方建设的绝大多数人工智能数据中心都不是这样设计的。所需的规模是如此之大，以至于公司纷纷在几乎没有电网基础设施可连接的农村地区设立分支机构。在那里建设意味着以天然气驱动的涡轮机的形式带来自己的电力（所谓的“表后”电力）。公司还制造备用柴油发电机。例如，据报道，Anthropic 同意支付 34 亿美元购买燃气轮机，这被称为人工智能公司最大的发电采购。

即使电网就在附近，它们也不太可能满足所需的电力需求。对 AI 训练有吸引力的最小数据中心为 300 兆瓦。对于一个工业场地来说，这是很大的电力，但并非史无前例：一位数据中心开发商告诉我，他正在关注一家已经具备从电网获取这么多电力的前钢铁厂的设施。

但理想的设施更像是 6,000 兆瓦。这是芝加哥市的估计耗电量，仅该市就有 20 多个发电厂（还有数十个更远的发电厂）为该市提供电力。

数据中心公司自带电力的想法乍一看似乎很有吸引力，因为它们不会给电网带来压力。但如此规模的发电不可避免地会影响周边社区，而当公用事业建设如此规模的基础设施时，社区传统上期望对电力的去向拥有发言权。现在，私营公司正在开展类似规模的项目。
fact_bullets_zh: 【核心事件】科技巨头与数据中心运营商在美国数据中心枢纽区域（如阿什本：揭示数据中心遭社区抵制的真相非文化战争，而是能源供应短缺引发的真实生存危机。
【起因与机理】AI算力爆发式增长导致的电力负荷让地方基础设施不堪重负，引发公众对能源定价及稳定性的恐慌。
【关键技术规格】数据中心抵制潮背后的能源本质。
【观点态度】AI扩张对电网稳定性带来的生存级挑战。

title: Anthropic says during prerelease testing Mythos 5.2 and Fable 5.2 formalized the proof of Fermat's Last Theorem and solved two open black hole physics problems (Jay Peters/The Verge)
title_en: Anthropic says during prerelease testing Mythos 5.2 and Fable 5.2 formalized the proof of Fermat's Last Theorem and solved two open black hole physics problems (Jay Peters/The Verge)
author: The Verge
article_content:
Posts from this topic will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Claude Fable 5.2 is designed to take on big technical challenges, and it’s available today.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Anthropic is announcing two new models today: Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2, which it says are designed to take on “daunting” technical challenges. The company claims the new models show improvements in coding, reasoning, and vision, and can generate outputs faster than the 5.1 versions of the Fable and Mythos models.

Claude Fable 5.2 is good at challenging software engineering problems, Anthropic says, and can orchestrate agent teams and tackle long-running projects. The new model has also solved some complex scientific problems, including two open theoretical physics problems.

During prerelease testing, the two models have “helped our engineers complete otherwise-infeasible software migrations, designed three working electronic devices from scratch, solved two open problems in the physics of black holes, made substantial progress on robotics evaluations, and formalized the proof of Fermat’s Last Theorem in 30 hours,” Anthropic says.

Claude Fable 5.2 is launching today. As for Claude Mythos 5.2, only vetted organizations will have access to start. The new 5.2 models follow the release of Claude Fable 5.1 and Claude Mythos 5.1 in September.

title: Apple’s $50 Intelligence Usage Packs extend access to some AI features
title_en: Apple’s $50 Intelligence Usage Packs extend access to some AI features
author: The Verge AI
article_content:
Posts from this topic will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Logic Pro is Apple’s first app to charge for extended usage of Apple Intelligence.﻿

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

After publishing a support article in early September outlining usage limits for some Apple Intelligence features, the company has updated Logic Pro with an option to “Buy More Usage” for a one-time purchase price of $49.99, as spotted by 9to5Mac. It has a built-in AI assistant to do things like “start a new song, set up a vocal track from a single prompt, or refine an active project.”

These Intelligence Usage Packs, as Apple calls them, will allow users to continue accessing certain Apple Intelligence features that have usage limits because they rely on cloud-based AI models from OpenAI or Google Gemini. The Usage Packs can only be used by the Apple Account that purchased them (Family Sharing isn’t supported) and, as Apple explains on its website, any unused additional usage will roll over from month to month, but will expire 12 months after it was purchased.

For Logic Pro, Apple says the usage limit is “impacted by the complexity of conversations you have with the assistant.” Users finding themselves running out of access can find the option to buy an Intelligence Usage Pack in the Intelligence Features > Show Usage section of the app’s main menu. Currently, only Logic Pro has the option to buy more usage, but it’s expected to be added to other Apple Creator Studio apps this month, including Pixelmator Pro, Final Cut Pro, Motion, plus Pages, Keynote, and Numbers that are getting access to Apple’s AI chatbot.

title: Anthropic releases Mythos 5.2 and Fable 5.2, saying they are "best for the most ambitious, open-ended technical work", for $8/1M input and $40/1M output tokens (Anthropic)
title_en: Anthropic releases Mythos 5.2 and Fable 5.2, saying they are "best for the most ambitious, open-ended technical work", for $8/1M input and $40/1M output tokens (Anthropic)
author: Anthropic
article_content:
We’ve upgraded Claude Fable and Claude Mythos—models that are designed to tackle the most daunting technical challenges.

Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 show improvements in areas like coding, reasoning, and vision. During prerelease testing they’ve helped our engineers complete otherwise-infeasible software migrations, designed three working electronic devices from scratch, solved two open problems in the physics of black holes, made substantial progress on robotics evaluations, and formalized the proof of Fermat’s Last Theorem in 30 hours—among many other applications we’ll discuss below.

Claude Fable and Claude Mythos are the same underlying model. Fable has strong cybersecurity and biology safeguards to guard against misuse, which allows us to make it available to all users. Organizations pursuing beneficial applications in cybersecurity or biomedical research can apply for access to Mythos through our recently expanded Life Sciences and Cyber Verification Programs.

Testers have found that Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 communicate more clearly than past Fable and Mythos models. They generate outputs up to 30% faster than Claude Fable 5.1 and Claude Mythos 5.1, and they’re available at a lower price: $8 per million input tokens and $40 per million output tokens.

Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 also come with an optional fast mode, which speeds up token generation by up to 2.5 times. Fast mode is available for $16 per million input tokens and $80 per million output tokens.

Safety and alignment. To help ensure safety and alignment keep step with growing model capabilities, we ran extensive prerelease safety testing on the model that underlies Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2. This included developing novel evaluations that give deeper insight into specific concerning behaviors like sandbox escapes. We believe high-stakes risks from misalignment remain low, and the model performed as well as, or better than, our recent models on most alignment measures. Fable 5.2’s cyber and biology safeguards are as robust as those of Fable 5.1’s but produce fewer unnecessary blocks, and we have implemented our strongest-ever protections against distillation attacks.

We describe more about our safety testing below, and full details can also be found in the Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 system card.

When to use Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2. Fable and Mythos are best for the most ambitious, open-ended technical work. For most coding and knowledge tasks, we recommend that users start with Claude Opus 5.5, our strongest daily driver, and then switch to a different model as required, depending on the scope and complexity of their work—upward to Fable or Mythos, or downward to Claude Sonnet 5.5 or Claude Haiku 5.5. Fable 5.2 can also play the role of Advisor (where Haiku, Sonnet, or Opus models consult it to help solve harder problems) or Orchestrator (where it delegates simpler tasks to smaller models).

Benchmark performance. The benchmarks table below shows that Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 are a step above Opus 5.5 in almost all the capabilities we evaluated:

For details on evaluation methodology, see the Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 System Card. Scores for Fable 5.2, Fable 5.1, and Opus 5.5 show results with safeguards on unless otherwise noted. All scores show each model’s highest-available effort unless otherwise noted. † On CyScenarioBench, each lab’s scores are based on unique tasks. ‡ RoboDojo Sim shows the highest-available effort and was run internally.

Effort and efficiency. On Medium effort (the default in Claude apps and Claude Code), Fable 5.2 can accomplish challenging tasks with fewer tokens than Fable 5.1. In early testing on the FrontierCode 2.0 evaluation, Fable 5.2 at High effort scored about level with Opus 5.5 at Max effort, for roughly half the cost per task. At Xhigh effort, it also scored the highest of any released model tested.

FrontierCode measures whether a model’s code changes would be merged by the maintainers of open-source repositories. At High effort, Fable 5.2 scores about the same as Opus 5.5’s best score (45.3% vs. 45.5%) for roughly half the cost per task, and ahead of GPT-6 Astra’s best (42.8%) at about the same cost. At Xhigh effort, Fable 5.2 reaches 49.1%, the highest score of any released model we’ve tested.

Perplexity’s WANDR benchmark measures agents on large data-collection tasks. At Medium effort, Fable 5.2 matches Opus 5.5’s top score for about 40% of the cost per task.

BenchCAD 2.1 measures hardware engineering, specifically how closely a model’s designs match reference geometry and circuits, and is scored 0–100 with partial credit. At Max effort, Fable 5.2 scores 83.5, ahead of Opus 5.5 (65.3) and Fable 5.1 (44.4).

Humanity’s Last Exam (HLE) is a test of expert-level academic knowledge and reasoning. At Low effort, Fable 5.2 matches Opus 5.5’s top score for less than one-tenth of the cost per task.

Chartography tests how accurately a model can read charts and figures. At Medium effort, Fable 5.2 scores 66.4%, ahead of Opus 5.5 at Max effort (64.4%) for less than one-tenth of the cost per task.

Over 90% of the changes merged into Anthropic’s core codebase are now written by Claude (with human guidance). We’ve used Fable 5.2 to fix stubborn bugs in minutes, optimize performance across all of our services, and complete high-value software projects that would otherwise have been too slow or too costly to attempt. A team of agents running an earlier version of Fable 5.2 migrated a critical production service from Python to Rust—the service is now more efficient, more reliable, and starts about 26 times faster. We’ve found that Fable 5.2 exercises strong engineering judgement and can produce high-quality results from even ambiguous requests.

As an experiment, one Anthropic engineer gave Fable 5.2 the task of designing a prototype operating system. Starting from an empty folder, the model coordinated over 1,000 subagents, working around the clock for eight days writing, testing, and reviewing code. It produced a working operating system that boots on a laptop, with its own core that runs the machine, drivers for the disk, keyboard, and network, permanent file storage, windows, a login screen, an installer, and built-in Claude functionality (see the video below).

Early testers have been impressed at how successfully Fable 5.2’s coding skills can be applied to a wide range of tasks:

“The model is in my head. It understands the intent behind every prompt I’ve given it. I haven’t had to say ‘No, I meant…’ a single time. Projects we’ve been pushing along with other models for weeks got finished and approved by our teammates in a few days with Claude Fable 5.2, and the humans reviewing its code had less to say.”

“Claude Fable 5.2 is great for taking a loose idea and refining it. Its answers are really well-considered, and within a few turns I can almost always say ‘ok, go do that,’ and trust that it’ll complete it with little intervention. It feels like working with another staff-level engineer.”

“You can just throw Claude Fable 5.2 at new, ambiguous systems it has never seen before, and it will figure out how to actually work within them. It’s almost like an incident commander that can send out faster models to get quick signals and coordinate, which removes that burden from me as an operator.”

“Claude Fable 5.2 can complete tasks that previous models struggled with. The clearest examples so far are building higher-quality 3D scenes from scratch and rebuilding an experience from a visual reference. It’s very strong on the harder game-dev tasks, where it keeps iterating and improving instead of getting stuck.”

“I had Claude Fable 5.2 run a 10–12 hour security audit. It sent out about 170 reviewer agents and came back with a write-up, fix pull requests and a policy proposal. It works until the job is actually complete instead of stopping at a plausible checkpoint. Its self-correction and honesty about gaps impressed me. At High effort, I’d use this over what I run today for long unattended audits and doc-heavy work.”

“In one test combining country debt summaries, repayment history, and regional benchmarks, Claude Fable 5.2 generated SQL that returned the expected results. The SQL generated by two other models also ran successfully, but incorrectly summed country-level summary amounts, producing values 5–8x the expected amounts. Getting these business calculations right is why we see value in using Fable 5.2 for enterprise SQL generation.”

“In a single session, Claude Fable 5.2 built a hypervisor, the software that walls off virtual computers sharing one machine. Its core is mathematically proven to keep them apart. More than 3,500 machine-checked proofs cover every case, not just the ones you test. It’s the first model I’ve seen break a problem this large into pieces it can prove, fit them together, and keep taking on more ambitious work. A very clear upgrade from Fable 5.1.”

“Claude Fable 5.2 is the strongest model we have measured on data-eng-bench, our open-source benchmark of 103 data-engineering tasks. It solved tasks consistently across repeated runs and passed every interactive coding task we gave it.”

“Claude Fable 5.2 says it doesn’t know things instead of hallucinating. At one point it told me its last estimate was wrong and that it wouldn’t give a number until it had measured the change. Very impressive!”

Claude Mythos 5.2 is our most capable model for cybersecurity engineering. It catches more vulnerabilities than our previous models, and is better at reproducing and fixing them (note that Claude Fable 5.2’s safeguards will block most cybersecurity-related tasks). A security company found that one in six confirmed bugs found by Claude Mythos 5.2 were missed by all of the other frontier models they tested. On our internal evaluation, CVE Rediscovery,¹ Claude Mythos 5.2 found 10.2% more vulnerabilities than Claude Opus 5.5 and 14.4% more than Claude Mythos 5.1. Claude Mythos 5.2 also shows better judgement and calibration—one tester found that previous models had overstated the seriousness of about one in twenty findings, whereas Claude Mythos 5.2 hadn’t overstated any.²

CVE Rediscovery is an internal cybersecurity evaluation that assesses how many published CVEs (Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures) a model can independently find when given a snapshot of the project before a CVE was fixed. Our October 2026 run against 1,829 CVEs showed Claude Mythos 5.2 outperformed Claude Mythos 5.1 and Claude Opus 5.5 at every effort level.

Claude Mythos 5.2’s cyber capabilities are accessible through our Cyber Verification Program, which we’re continuing to expand and improve. Claude Enterprise customers (even if they aren’t members of the Cyber Verification Program) can access Claude Security, which scans codebases for vulnerabilities using our most capable models—which now includes Claude Mythos 5.2. A recent update to Claude Security helps it watch repositories as code is updated, track any findings to ensure they’re fixed, learn from additional context, and connect to a user’s tools through an API and MCP.

“We have worked closely with Anthropic’s new model, Claude Mythos 5.2, to do a next round of high-fidelity threat discovery and elimination within our own systems for potential issues we did not uncover with earlier Mythos models. The output is more readable and empowered our team to spot-check faster and more easily. We built our Code Guardian harness with Mythos 5.1, and we’d switch to Mythos 5.2 to give our customers more powerful cyber capabilities.”

“Claude Mythos 5.2 is astonishingly good. We’ve worked closely with the Anthropic team all year to harden Firefox with successive generations of Claude models, and each round has left fewer, subtler bugs to find. Even so, Mythos 5.2 roughly doubled the vulnerability discovery metrics of Mythos 5.1 across respective scanning campaigns.”

Important tasks in science, engineering, and mathematics increasingly depend on coding: analyzing data, modeling molecules, designing parts, and controlling instruments are all done through software. Below, we discuss how Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 have helped researchers make progress on difficult problems in these areas.

Claude Fable 5.2 solved two open problems in theoretical physics. Both concern black holes, and the effort to unite the two linchpin theories of modern physics, relativity, and quantum mechanics.

Both of Claude’s results rely on holographic duality, the idea that certain universes containing gravity can be precisely described by a quantum theory containing no gravity at all. In the first problem, physicists in 1983 had shown that as these universes heat up, black holes form abruptly, like water boiling; but their method worked only in large universes that were big enough for relativity to apply. A calculation to determine whether the same was true in very small universes, where only the quantum description can be used, was laid out in 2003 but was too laborious to complete. Fable 5.2, working largely autonomously, completed it and found the transition is abrupt there, too. In the second problem, Fable 5.2 found the exact limit of a technique physicists have used for more than 15 years to rule out candidate theories of quantum gravity in a simplified universe. Read more about these results in their respective preprints, here and here.

Adeno-associated viruses are small, harmless viruses whose protein shell, the capsid, can be used to deliver gene therapies. The protein structure of the capsid is important—for example, it affects whether the therapy will be blocked by a patient’s immune system—but it’s also highly complex. Existing protein-folding models like AlphaFold can predict individual proteins, but a capsid is built from dozens of them. Building on two open-source protein-folding models, Claude Mythos 5.2 found a novel way to accurately predict a whole capsid’s structure. It wrote code that ran these models on overlapping groups of protein chains, and used the information on the known symmetries of the capsid to merge them together.

Claude’s method worked across several capsids, both natural and engineered (in our tests, it accurately modeled 28 of the 34 it attempted)³. Three computational biologists shared the following reflections on how Claude’s skills could be used to speed up their research into gene therapies:

“This acceleration could save meaningful time and cost from our capsid folding pipeline, enabling us to deploy compute more efficiently across many capsid properties that are needed for a genetic medicine. We are excited to help Anthropic push the reasoning capabilities further to reduce the cost of designing capsids overall.”

“Large protein assemblies, including capsids, remain an open problem for protein modeling, due to the complexity of accurately predicting and positioning the structures of dozens of individual macromolecules, not to mention the inordinately high computational costs involved. Claude’s approach cleverly tackles this problem for symmetric assemblies, making it possible for individual scientists to model systems on personal workstations that would otherwise require dedicated clusters.”

“Biohub’s goal in open-sourcing ESMFold2 was to enable the scientific community to build on the biology it has learned. We are excited to see Claude prototype a new sampling procedure that enables predictions of large, symmetric complexes such as AAV capsids—a protein used to deliver gene therapies. We will continue to incorporate such contributions from the community that extend our tools to important application domains.”

Mathematical formalization. Formalization is the process of translating a mathematical proof into a language that a computer can check step by step. It can help human mathematicians gain confidence in results without having to check them by hand (this matters even more when AI models generate results that are hard for humans to verify). Because formalization is such a laborious process, if AI could assist with it, mathematicians could spend more time exploring novel ideas.

Our first formalization of Fermat’s Last Theorem, performed by an unreleased research version of Claude, took 11 days. It relied on a purpose-built harness along with guidance from a human researcher. By contrast, a team of 1,000 Fable 5.2 agents fully formalized the theorem in just 30 hours, with minimal human intervention. Fable 5.2 started from minimal prompts, built its own ways to coordinate, and used no mathematical references, only a list of intermediate theorem statements to score progress. It needed one-third of the action tokens as our first formalization and produced a proof seven times shorter. As can be seen in the figure below, Opus 5.5 (with the same 1,000-agent setup) completed only 26% of the formalization in 18 hours, and barely made any more progress after 30.

Formalizing the proof of Fermat’s Last Theorem in the mathematical programming language Lean. Each line shows the proportion of the full formalization that Fable 5.2 (green line) and Opus 5.5 (orange line) had completed over 30 hours with about 1,000 agents, and a single run per model. At the dashed line (18 hours), both teams resumed from their last save with 12 more hours.

Many of AI’s potential benefits—for example in speeding up laboratory research—depend on it being able to act in the physical world. Claude Fable 5.2 continues our models’ trend of increasing usefulness in the real world, showing promising results on tasks such as designing hardware devices and substantial advances in controlling physical robots.

Hardware engineering. We tested Fable 5.2’s skills in hardware engineering, asking it in a one-paragraph prompt to design and produce three working, electronic devices with their own circuit boards, 3D-printed enclosures, and software. The devices, pictured below, were a home voice-assistant hub, a USB speakerphone, and a handheld virtual pet. We collaborated on this project with Diode, a company that designs and manufactures circuit boards.

Claude wrote its own specifications, selected available electronic components from US distributors, routed each device’s four-layer circuit board, modeled the enclosures with computer-aided design, and programmed the devices’ software. Each board was ready for manufacturing in under a day, with minimal human input. Once Diode had built the boards, Claude guided the company’s engineers through the testing and assembly of the devices. All three devices worked without needing any electrical modifications. Read more about Claude’s hardware engineering skills here.

Robotics. Compared with earlier Claude models, Fable 5.2 shows substantially improved skills in controlling physical robots—even for robotics tasks on which it has never explicitly been trained. The video below shows robots controlled by Fable 5.2 completing a variety of tasks including solving a puzzle cube, unscrewing a bottle cap, and drawing a picture of a robot. On the public RoboDojo benchmark, which tests how AIs can control a simulated two-arm robot from camera images, Fable 5.2 outperformed other frontier models that were run on the same harness as well as most AI systems built specifically to control robots.

RoboDojo Sim tests control of a simulated two-arm robot. Scores are based on our internal runs for each model using the highest available effort level. At Max effort, Fable 5.2 scores 64.9%, more than double GPT-6 Astra (29.8%) and Fable 5.1 (27.6%).

Early testers using Claude Fable 5.2 for research and analysis tasks found that it can handle more ambiguous, data-heavy tasks than previous models and has better judgement on ambiguous tasks—particularly those that require abstract reasoning and design. Proprietary trading firm Jump Trading tested Fable 5.2 on proxy evaluations that resemble some of its quantitative research tasks, embedding it in a harness similar to the one the firm uses for its own research. In one run, Fable 5.2 effectively played all the necessary roles: code-writer, coordinator, planner, and job-submitter. Previous models had required substantial investments of time to manually rebalance roles to accommodate different models’ strengths and weaknesses.

Other testers from research and analysis organizations sent us the following statements on their experiences with Fable 5.2:

“Claude Fable 5.2 is incredible at playing every major role within a research system: defining questions, interpreting, coordinating, and of course finding and implementing the key ideas. Definitely one of the strongest on taste and judgment that we’ve seen. In an internal research automation benchmark, it achieved a full 10% lower error than the next best model.”

“In a recent evaluation, we asked Claude Fable 5.2 to investigate how one organization tested a new integration in its core technology systems. It traced the answer to the right sources and didn’t overstate what the evidence showed. It also flagged that the question’s framing could be misleading. In investment research, that restraint makes clear what remains unknown and where the market may be mispricing risk or opportunity.”

“Phonon calculations are one of the most expensive routine steps in computational materials science, which is why labs often skip stability checks when screening new materials. Claude Fable 5.2 made Quantum ESPRESSO’s phonon code about 36 times faster on average than stock on the same GPU, taking our 13 benchmark cases from 3.3 hours to under four minutes. That beats Fable 5.1’s speedup by 3–4 times.”

“With Fable 5.1 we saw the first glimmers of a model coming up with truly innovative research ideas. Claude Fable 5.2 continues that trend. It had the same insight we were impressed with from Fable 5.1 and then came up with a second, entirely new angle. It achieved new best scores on three of the four quant research problems we’ve finished. We’d like to use it for high-impact, long-running research tasks, or for coordinating teams of other models.”

“In an I-9 compliance review, Claude Fable 5.2 gave the client clearer direction than Fable 5.1. It identified the employees needing immediate attention and explained how to correct each issue and who should act. It’s an exciting improvement in the model’s ability to give practical legal guidance.”

“On one task, Claude Fable 5.2 had to pull a company’s financials out of its 10-K into a forecasting model, and the template didn’t say whether a metric should be the reported figure or calculated. It inferred the author’s intent from the cell formatting, caught that the regional numbers didn’t sum to the reported total, and got every cell right. Better judgment calls like that are the main reason it scored 91% on our eval versus 86% for the next best model.”

“In our quantitative research work, Claude Fable 5.2 delivered very strong improvements versus Fable 5.1, especially in the setup with multiple coordinating agents. Its maths research capabilities represent another meaningful advance, too.”

“Before putting AI to work across workflows, you need to trust its approach and conclusions. In our testing, Claude Fable 5.2 identified inconsistencies, drew on context across entire document sets, and adjusted recommendations based on relevant evidence. For example, when reviewing files attached to a loan application, it flagged that the salary deposits and the bank statement’s balance didn’t match, so the underwriter could focus on what to check.”

No single test can tell us how a highly capable model will behave once it’s deployed, so we rely on many different tests and many different types of evidence before release. For the model underlying Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2, our predeployment safety work included alignment training and testing, newly designed evaluations on the model’s propensity to take unhelpful actions, building stronger safeguards against misuse, and scaling up our behavioral monitoring. The model was also tested before release by external evaluators, including the UK AI Security Institute, Frontier Design, and METR. See the Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 System Card for a summary of their reports⁴ and for a full description of our own safety and capabilities testing.

We ran a suite of evaluations for how well-aligned Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 are in behavioral terms, testing how often they behave in unintended and potentially unsafe ways. Weighing everything we’ve seen across a range of evaluations, we’ve assessed the risk of these models behaving in unsafe ways in high-stakes situations to be low (as with our other recent models).

We tested Claude Mythos 5.2 (the same underlying model as Fable 5.2 without certain cybersecurity or biology safeguards), on our automated behavioral audit, which tests how a model behaves across approximately 1,900 scenarios. Claude Mythos 5.2 perf...

article_content_zh:
我们升级了克劳德寓言和克劳德神话，这些模型旨在解决最艰巨的技术挑战。

Claude Fable 5.2 和 Claude Mythos 5.2 显示了编码、推理和视觉等领域的改进。在预发布测试期间，他们帮助我们的工程师完成了原本不可行的软件迁移，从头开始设计了三种工作电子设备，解决了黑洞物理学中的两个开放问题，在机器人评估方面取得了实质性进展，并在 30 小时内正式证明了费马大定理，以及我们将在下面讨论的许多其他应用。

克劳德寓言和克劳德神话是相同的底层模型。 《神鬼寓言》拥有强大的网络安全和生物学保障措施来防止滥用，这使我们能够将其提供给所有用户。在网络安全或生物医学研究中寻求有益应用的组织可以通过我们最近扩展的生命科学和网络验证计划申请访问 Mythos。

测试人员发现，Fable 5.2 和 Mythos 5.2 比过去的 Fable 和 Mythos 模型的沟通更加清晰。它们生成输出的速度比 Claude Fable 5.1 和 Claude Mythos 5.1 快 30%，并且价格更低：每百万输入代币 8 美元，每百万输出代币 40 美元。

Fable 5.2 和 Mythos 5.2 还配备了可选的快速模式，可将代币生成速度提高高达 2.5 倍。快速模式的价格为每百万输入代币 16 美元，每百万输出代币 80 美元。

安全和对齐。为了帮助确保安全性和一致性与不断增长的模型功能保持同步，我们对 Fable 5.2 和 Mythos 5.2 的基础模型进行了广泛的预发布安全测试。这包括开发新颖的评估，以更深入地了解沙箱逃逸等特定相关行为。我们认为，错位带来的高风险仍然很低，并且该模型在大多数对齐措施上的表现与我们最近的模型一样好，甚至更好。 《神鬼寓言 5.2》的网络和生物防护措施与《神鬼寓言 5.1》一样强大，但产生的不必要的区块更少，而且我们已经实施了有史以来最强大的蒸馏攻击保护措施。

我们在下面描述了有关安全测试的更多信息，完整的详细信息也可以在 Claude Fable 5.2 和 Mythos 5.2 系统卡中找到。

何时使用克劳德寓言 5.2 和神话 5.2。寓言和神话最适合最雄心勃勃、开放式的技术工作。对于大多数编码和知识任务，我们建议用户从我们最强的日常驱动程序 Claude Opus 5.5 开始，然后根据工作的范围和复杂性根据需要切换到不同的模型 - 向上到 Fable 或 Mythos，或向下到 Claude Sonnet 5.5 或 Claude Haiku 5.5。 Fable 5.2 还可以扮演顾问（Haiku、Sonnet 或 Opus 模型参考它来帮助解决更困难的问题）或 Orchestrator（它将更简单的任务委托给更小的模型）的角色。

基准性能。下面的基准测试表显示，在我们评估的几乎所有功能中，Claude Fable 5.2 和 Mythos 5.2 都比 Opus 5.5 高出一步：

有关评估方法的详细信息，请参阅克劳德寓言 5.2 和克劳德神话 5.2 系统卡。除非另有说明，《神鬼寓言 5.2》、《神鬼寓言 5.1》和《Opus 5.5》的分数显示的结果均已启用防护措施。除非另有说明，所有分数均显示每个模型的最高可用成果。 † 在 CyScenarioBench 上，每个实验室的分数均基于独特的任务。 ‡ RoboDojo Sim 显示了最高的可用努力并且是内部运行的。

努力和效率。在中等难度下（Claude 应用程序和 Claude Code 中的默认设置），Fable 5.2 可以使用比 Fable 5.1 更少的令牌完成具有挑战性的任务。在 FrontierCode 2.0 评估的早期测试中，Fable 5.2 在高工作量下的得分与 Opus 5.5 在最大工作量下的得分大致相同，而每项任务的成本大约是 Opus 5.5 的一半。在 Xhigh 的努力下，它的得分也是所有已发布测试型号中最高的。
