title: Nvidia espionage scandal weakens Huang's lobby against tighter AI chip export controls
title_en: Nvidia espionage scandal weakens Huang's lobby against tighter AI chip export controls
author: THE DECODER
article_content:
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has admitted to an extramarital affair with a woman US intelligence agencies classify as a suspected Chinese informant. The board has launched an independent investigation. The affair weakens Huang's lobbying efforts against stricter AI chip export controls, with a newly elected Democratic Congress poised to ramp up scrutiny of AI chip smuggling to China and push for tighter restrictions.

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang acknowledged an extramarital relationship with Alice Huang (Huang Le), a former executive at Singaporean data center operator Megaspeed International, in a company-wide memo. This is according to Bloomberg. US intelligence agencies have classified the woman as a suspected informant for a Chinese intelligence service. Secretary of State Marco Rubio reportedly wrote a memo to senior government officials warning about the closeness between Huang and the woman.

As recently as late October, the Nvidia CEO had described the relationship to Bloomberg as "normal." Nvidia's board has now announced an independent investigation led by a committee of independent directors. The Chinese embassy denied the espionage allegations.

Megaspeed operates data centers across Southeast Asia and provides computing capacity to companies including Chinese tech giant Alibaba. US authorities suspect the company serves as a backdoor for transferring export-controlled Nvidia chips to China. A Malaysian sister company reportedly purchased AI hardware containing Nvidia chips worth at least $4.8 billion between June 2024 and February 2026.

The Megaspeed case points to a broader problem. Despite US export bans, billions of dollars' worth of Nvidia chips are reaching China through smuggling networks in Southeast Asia. Nvidia recently responded with tighter chip tracking. Its "Fleet Intelligence" system logs the location of AI accelerators and is now a requirement for the coveted Nvidia Cloud Partner (NCP) status in the region, Bloomberg reports. Sharing location data with Nvidia or the US government remains voluntary, though. Nvidia also removed half of its pre-approved Asian buyers from its list earlier this year and capped the resale of computing capacity to Chinese firms at 50 percent.

Washington and Capitol Hill consider these measures insufficient, according to Bloomberg. Nvidia counters that it complies with existing law and that identifying illegal actors is the government's job.

Huang has spent years pushing for Nvidia and other US chipmakers to keep selling AI processors to China. His argument: shutting out the world's second-largest chip market would push China to build an independent and potentially superior AI industry. He made this case directly to the Trump administration and accompanied President Trump on a trip to Beijing in May.

The affair now undermines that lobbying effort. Republican lawmakers had already demanded a briefing with Huang before his admission. After the US midterms, where Democrats won both chambers of Congress, stricter export controls have become more likely. Bloomberg Intelligence notes that the affair weakens Nvidia's bargaining position right as the new Democratic Congress takes over committee chairs in January and plans to scrutinize AI chip exports to China more closely.

Nvidia has a market cap of roughly $4.5 trillion, making it the second most valuable company in the world. Huang built the company without a conventional hierarchy: about 60 people report directly to him, and there is no public succession plan. Bernstein analyst Stacy Rasgon warned that Huang "is Nvidia" and personally pulls most of the strings at the company. Unlike Mark Zuckerberg at Meta, Huang doesn't hold dual-class shares. His stake of just under four percent offers him no protection against removal by the board or shareholders.

title_zh: 黄仁勋卷入间谍风波，AI芯片出口游说遇重挫
summary_zh: 黄仁勋承认与被美情报部门列为疑似中国线人的前高管存在婚外情，公司已启动独立调查，或将引发美方更严苛的芯片出口管制
article_content_zh:
英伟达首席执行官黄仁勋承认与一名被美国情报机构列为可疑中国线人的女性发生婚外情。该委员会已展开独立调查。这一事件削弱了黄仁勋针对更严格的人工智能芯片出口管制的游说努力，新当选的民主党国会准备加强对向中国走私人工智能芯片的审查，并推动实施更严格的限制。

Nvidia 首席执行官黄仁勋在一份全公司备忘录中承认与新加坡数据中心运营商 Megaspeed International 前高管 Alice Huang（黄乐）存在婚外关系。据彭博社报道。美国情报机构已将这名女子列为中国情报部门的可疑线人。据报道，国务卿马可·卢比奥向政府高级官员写了一份备忘录，警告黄与这名女子之间的亲密关系。

就在 10 月底，Nvidia 首席执行官还称与彭博社的关系“正常”。英伟达董事会现已宣布一项由独立董事委员会领导的独立调查。中国大使馆否认了间谍指控。

Megaspeed 在东南亚各地运营数据中心，并为包括中国科技巨头阿里巴巴在内的公司提供计算能力。美国当局怀疑该公司充当将受出口管制的英伟达芯片转移到中国的后门。据报道，一家马来西亚姐妹公司在 2024 年 6 月至 2026 年 2 月期间购买了价值至少 48 亿美元的包含 Nvidia 芯片的人工智能硬件。

Megaspeed 案例指出了一个更广泛的问题。尽管美国实施出口禁令，价值数十亿美元的英伟达芯片仍通过东南亚的走私网络到达中国。英伟达最近采取了更严格的芯片跟踪措施作为回应。据彭博社报道，其“舰队智能”系统记录了人工智能加速器的位置，现在是获得该地区令人垂涎的 Nvidia 云合作伙伴 (NCP) 地位的必要条件。不过，与 Nvidia 或美国政府共享位置数据仍然是自愿的。英伟达今年早些时候还从其名单中删除了一半预先批准的亚洲买家，并将向中国公司转售的计算能力限制在 50%。

华盛顿和国会山认为这些措施还不够。英伟达反驳称，它遵守现行法律，识别非法行为者是政府的工作。

多年来，黄仁勋一直在推动英伟达和其他美国芯片制造商继续向中国销售人工智能处理器。他的论点是：将世界第二大芯片市场拒之门外将推动中国建立一个独立的、可能更优越的人工智能产业。他直接向特朗普政府提出了此事，并于五月陪同特朗普总统访问了北京。

现在这件事破坏了游说努力。共和党议员已经要求在黄入院前向他通报情况。美国中期选举后，民主党赢得国会参众两院，更严格的出口管制变得更有可能。彭博资讯指出，这一事件削弱了英伟达的讨价还价地位，因为新的民主党国会在一月份接任委员会主席，并计划更严格地审查对中国的人工智能芯片出口。

Nvidia 的市值约为 4.5 万亿美元，使其成为全球第二大市值公司。黄建立的公司没有传统的等级制度：大约 60 人直接向他汇报，并且没有公开的继任计划。伯恩斯坦分析师斯塔西·拉斯贡警告说，黄仁勋“就是英伟达”，并且亲自掌控着该公司的大部分事务。与 Meta 的马克·扎克伯格不同，黄仁勋并不持有双重股权。他持有的不到百分之四的股份并不能保护他免受董事会或股东的罢免。

title: Amsterdam police arrested between 150 and 200 protesters for trespassing and violence at a Microsoft data center construction site owned by Pure Data Centers (Jowi Morales/Tom's Hardware)
title_en: Amsterdam police arrested between 150 and 200 protesters for trespassing and violence at a Microsoft data center construction site owned by Pure Data Centers (Jowi Morales/Tom's Hardware)
author: Tom's Hardware
article_content:
The people were protesting against the use of fossil fuel generators to power data centers.

This protest is a continuation of the action that started last Friday, where protesters breached the Microsoft data center, which was being owned by Pure Data Centers. It is also the first of many organized by the “Stop Dirty Data Centers” coalition across Europe, with actions planned for Amsterdam, Dublin, Warsaw, Denmark, and several other cities across the continent. The Dutch publication NOS [machine translated] identified the exact group at the site today as Fossielvrij, who are against the use of fossil fuels in data centers such as the jet engines that Elon Musk installed at xAI’s Mississippi data center.

“Gas prices are going through the roof, and new houses are being postponed because of the overcrowded power grid. Yet tech billionaires like Elon Musk and Jeff Bezos are building energy-guzzling, hideous data centers,” the group said on its website. “We can take back the power of Big Tech by pressing the pause button now. Give us the opportunity to democratically decide what we do and do not use AI for, so that it is not at the expense of our living environment and everything that makes our lives beautiful. Then we look at how many more data centers are needed.”

The protest comes amid the AI data center build-out, which has been facing increased opposition across the United States. A Google data center site in Finland is also in trouble after it cleared out around 1,300 acres worth of forest and trees without an environmental impact assessment, displacing wildlife, and leading to a criminal probe on Tuike Finland Oy, the Google subsidiary in charge of the site.

Fossielvrij’s action was supposed to be peaceful, but it appears that another group joined the demonstration and broke through the fences around the site, leading to the police confrontation. The suspects were arrested for domestic violence and then taken to a cell complex, where it will be decided if they will be detained longer. The police also said that “All suspects will be heard afterward.”

人们抗议使用化石燃料发电机为数据中心供电。

此次抗议活动是上周五开始的行动的延续，当时抗议者闯入了 Pure Data Centers 拥有的微软数据中心。这也是欧洲“停止肮脏数据中心”联盟组织的众多活动中的第一个，计划在阿姆斯特丹、都柏林、华沙、丹麦和欧洲大陆的其他几个城市采取行动。荷兰出版物 NOS（机器翻译）将今天现场的确切组织确定为 Fossielvrij，他们反对在数据中心使用化石燃料，例如埃隆·马斯克在 xAI 密西西比州数据中心安装的喷气发动机。

该组织在其网站上表示：“天然气价格飞涨，由于电网过度拥挤，新房建设被推迟。然而，像埃隆·马斯克和杰夫·贝佐斯这样的科技亿万富翁正在建造耗能、丑陋的数据中心。” “我们现在可以按下暂停按钮来夺回大型科技的力量。让我们有机会民主地决定我们使用人工智能做什么和不做什么，这样就不会以牺牲我们的生活环境和让我们生活美好的一切为代价。然后我们看看还需要多少数据中心。”

此次抗议活动正值人工智能数据中心扩建之际，该项目在美国各地面临越来越多的反对。位于芬兰的谷歌数据中心也陷入了麻烦，因为它在没有进行环境影响评估的情况下砍伐了约 1,300 英亩的森林和树木，导致野生动物流离失所，并导致负责该数据中心的谷歌子公司 Tuike Finland Oy 受到刑事调查。

福西尔弗里的行动本应是和平的，但似乎另一群人也加入了示威活动，并冲破了现场周围的围栏，导致与警方的对峙。嫌疑人因家庭暴力被捕，然后被带到牢房，在那里将决定是否延长拘留时间。警方还表示，“随后将听取所有嫌疑人的陈述。”

title: Authors Can Defend Against AI Allegations With ‘Paper Trail’ Tools. Is It Enough?
title_en: Authors Can Defend Against AI Allegations With ‘Paper Trail’ Tools. Is It Enough?
author: Wired AI
article_content:
She also has a legal claim to fame: Bartz was the lead plaintiff in a class-action suit against Anthropic that alleged the company had downloaded millions of copyrighted books from pirate sites to use as training data for its models. Anthropic last year agreed to pay $1.5 billion in the largest copyright settlement in US history.

But while Bartz and many other writers were on guard against this plunder of their work, another AI threat was brewing. What happens when authors are accused of relying on artificial intelligence themselves?

This past March, the publishing industry found out: Following widespread speculation on social media that a horror novel titled Shy Girl was largely AI-generated, and a Times article about those claims, Hachette Book Group canceled an upcoming US publication run for the novel and discontinued it in the UK, where it had already been released. According to Pangram, a robust but by no means infallible AI detection tool, some 78 percent of the text was AI-generated.

Mia Ballard, the author of Shy Girl, has denied allegations that she used AI to write the novel, claiming that an editor was responsible for AI-assisted changes to a previously self-published version of the book. She has also said that she is pursuing legal action. Since that scandal broke, several more fiction authors have run afoul of AI suspicions, one after winning a short story prize, another after publishers bid into the millions for his crime novel. Both have denied these allegations as well.

But Bartz notes that once the accusations start, the damage is done. As the Shy Girl scandal erupted, she says, “I kind of immediately felt like this was going to lead to a potential witch hunt.” The unavoidable emergence of AI in publishing, she explains, will “have the unintended effect of leading anyone to be able to accuse anyone of using AI,” and at the moment, authors have little recourse in defending themselves against these charges. “There’s no agreed upon standard,” Bartz says, in proving human authorship.

The developers of a host of new software tools hope to change that. Platforms including Workings, Blindproof, Wintertext, Human Ink, and ObraVera promise the means to track and document an author’s writing process, in some cases encrypting and fingerprinting the written work or typing rhythms with unique codes, in order to produce a record of authorship (whether entirely human or AI-assisted). The idea is not just to create a paper trail that writers can point to if someone questions whether they used an LLM but to demonstrate provenance when, for example, text is scraped into AI training sets without attribution or other identifying metadata.

Mary Rasenberger, CEO of the Authors Guild, a professional organization focused on free expression and copyright protection, says that the guild can’t recommend any one of these tools over another but wants writers to know they exist as something of a security net. (Many of the companies have approached the Authors Guild to pitch their services, according to Umair Kazi, the guild’s director of policy and advocacy.)

At the same time, Rasenberger tells WIRED, it’s “insulting” and a “burden” to have to jump through this hoop, and “we don't feel it should be required” for authors to preserve receipts.

“If what you're selling are your words and your voice and your imagination, your creativity, using AI doesn't make sense,” Rasenberger says, noting that authors’ pride in their own work means AI slop is far less common in publishing than one might think. “I've talked to editors, particularly editors of literary nonfiction and fiction,” Rasenberger says, “and some of them will say, ‘I never see AI-generated submissions, I'd know it if I did.’”

Rasenberger worries that authors are up against a climate of distrust—they should “refrain from accusations of other authors because it just does not support a healthy literary community,” she says—and overconfidence in AI detection tools, which can be fooled and have been known to produce false positives. While Pangram claims an “industry-leading” false positive rate of 0.01 percent when used on creative writing, Rasenberger said the Authors Guild has “heard of lots of instances where people have put their own human-authored work in Pangram and gotten a result back saying it was AI-generated.” There are a variety of factors, she adds, that can “make an AI detector think something's AI-generated when it's not.”

By the same token, a process-tracking app isn’t foolproof; the AI arms race means there’s an ongoing cycle of vulnerabilities and fixes on both sides.

“We offer a product that [tracks writing] in Google Docs, and many users find it helpful,” says Max Spero, cofounder and CEO of Pangram. “With that said, ‘paper trail’ tools are not a perfect catch-all. For example, someone could hand-type AI text, or use an auto-typer.” Spero points out that the messiness of writing itself creates further problems. “The average writer doesn't just sit down and type out a book,” he says. “They work with multiple files, send drafts back and forth, use voice notes while on the go. Not all of this gets captured in writing process tools.”

The tools, meanwhile, may be more geared toward copyright concerns than confirmation of human or AI authorship. Brady Ridgway, technical founder of ObraVera—which can cryptographically “fingerprint” patterns in writing as well as audio voice recordings—says his platform is designed to trace reuse of material you have stored in their database as a registered human user. With a time stamp and a crypto hash, he explains, if the content “crops up later somewhere it's not supposed to be, or somebody else claims it as theirs, we can search the database and say, ‘These words were created at this time, by this person.’”

That may demonstrate provenance and ownership, Ridgway says, yet it’s up to the registered individual to declare whether they used AI or not in the creation of the text. He refers to the kerfuffle in May over the writer who was accused of winning a Commonwealth Short Story Prize with an AI-generated submission. “Everybody seems to agree that he's the person who submitted the short story,” Ridgway says. “That's all that the software would do. It would say that somebody on this day made a declaration that it was human only or not AI-assisted.” It can’t confirm whether that’s a true statement or not.

Friedman tells WIRED that agents and publishers are unlikely to implement any method of verifying human authorship that “costs extra money or extra time,” not least because it would be impossible to get them to commit to a shared standard. She predicts that “it will be like herding cats to get agreement on this, because publishing is slow to adopt new technologies, especially new technologies developed by industry outsiders.”

Even if diverse publishers with highly variable needs and resources were to coalesce around some theoretical form of authentication, hurdles remain. Friedman alludes to the logistical problems of integrating this benchmark into existing production models, not to mention the lingering problem of “faked or manipulated” certification. “If any of this costs extra money or extra time, forget it,” she concludes. And while authors may be willing to pay for peace of mind, Friedman says, they won’t be able to trust that agents and publishers will accept proof of authorship from any given app.

In the absence of a clear solution, writers are left to fend for themselves. Bartz says that she’s alarmed by how zealous readers are responding to the prospect of being deceived by AI. “I have heard of people getting review-bombed on Goodreads because some stranger felt that the book sounded like AI to them, and everyone else piled on,” she says. “I've seen readers saying, ‘I'm not gonna read anything published after 2022, because then I can be sure that it doesn't have generative AI in it.’ That's a great way to tank an entire industry all at once.”

It so happens that Bartz’s forthcoming 2027 book, Delete Your Account, tackles generative artificial intelligence head-on. Her protagonist is a blocked writer who opts for an unfortunate shortcut, prompting an AI chatbot to imitate her favorite thriller—only to find herself trapped in that original story, facing certain death.

Bartz wonders if the very choice to satirize AI has put her in a precarious spot. “I've written portions that are very much meant to sound like LLMs,” she says. “Transcripts I made up, and annoying, AI-sounding marketing materials from this made-up AI company. And I don't know—if any of that comes back as AI-written, what will I do?”

article_content_zh:
她还拥有合法的名声：巴茨是针对 Anthropic 的集体诉讼的主要原告，该诉讼指控该公司从盗版网站下载了数百万本受版权保护的书籍，用作其模型的训练数据。 Anthropic 去年同意支付 15 亿美元，达成美国历史上最大的版权和解协议。

但是，当巴茨和许多其他作家警惕自己的作品遭到这种掠夺时，另一个人工智能威胁正在酝酿之中。当作者被指控依赖人工智能时会发生什么？

今年三月，出版业发现：社交媒体上广泛猜测一部名为《害羞女孩》的恐怖小说主要是人工智能生成的，《泰晤士报》发表了一篇关于这些说法的文章，阿歇特图书集团取消了该小说即将在美国的出版活动，并停止在英国出版，该小说已经在英国发行。 Pangram 是一种强大但绝非万无一失的 AI 检测工具，根据 Pangram 的说法，大约 78% 的文本是 AI 生成的。

《害羞女孩》的作者米娅·巴拉德否认了有关她使用人工智能来写小说的指控，声称一名编辑负责在人工智能辅助下对该书之前自行出版的版本进行修改。她还表示正在采取法律行动。自那起丑闻爆发以来，又有几位小说作家陷入了对人工智能的怀疑，其中一位是在赢得短篇小说奖后，另一位是在出版商为他的犯罪小说出价数百万美元之后。两人也否认了这些指控。

但巴茨指出，一旦指控开始，损害就已经造成。她说，随着“害羞女孩”丑闻的爆发，“我立即感觉这将导致潜在的政治迫害。”她解释说，人工智能在出版领域不可避免的出现，将“产生意想不到的效果，导致任何人都能够指控任何人使用人工智能”，而目前，作者几乎没有办法为自己辩护以应对这些指控。巴茨在证明人类作者身份时说道：“没有一致同意的标准。”

许多新软件工具的开发人员希望改变这一现状。 Works、Blindproof、Wintertext、Human Ink 和 ObraVera 等平台承诺提供跟踪和记录作者写作过程的方法，在某些情况下对书面作品进行加密和指纹识别，或使用独特的代码输入节奏，以生成作者身份记录（无论是完全由人类还是人工智能辅助）。这个想法不仅仅是创建一个书面记录，如果有人质疑他们是否使用了法学硕士，作者可以指出，而且当文本被刮入人工智能训练集中而没有归属或其他识别元数据时，可以证明出处。

专注于自由表达和版权保护的专业组织作家协会的首席执行官玛丽·拉森伯格 (Mary Rasenberger) 表示，该协会不能推荐其中任何一种工具而不是另一种工具，但希望作家知道它们作为安全网的存在。 （据作家协会政策和宣传总监 Umair Kazi 称，许多公司已与作家协会接洽以推销他们的服务。）

与此同时，拉森伯格告诉《连线》杂志，必须跨越这个障碍是“侮辱”和“负担”，而且“我们认为不应该要求”作者保留收据。

拉森伯格说：“如果你卖的是你的文字、你的声音、你的想象力、你的创造力，那么使用人工智能就没有意义。”他指出，作者对自己的作品感到自豪，这意味着人工智能的失误在出版业远没有人们想象的那么常见。 “我和编辑们谈过，尤其是非小说类和小说类的编辑，”拉森伯格说，“他们中的一些人会说，‘我从来没有看到过人工智能生成的投稿，如果我看到了我就会知道。’”

拉森伯格担心作者面临一种不信任的氛围——她说，他们应该“避免对其他作者的指控，因为这不利于健康的文学社区”——以及对人工智能检测工具的过度自信，因为人工智能检测工具可能会被愚弄，并且会产生误报。虽然 Pangram 声称在创意写作中使用时误报率为 0.01%，处于“行业领先”地位，但 Rasenberger 表示，作家协会“听说过很多例子，人们将自己的人类创作作品放入 Pangram，并得到结果说它是人工智能生成的。”她补充说，有多种因素可以“让人工智能探测器认为某些东西是人工智能生成的，而实际上它不是。”

同样，流程跟踪应用程序也并非万无一失。人工智能军备竞赛意味着双方都会不断地进行漏洞修复。

Pangram 联合创始人兼首席执行官 Max Spero 表示：“我们提供了一款可以在 Google Docs 中[跟踪写作]的产品，许多用户发现它很有帮助。” “话虽如此，‘书面记录’工具并不是完美的包罗万象。例如，有人可以手动输入人工智能文本，或使用自动打字机。”斯佩罗指出，写作本身的混乱会带来更多问题。 “一般作家不会只是坐下来写一本书，”他说。 “他们处理多个文件，来回发送草稿，在旅途中使用语音笔记。并非所有这些都可以在编写流程工具中捕获。”

与此同时，这些工具可能更适合版权问题，而不是确认人类或人工智能的作者身份。 ObraVera 的技术创始人布雷迪·里奇韦 (Brady Ridgway) 可以对书写和音频录音进行加密“指纹”模式，他表示，他的平台旨在跟踪您作为注册人类用户存储在其数据库中的材料的重复使用情况。他解释说，有了时间戳和加密哈希，如果内容“后来出现在不应该出现的地方，或者其他人声称它是他们的，我们可以搜索数据库并说，‘这些词是这个人在这个时候创建​​的。’”

Ridgway 说，这可能会证明出处和所有权，但由注册个人来声明他们在创建文本时是否使用了人工智能。他提到了五月份因一位作家被指控通过人工智能生成的提交作品赢得英联邦短篇小说奖而引发的混乱。 “每个人似乎都同意他是提交短篇小说的人，”里奇韦说。 “这就是软件要做的全部事情。它会说，今天有人声明它只是人类或没有人工智能辅助。”它无法确认这是否是真实的陈述。

title: The climate case for AI has not been made
title_en: The climate case for AI has not been made
author: MIT Tech Review
article_content:
This week, as countries meet in Antalya, Turkey for the United Nations climate conference, one topic likely to dominate the conversation is artificial intelligence. The host has already called on countries to commit to ensuring that AI is designed, powered, and deployed in ways that support climate action.

But so far, industries around the world aren’t doing nearly enough to harness the technology to actually drive down the greenhouse-gas emissions heating up the planet, despite some very optimistic claims from AI companies.

In 2024, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman declared that AI would unleash “astounding triumphs,” including “fixing the climate.” The year before, in a 2023 op-ed, the head of sustainability at Google and her coauthor wrote that AI could reduce global emissions 5% to 10% by 2030.

Some academic researchers have examined these AI-related climate claims. A peer-reviewed study published last year, led by researchers at the London School of Economics’ Grantham Research Institute and the firm Systemiq, estimated that AI could help cut global emissions by the equivalent of 3.2 to 5.4 billion tons of carbon dioxide annually by 2035—roughly on par with the US’s annual energy-related emissions on the high end, even after subtracting AI’s own energy footprint. Those potential gains are mostly concentrated in three sectors: power, meat and dairy, and vehicles.

But projections like these are only as good as our willingness to test them against present-day reality. So is there evidence that the largest companies in these three sectors are beginning to integrate AI in line with the study’s projections, and if so, do the results match expectations? Or is the 2035 number still mostly aspirational?

Companies across these sectors have announced plenty of initial efforts to incorporate AI into various business practices. But an AI-assisted review of public information from significant market actors in each sector, conducted and reviewed by the second author of this piece, found that few have announced they’re pursuing the specific emissions-reducing routes that informed the projections in the study—and fewer still claim they’ve used them to achieve meaningful climate progress.

The power sector is where the earlier study’s underlying math is most concrete: AI-driven forecasting of supply and demand could increase the amount of renewable electricity that reaches the grid from already-built solar and wind facilities by up to 20%, which could prevent an estimated 1.8 billion tons of emissions a year.

Yet of the grid operators reviewed in China, the United States, and Europe, only one deployed a known meaningful, working AI program of this sort, according to the analysis. A partnership between the UK’s National Grid ESO and Open Climate Fix halved the grid operator’s solar-forecast error (the difference between the amount of incoming sunlight predicted and the amount that actually reaches solar panels), avoiding hundreds of thousands of tons of carbon dioxide a year. Beyond this example in the UK, though, many other grid operators in the EU, the US, and China had little to show in the public record in terms of the AI integration envisioned by the study.

The meat and dairy sector offers the starkest contrast between technology readiness and market reality. To achieve the 2035 emission reductions anticipated in the earlier study, AI would need to close the taste and cost gap between traditional proteins and alternative ones, such as lab-grown or plant-based burgers and milk substitutes.

In one of the clearest efforts to achieve this, the AI and food tech company NotCo recently formed a joint venture with Kraft Heinz using its platform Giuseppe, which analyzes plant molecular data to pinpoint combinations replicating the taste, texture, and smell of animal products.

But few other alternative-protein companies had such a deeply integrated way of using AI in product development, the AI-assisted review suggests. Meanwhile, the sector seems to be facing more fundamental problems, including stubbornly slow mainstream consumer adoption and declining funding levels. Most notably, venture capital flowing into cultivated meat fell from a $989 million peak in 2021 to around $83 million last year.

The transportation sector offers some hopeful examples of the type of AI integration necessary to achieve the study’s projections, particularly among battery manufacturers and ride-sharing platforms. CATL—which controls roughly 40% of the global market for electric-vehicle batteries—launched an AI system trained on more than 100,000 battery design cases and 600 terabytes of test data. It cut the time needed to screen candidate materials by two orders of magnitude, according to the company. Independent researchers also found that the ride-sharing platform Didi Chuxing was able cut per-trip emissions 16% on average by using AI-optimized routing to minimize detours.

There’s another big problem in the climate case for AI, though: Oil and gas companies are also interested in these tools for many reasons, including the potential to increase production of fossil fuels. Technology firms that committed to sustainability goals in the past should answer questions about how their tools could be used to boost old, dirty energy as well as clean, renewable energy.

Finally, it’s also worth noting that integrating AI is just the first step, and it remains unclear to what degree the technology can accelerate the sorts of improvements and innovations envisioned. AI also does little to shorten the standard paths to certifying, permitting, building, packaging, marketing, and selling any resulting products, facilities, or services.

The findings of the analysis, carried out by Anthropic’s Claude Code, were reviewed against public documents and media accounts to ensure their accuracy. It is possible that some companies and utilities in these industries are pursuing AI-assisted applications that would fit into the initial study’s scenarios but haven’t yet been disclosed publicly.

Greater and better-targeted AI integration and efficiency gains in these three sectors may well materialize, bringing the 2035 projections closer to reality. But it won’t happen without deliberate and sustained efforts to ensure that AI delivers more environmental benefits than harms.

Notably, so far the rapid adoption of AI models and buildout of data centers has driven a huge increase in energy consumption and emissions, and this has led major tech companies like Microsoft, Google, and others to fall well off track in their corporate climate goals. At this point it would be surprising if the sector even manages to zero out its climate pollution: Emissions associated with global data centers (which may handle AI as well as non-AI computing tasks) could exceed 300 million tons annually in 2035, according to the IEA’s base forecast.

Industry leaders must implement the technology in the ways that promise to do the most to drive down emissions. Corporate customers should select models with the lowest environmental impacts and opt to work with the AI developers doing the most to reduce their climate footprint. And states and regions need to do more to incentivize or require all these companies to operate in more responsible ways.

Mary Nichols is distinguished counsel at the UCLA School of Law and the former chair of the California Air Resources Board.

Jeremy Tamanini is the founder of Dual Citizen, a sustainability research and advisory firm.

article_content_zh:
本周，当各国在土耳其安塔利亚召开联合国气候会议时，人工智能可能成为主导对话的一个话题。东道主已经呼吁各国承诺确保人工智能的设计、驱动和部署都支持气候行动。

但到目前为止，尽管人工智能公司提出了一些非常乐观的说法，但世界各地的行业在利用这项技术来实际减少使地球升温的温室气体排放方面还远远不够。

2024 年，OpenAI 首席执行官 Sam Altman 宣称人工智能将带来“惊人的胜利”，包括“修复气候”。前一年，在 2023 年的一篇专栏文章中，谷歌可持续发展主管和她的合著者写道，到 2030 年，人工智能可以将全球排放量减少 5% 至 10%。

一些学术研究人员研究了这些与人工智能相关的气候主张。去年，由伦敦经济学院格兰瑟姆研究所和 Systemiq 公司的研究人员领导的一项同行评审研究估计，到 2035 年，人工智能每年可以帮助减少相当于 3.2 至 54 亿吨二氧化碳的全球排放量——即使在扣除人工智能自身的能源足迹之后，这与美国每年与能源相关的排放量大致相当。这些潜在收益主要集中在三个行业：电力、肉类和乳制品以及汽车。

但此类预测的好坏取决于我们是否愿意根据当今的现实对其进行检验。那么，是否有证据表明这三个行业中最大的公司正在开始按照研究的预测整合人工智能？如果是，结果是否符合预期？ Or is the 2035 number still mostly aspirational?

这些行业的公司已经宣布了许多初步努力，将人工智能融入到各种商业实践中。但本文的第二作者在人工智能辅助下对每个部门重要市场参与者的公共信息进行了审查，发现很少有人宣布他们正在追求为研究中的预测提供依据的具体减排路线，而声称他们已经利用这些路线来实现有意义的气候进展的人更少了。

电力行业是早期研究的基础数学最为具体的领域：人工智能驱动的供需预测可以将已建成的太阳能和风能设施到达电网的可再生电力数量增加高达 20%，预计每年可以减少 18 亿吨的排放。

然而，根据分析，在中国、美国和欧洲审查的电网运营商中，只有一家部署了已知的有意义的、有效的此类人工智能程序。英国国家电网 ESO 和 Open Climate Fix 之间的合作将电网运营商的太阳能预测误差（预测的入射阳光量与实际到达太阳能电池板的阳光量之间的差异）减少了一半，每年避免了数十万吨二氧化碳的排放。然而，除了英国的这个例子之外，欧盟、美国和中国的许多其他电网运营商在公共记录中几乎没有显示出该研究设想的人工智能集成的情况。

肉类和乳制品行业的技术成熟度与市场现实之间存在着最鲜明的对比。为了实现早期研究中预期的 2035 年减排目标，人工智能需要缩小传统蛋白质与替代蛋白质（例如实验室种植或植物性汉堡和牛奶替代品）之间的口味和成本差距。

人工智能和食品科技公司 NotCo 最近与卡夫亨氏 (Kraft Heinz) 成立了一家合资企业，利用其平台 Giuseppe 来实现这一目标，这是实现这一目标的最明显的努力之一，该平台分析植物分子数据，以精确地复制动物产品的味道、质地和气味的组合。

但人工智能辅助审查表明，很少有其他替代蛋白质公司能够在产品开发中采用如此深度集成的人工智能方式。与此同时，该行业似乎面临着更根本的问题，包括主流消费者采用速度缓慢和资金水平下降。最值得注意的是，流入人造肉的风险资本从 2021 年 9.89 亿美元的峰值下降到去年的 8300 万美元左右。

交通运输行业提供了一些有希望的例子，说明实现研究预测所需的人工智能集成类型，特别是在电池制造商和乘车共享平台之间。 CATL 控制着全球约 40% 的电动汽车电池市场，推出了一款人工智能系统，该系统经过超过 100,000 个电池设计案例和 600 TB 的测试数据进行训练。据该公司称，它将筛选候选材料所需的时间缩短了两个数量级。独立研究人员还发现，乘车共享平台滴滴出行通过使用人工智能优化的路线来尽量减少弯路，平均每次行程排放量减少了 16%。

不过，人工智能的气候案例还存在另一个大问题：石油和天然气公司也出于多种原因对这些工具感兴趣，包括增加化石燃料产量的潜力。过去致力于可持续发展目标的科技公司应该回答有关如何使用其工具来促进旧的、肮脏的能源以及清洁的可再生能源的问题。

最后，还值得注意的是，集成人工智能只是第一步，目前尚不清楚该技术能够在多大程度上加速所设想的各种改进和创新。人工智能也几乎没有缩短认证、许可、建造、包装、营销和销售任何最终产品、设施或服务的标准路径。

title: Toronto-based Ada and SF-based Dialpad, both makers of AI customer service software, agree to merge in an all-share deal valuing Ada at ~$430M, sources say (Globe and Mail)
title_en: Toronto-based Ada and SF-based Dialpad, both makers of AI customer service software, agree to merge in an all-share deal valuing Ada at ~$430M, sources say (Globe and Mail)
author: Globe and Mail
article_content:
Ada chief executive Mike Murchison, shown earlier this year, co-founded the AI customer service company in 2016. Along with answering questions, Ada's tech connects to clients' other software systems to perform administrative tasks.Jon Laytner/The Globe and Mail

Ada Support Inc., the Toronto-based company that makes AI customer service software for businesses, has agreed to combine with U.S. company Dialpad Inc. in an all-share deal valuing the Canadian enterprise at around $600-million, or about US$430-million, two sources familiar with the matter said.

That’s down from Ada’s US$1.2-billion valuation when it raised money at the peak of the pandemic technology bubble in a US$130-million financing round led by Silicon Valley venture capital firm Spark Capital. At the time, that financing made it part of a cohort of Canadian “unicorns,” or privately held technology companies that achieve a valuation of US$1-billion or more.

Tech valuations subsequently plummeted starting in late 2021 and those of legacy software providers have remained depressed owing to lingering questions about how much large language model-powered (LLM) artificial-intelligence software will disrupt the market. Like other emerging technology companies, Ada went on to make a series of layoffs and cost cuts, including eliminating half its marketing team in July and laying off 25 employees last week, two other sources told The Globe and Mail.

The Globe is not identifying the sources as they are not authorized to discuss the matters.

Chief executive officer Mike Murchison and David Hariri co-founded Ada in 2016 after launching an earlier social-media startup. The firm sold a software system that let businesses set up their own customer service chatbots, initially using elaborate prewritten scripts.

In addition to answering questions, Ada’s technology connects to clients’ other software systems to do tasks such as updating contact information, changing bookings or issuing refunds.

The firm’s website lists customers including Caribbean telecom provider Digicel, Canadian retailer Indigo Books & Music Inc. and Asian consumer superapp Grab. It’s also counted Shopify Inc., AirAsia Group BHD and Telus Corp. among its clients.

Mr. Murchison did not immediately respond to a request for comment about the transaction.

Ada grew rapidly in its early years, generating tens of millions of dollars in annual revenue by the early 2020s, and raising money from several leading Canadian venture capital firms as well as U.S. heavyweights Accel, Bessemer Venture Partners, FirstMark Capital and Tiger Global Management.

While Ada was early to the business of AI chatbots, it’s faced increasing competition in recent years, particularly following OpenAI’s launch of ChatGPT in November 2022.

Ada rebuilt its technology to use LLMs, letting the bots more dynamically take in and respond to users’ questions. In April 2023, it rolled out voice agents that could answer customer-service phone calls. That led to a rapid decline in revenues from its older products but an equally quick expansion of its LLM-based offering. But the net result, said the two sources familiar with the deal terms, was that Ada’s overall revenue expansion has not kept pace with other rapidly growing AI-based companies and was recently running at about US$50-million in revenues on an annual basis.

Dialpad is a privately held San Francisco Bay Area software company that sells contact-centre software to businesses and has been in operation since 2011. It’s much larger than Ada, which has roughly 200 employees. Dialpad, which like Ada achieved unicorn status during the pandemic, also has a deep bench of top-flight U.S. early-stage investors, including Andreessen Horowitz, Google Ventures, SoftBank Corp., ICONIQ Capital and Salesforce Ventures, as well as the growth equity arm of the Ontario Municipal Employees’ Retirement Systems.

Last October, Dialpad launched an agentic AI platform, supplying the software for businesses to build autonomous voice-and-text AI agents. Some of its clients include Randstad, Nasdaq and T-Mobile. AI agents make decisions or execute on actions autonomously on behalf of human users.

One of the sources familiar with the deal said Dialpad has a strong user base in enterprise telephony for internal and customer support, and that the deal is seen as a way to help both companies generate continued market growth with Ada’s advanced technology.

The deal is expected to close as soon as next week.

There have been significant shifts in Ada’s work force in recent months. In a recording of the July layoffs, obtained by The Globe, Mr. Murchison can be heard telling employees that his decision to terminate their employment was related to a “change we are making around how Ada is building products.” Two of those laid-off employees, who spoke to The Globe on condition of anonymity, said that Mr. Murchison had been keen on amplifying the use of the AI agent Claude in workflows, especially on the marketing team, to cut costs. They believed that their layoffs were the direct impact of AI use within the company.

Ada co-founder Mr. Hariri left the firm in July for a product management role at Shopify, according to his LinkedIn profile, although he remains on the board. Ada’s chief marketing officer and chief customer officer have also exited this year.

summary_en: Toronto-based Ada has agreed to merge with U.S.-based Dialpad in an all-share deal, valuing the Canadian AI customer service firm at approximately $430 million. Once a unicorn with a $1.2 billion valuation, Ada's market value has plummeted by nearly two-thirds due to the post-pandemic tech correction and market disruption from LLMs.
title_zh: AI客服双雄合并：独角兽估值腰斩
summary_zh: 多伦多AI客服厂商Ada与旧金山Dialpad达成全股合并协议，Ada估值约4.3亿美元
article_content_zh:
今年早些时候出现的 Ada 首席执行官迈克·默奇森 (Mike Murchison) 于 2016 年共同创立了这家人工智能客户服务公司。除了回答问题，Ada 的技术还连接到客户的其他软件系统来执行管理任务。Jon Laytner/《环球邮报》

两位知情人士称，总部位于多伦多的企业人工智能客户服务软件公司 Ada Support Inc. 已同意与美国公司 Dialpad Inc. 进行全股合并，这家加拿大企业的估值约为 6 亿美元（约合 4.3 亿美元）。

这低于 Ada 在大流行科技泡沫高峰期筹集资金时的 12 亿美元估值，该轮融资由硅谷风险投资公司 Spark Capital 领投，融资金额为 1.3 亿美元。当时，这笔融资使其成为加拿大“独角兽”（即估值达到 10 亿美元或以上的私营科技公司）的一员。

随后，科技公司的估值从 2021 年底开始大幅下跌，而传统软件提供商的估值仍然低迷，原因是人们对大型语言模型驱动 (LLM) 人工智能软件将在多大程度上扰乱市场这一问题挥之不去。另两位消息人士告诉《环球邮报》，与其他新兴科技公司一样，Ada 随后进行了一系列裁员和成本削减，包括 7 月份裁撤了一半的营销团队，以及上周解雇了 25 名员工。

《环球报》没有透露消息来源，因为他们无权讨论此事。

首席执行官 Mike Murchison 和 David Hariri 在创立了一家早期社交媒体初创公司后，于 2016 年共同创立了 Ada。该公司销售了一款软件系统，允许企业建立自己的客户服务聊天机器人，最初使用精心设计的预先编写的脚本。

除了回答问题之外，Ada 的技术还可以连接到客户的其他软件系统来执行更新联系信息、更改预订或发放退款等任务。

该公司网站列出的客户包括加勒比电信提供商 Digicel、加拿大零售商 Indigo Books & Music Inc. 和亚洲消费者超级应用 Grab。 Shopify Inc.、AirAsia Group BHD 和 Telus Corp. 也是该公司的客户。

默奇森先生没有立即回应有关该交易的置评请求。

Ada 早年发展迅速，到 2020 年代初年收入达到数千万美元，并从加拿大几家领先的风险投资公司以及美国重量级企业 Accel、Bessemer Venture Partners、FirstMark Capital 和 Tiger Global Management 筹集资金。

虽然 Ada 很早就涉足人工智能聊天机器人业务，但近年来它面临着日益激烈的竞争，特别是在 OpenAI 于 2022 年 11 月推出 ChatGPT 之后。

Ada 重建了其技术以使用法学硕士，让机器人更动态地接受并回答用户的问题。 2023 年 4 月，它推出了可以接听客户服务电话的语音代理。这导致其旧产品的收入迅速下降，但其基于法学硕士的产品同样快速扩张。但两位熟悉交易条款的消息人士称，最终结果是 Ada 的整体收入扩张未能跟上其他快速增长的人工智能公司的步伐，最近的年收入约为 5000 万美元。

Dialpad 是旧金山湾区一家私营软件公司，向企业销售联络中心软件，自 2011 年开始运营。它比 Ada 规模大得多，后者约有 200 名员工。与 Ada 一样，Dialpad 在疫情期间获得了独角兽地位，它也拥有大量顶级美国早期投资者，包括 Andreessen Horowitz、Google Ventures、SoftBank Corp.、ICONIQ Capital 和 Salesforce Ventures，以及安大略省市政雇员退休系统的成长型股权部门。

去年 10 月，Dialpad 推出了代理人工智能平台，为企业提供构建自主语音和文本人工智能代理的软件。其部分客户包括任仕达 (Randstad)、纳斯达克 (Nasdaq) 和 T-Mobile。人工智能代理代表人类用户自主做出决策或执行操作。

title: Bikers and Bug-Lovers Join Forces to Fight a New Google Data Center
title_en: Bikers and Bug-Lovers Join Forces to Fight a New Google Data Center
author: Wired AI
article_content:
Robins works for wildlife conservation trust Buglife, part of an unlikely alliance of special-interest groups trying to block the Thurrock development. Buglife and local wildlife groups fear for an endangered plant, rare bumblebee, and other invertebrates whose habitat they say will be destroyed. Nonprofit Foxglove says the data center will emit too much pollution. The Thurrock Hammers motorcycle club wants to return to racing on the site.

Members of the various groups joined Robins outside Google’s office last Wednesday, holding placards demanding the company “search elsewhere” for somewhere to put its facility.

Across the UK, companies like Google are preparing to build industrial-scale data centers, part of a scramble to meet the swelling demand for the compute needed to run artificial intelligence models and other digital services. The UK government is eager to encourage them, hoping to capture a share of the hundreds of billions of dollars flowing into the AI industry and minimize the country’s dependence on foreign partners for compute. But like in the US, people living near to the proposed developments are making their objections known and trying to gum up the works.

Google says its plans for the Thurrock site prioritize biodiversity and the reduction of emissions. “We share the concerns that Buglife and others have—and their expectation that this site should be developed sustainably,” Adam Elman, director of sustainability EMEA at Google, tells WIRED. But the situation in Thurrock underscores the level and breadth of resistance that data center developers face as the public mood towards them appears to sour. Though small, the demonstration outside Google was one of a number of anti-data center protests that took place across Europe last week. In Amsterdam, protesters scaled a crane at a Microsoft data center site and unfurled a “fuck AI” banner.

“There’s local campaign groups against data centers popping up every week,” says Robins. “People are angry about data centers turning up in their back gardens. They’re angry about data centers flouting local opinion—and about the impact it has on wildlife.”

The Thurrock site is located next to a fuel stop, where an arterial road meets the highway that encircles London. On the plot, the remnants of Arena Essex, a disused motorcycle racing stadium, border grassland scribbled with old footpaths, and a lake.

Google acquired the site through a subsidiary in 2023. In May last year, it applied for permission to build a data center campus there. When locals caught wind, they coordinated with national wildlife and environmental groups and began to kick up a fuss. Of the 1,000 responses submitted by members of the public to the planning authority, only one supported the project. (Thurrock Council says that many of the responses were submitted by people living outside the local area.)

The protest group argues that Google’s proposal fails to properly account for the negative effects of the data center development: the loss of the raceway sporting facility, the destruction of habitat for rare flora and fauna, and the up to 570,000 tonnes of emissions it could produce each year—which Foxglove claims cannot be accommodated under the UK government’s carbon budget.

“We’re an outlier. We object on different grounds. I think that’s why I think we’re quite useful to the whole campaign,” says Mark Sexton, director at the Thurrock Hammers motorcycle club. “The unlikely alliance has got some attention.”

Google says the objections are grounded in misconceptions about its plans. The company claims it will achieve a net gain in biodiversity by retaining habitat and transplanting endangered plants to another location; and that it will offset the emissions by financing new sources of renewable energy generation, with a view to becoming carbon-neutral by 2030. Google argues that razing the motorcycle stadium will not result in the loss of an invaluable community facility because the track has already been out of use for a number of years. “We want to be good neighbors,” says Elman. “We recognize the ecological value of these sites. Our goal is to minimize the impact as much as possible.”

Unconvinced by Google’s reassurances, the protesters intend to continue to fight the development—one small act of protest at a time. “Do I think we’ve got much hope? Not right now,” says Rob Pownall, founder of nonprofit Protect The Wild, who attended Wednesday’s demonstration. “But this is another chip off that massive ice block.”

There are some signs the grassroots anti-data center movement is starting to win concessions. In the US, some states have instituted permitting freezes and data center moratoria, and pro-data center candidates were roundly crushed in this week’s midterm elections. In the UK, Foxglove recently succeeded in a legal challenge that forced the government to withdraw planning permission for a data center to the west of London.

Thurrock Council tells WIRED it expects to rule on Google’s initial planning application early next year. After that, the company will need to come up with a more granular plan for developing the site, which will be subject to another lengthy vetting process. The protesters say they intend to make life hard for Google at every step.

“These planning campaigns can go on for years,” says Robins. “It’s a war of attrition.”

title_zh: 谷歌英国建数据中心遭当地“联军”抗议
summary_zh: 由于担心生态破坏与噪音污染，环保组织、摩托车俱乐部及公益机构在谷歌办公室门前抗议其拟建的数据中心项目
article_content_zh:
罗宾斯为野生动物保护信托公司 Buglife 工作，该信托公司是一个试图阻止瑟罗克开发的特殊利益集团联盟的一部分。 Buglife 和当地野生动物团体担心濒临灭绝的植物、稀有的大黄蜂和其他无脊椎动物，他们说这些动物的栖息地将被破坏。非营利组织 Foxglove 表示，该数据中心将排放过多的污染物。瑟罗克·哈默斯摩托车俱乐部希望重返现场比赛。

上周三，各个团体的成员在谷歌办公室外与罗宾斯一起举着标语牌，要求该公司“寻找其他地方”放置其设施。

在英国各地，谷歌等公司正准备建设工业规模的数据中心，这是满足运行人工智能模型和其他数字服务所需的不断增长的计算需求的一部分。英国政府急于鼓励他们，希望能从流入人工智能行业的数千亿美元中分一杯羹，并最大限度地减少该国在计算方面对外国合作伙伴的依赖。但就像在美国一样，居住在拟议开发项目附近的人们正在表达他们的反对意见，并试图把工程搞砸。

谷歌表示，瑟罗克工厂的计划优先考虑生物多样性和减少排放。谷歌欧洲、中东和非洲可持续发展总监 Adam Elman 告诉《连线》杂志：“我们与 Buglife 和其他人一样担心，也希望这个网站能够可持续发展。”但瑟罗克的情况突显了数据中心开发商面临的阻力的程度和广度，因为公众对他们的态度似乎在恶化。尽管规模较小，但谷歌外的示威活动是上周欧洲各地发生的众多反数据中心抗议活动之一。在阿姆斯特丹，抗议者爬上微软数据中心的起重机，并展开了“fuck AI”的横幅。

“每周都会出现反对数据中心的当地运动团体，”罗宾斯说。 “人们对数据中心出现在自家后花园感到愤怒。他们对数据中心无视当地意见及其对野生动物的影响感到愤怒。”

瑟罗克工厂位于加油站旁边，这里有一条主干道与环绕伦敦的高速公路交汇。情节中，埃塞克斯竞技场（Arena Essex）的遗迹、一座废弃的摩托车赛车场、布满旧人行道的边境草原和一个湖泊。

谷歌于 2023 年通过子公司收购了该网站。去年 5 月，它申请了在那里建设数据中心园区的许可。当当地人发现风声后，他们与国家野生动物和环保组织协调并开始大惊小怪。在公众向规划当局提交的 1,000 份回复中，只有一份支持该项目。 （瑟罗克委员会表示，许多回复是由居住在当地以外的人提交的。）

抗议组织认为，谷歌的提议未能正确考虑数据中心开发的负面影响：跑道体育设施的消失、稀有动植物栖息地的破坏，以及每年可能产生的高达 57 万吨的排放量——Foxglove 声称，英国政府的碳预算无法容纳这些排放量。

“我们是异类。我们以不同的理由反对。我想这就是为什么我认为我们对整个竞选活动非常有用，”瑟罗克·哈默斯摩托车俱乐部主任马克·塞克斯顿说。 “这个不太可能的联盟引起了一些关注。”

谷歌表示，这些反对意见是基于对其计划的误解。该公司声称，通过保留栖息地并将濒临灭绝的植物移植到另一个地方，将实现生物多样性的净增益；它将通过资助新的可再生能源发电来抵消排放，以期到 2030 年实现碳中和。谷歌辩称，夷平摩托车体育场不会导致宝贵的社区设施的损失，因为这条赛道已经闲置多年。 “我们想成为好邻居，”埃尔曼说。 “我们认识到这些地点的生态价值。我们的目标是尽可能减少影响。”

抗议者对谷歌的保证不相信，打算继续对抗事态的发展——一次小小的抗议行为。 “我认为我们有很大希望吗？现在还没有，”参加周三示威活动的非营利组织“保护野生动物”创始人罗布·鲍纳尔 (Rob Pownall) 说道。 “但这只是那块巨大冰块上的又一块碎片。”

有一些迹象表明，草根反数据中心运动开始赢得让步。在美国，一些州已经实行了许可冻结和数据中心暂停，支持数据中心的候选人在本周的中期选举中遭到全面压垮。在英国，Foxglove 最近成功解决了一项法律挑战，迫使政府撤回伦敦西部数据中心的规划许可。

瑟罗克委员会告诉《连线》杂志，预计明年初将对谷歌的初步规划申请做出裁决。之后，该公司将需要制定一个更细化的网站开发计划，这将需要经过另一个漫长的审查过程。抗议者表示，他们打算一步步让谷歌处境艰难。

“这些规划活动可以持续数年，”罗宾斯说。 “这是一场消耗战。”

title: Kuken Industries searches 70 years of drawings in minutes
title_en: Kuken Industries searches 70 years of drawings in minutes
author: OpenAI 官方动态
content_snippet: Kuken Industries uses the OpenAI API to search 70 years of cooling tower drawings. Engineers can find the drawing for a repair in 4.5 minutes, down from nearly an hour.
summary_en: Kuken Industries has integrated the OpenAI API to digitize and enable semantic search for its vast archive of cooling tower blueprints spanning 70 years. This initiative aims to streamline maintenance workflows, reducing the time engineers spend locating historical drawings from nearly an hour to just 4.5 minutes.
title_zh: 工业老厂接入AI：70年图纸秒级检索

title: Google rolls out a Googlebook update that frees up 3GB-6GB of RAM via on-device AI optimizations, reduces Chrome crashes, patches ~60 Android flaws, and more (Jay Bonggolto/Android Central)
title_en: Google rolls out a Googlebook update that frees up 3GB-6GB of RAM via on-device AI optimizations, reduces Chrome crashes, patches ~60 Android flaws, and more (Jay Bonggolto/Android Central)
author: Android Central
article_content:
Google's latest Googlebook update frees up to 6GB of RAM and fixes Chrome crashes.

The biggest change is in how Googlebook handles memory used by its on-device AI services. Google has updated its NPU driver and optimized AICore memory management, freeing up 3GB to 6GB of system RAM, as per a Reddit post by Google's Mishaal Rahman. That’s a significant bump for laptops with 16GB of RAM, especially when jumping between a lot of apps and browser tabs.

Chrome should also behave better under heavier workloads. The update improves the way the system reclaims memory when background AI services conflict with browser processes, reducing the chances of unexpected tab reloads and crashes. I’m almost tempted to say the update is the kind of fix that arguably should have been in place before Googlebook launched, but better late than never.

The November release covers a wide range of hardware and software issues. Convertibles should no longer lose keyboard and touchpad input when you switch between tablet and laptop modes. Google has also fixed Zoom crashes using simulated backgrounds, filters, blur effects, and 3D avatars.

External displays get a little love, too. Now you should be able to play DRM-protected streaming content such as Netflix, rather than just seeing a black screen. USB microphones and multichannel audio interfaces should work as expected too. Bluetooth users can also get lower audio-video synchronization delays and more reliable reconnection for wireless mice.

Google hasn't forgotten about those who use Googlebook for development work. The Linux Terminal beta brings in a bunch of fixes, including more reliable shell sessions after sleep, better SSH port forwarding, and improved multi-window management. Google also fixed a memory leak when closing terminal tabs and made Linux VM updates less destructive, preserving user storage and custom SSH configurations.

Security is another part of the release. The Android security patch for November 1, 2026 resolves around 60 vulnerabilities. Google also updated the Linux 6.18 kernel and Ti50 security chip firmware, fixing unexpected restarts, boot loops, and noisy fans.

Google says the update is being rolled out gradually to supported models, including devices from Acer, ASUS, Lenovo, HP, and Dell. Owners can find it under Settings > System > System Update. You want the build number CL3B.260622.286.R2.

Early reactions on Reddit have been largely positive, with some owners already reporting smoother performance. That said, users are reporting issues, including Chrome spell check and notification syncing problems after waking from sleep.

Jay Bonggolto always keeps a nose for news. He has been writing about consumer tech for as long as he can remember, and he has used a variety of Android phones since falling in love with Jelly Bean. Send him a direct message via X or LinkedIn.

article_content_zh:
Google 最新的 Googlebook 更新释放了高达 6GB 的 RAM 并修复了 Chrome 崩溃问题。

最大的变化在于 Googlebook 如何处理其设备上人工智能服务使用的内存。根据 Google 的 Mishaal Rahman 在 Reddit 上发布的帖子，谷歌已经更新了其 NPU 驱动程序并优化了 AICore 内存管理，释放了 3GB 至 6GB 的系统 RAM。对于具有 16GB RAM 的笔记本电脑来说，这是一个显着的提升，尤其是在大量应用程序和浏览器选项卡之间切换时。

Chrome 在较重的工作负载下也应该表现得更好。此更新改进了当后台 AI 服务与浏览器进程发生冲突时系统回收内存的方式，从而减少了意外选项卡重新加载和崩溃的可能性。我几乎想说，这次更新应该是在 Googlebook 推出之前就应该进行的修复，但迟做总比不做好。

11 月版本涵盖了广泛的硬件和软件问题。当您在平板电脑和笔记本电脑模式之间切换时，敞篷车不应再丢失键盘和触摸板输入。谷歌还修复了使用模拟背景、滤镜、模糊效果和 3D 头像的 Zoom 崩溃问题。

外接显示器也受到了一些人的喜爱。现在您应该能够播放受 DRM 保护的流媒体内容，例如 Netflix，而不仅仅是看到黑屏。 USB 麦克风和多通道音频接口也应该按预期工作。蓝牙用户还可以获得更低的音视频同步延迟和更可靠的无线鼠标重新连接。

Google 并没有忘记那些使用 Googlebook 进行开发工作的人。 Linux Terminal Beta 版带来了一系列修复，包括睡眠后更可靠的 shell 会话、更好的 SSH 端口转发以及改进的多窗口管理。谷歌还修复了关闭终端选项卡时的内存泄漏问题，并降低了 Linux VM 更新的破坏性，保留了用户存储和自定义 SSH 配置。

安全性是该版本的另一部分。 2026 年 11 月 1 日的 Android 安全补丁解决了大约 60 个漏洞。谷歌还更新了 Linux 6.18 内核和 Ti50 安全芯片固件，修复了意外重启、启动循环和风扇噪音等问题。

谷歌表示，该更新正在逐步推广到支持的型号，包括宏碁、华硕、联想、惠普和戴尔的设备。用户可以在“设置”>“系统”>“系统更新”下找到它。您需要内部版本号 CL3B.260622.286.R2。

Reddit 上的早期反应基本上是积极的，一些所有者已经报告了性能更加平稳。也就是说，用户报告了一些问题，包括 Chrome 拼写检查和从睡眠中醒来后的通知同步问题。

杰伊·邦戈尔托总是密切关注新闻。从他记事起，他就一直在撰写有关消费者技术的文章，自从爱上 Jelly Bean 以来，他已经使用过各种 Android 手机。通过 X 或 LinkedIn 向他发送直接消息。

title: When talking about AI safety, President Trump says "I don't mind guardrails. But I don't wanna put us in a deep second position", and "China has no guardrails" (CBS News)
title_en: When talking about AI safety, President Trump says "I don't mind guardrails. But I don't wanna put us in a deep second position", and "China has no guardrails" (CBS News)
author: CBS News
article_content:
This past Tuesday, President Donald Trump's Republican Party suffered an extraordinary midterm repudiation â losing not just the House and Senate, but statewide offices in red states, from Texas to Kansas to South Carolina, that Democrats hadn't won in decades. In the past, this president has met defeat with claims of fraud and the effort to overturn the 2020 election.

But when we met with him in the White House on Friday for his first sit-down interview since the midterms, we found him in a surprisingly reflective mood, and seemingly accepting of defeat. Our wide-ranging conversation covered: immigration and corruption, Iran and artificial intelligence, his potential successors and his own mortality.

But we began with the election results.Ross Douthat: Two years ago, you won a big, some might say historic, victory. Just now, the Republican party in the midterms suffered a big, some might say, historic defeat. Give me your political analysis of what just happened.President Donald Trump: Well, number one, I was not on the ballot.

But I campaigned hard for some people. And-- I think if I was on the ballot, it would've been a much different situation because you saw the level of popularity and love. There was love.

We had massive rallies. You had to transfer those voters, however, to candidates that they didn't like. But there's something beyond that.

They didn't like the war. They didn't like the fact that gasoline went up, 'cause I had it down at a low, and there's-- a great dislike, incredibly, for Israel. Ross Douthat: Let's go through those then one by one.President Donald Trump: Go ahead.Ross Douthat: Start-- start with the candidates, right?

You said it was tough to transfer your own appeal to candidatesPresident Donald Trump: Yeah.Ross Douthat: But in a lot of cases, you picked the candidates. You endorsed Ken Paxton--President Donald Trump: Well, I--Ross Douthat: --in Texas.President Donald Trump: I--Ross Douthat: He had a tough time.President Donald Trump: Sure.Ross Douthat: You endorsed Darline Graham--President Donald Trump: But-- but Cornyn--Ross Douthat: --in South Carolina.President Donald Trump: --Cornyn would've lost also.

Darline, I did that in-- honor of a man named Lindsey, who was a friend of mine. And she fought hard. She fought hard.

She really did. Ross Douthat: She lost a very Republican state.President Donald Trump: Oh--Ross Douthat: To a very liberal challenger--President Donald Trump: I won-- I won South Carolina by the highest vote in history by far. I won Texas by the highest vote in history by far.

I won Florida who, by the way, I did endorse. And he's gonna be-- a great governor and a great senator. I endorsed both of them.

And, had I not endorsed them, they wouldn't have won.Ross Douthat: Why can't it transfer? You-- you were out on the trail, and you said--President Donald Trump: It didn't transfer--Ross Douthat: You said, "Vote like I'm on the ballot."President Donald Trump: Yeah. It didn't--Ross Douthat: And people didn't?

Or-- or did they? Did they vote because they were mad at you--President Donald Trump: No, they--Ross Douthat: About--President Donald Trump: I think they didn't vote, really. I think in some cases, they didn't like the candidates.

And that's, you know, their prerogative. Ross Douthat: Couple days ago your vice president, JD Vance, wrote a social media post where he says, "The reason we lost is the war," meaning Iran. And he said things in that post--President Donald Trump: I don't disagree--Ross Douthat: About Israel.

Yeah. So you agree with his analysis?President Donald Trump: I don't disagree with it Ross Douthat: Did you know he was gonna write that post?President Donald Trump: He asked me what do I think. I said, "You write what you're--" I said--Ross Douthat: "Write what you--"President Donald Trump: You write what you want--"Ross Douthat: "Write what you feel"?President Donald Trump: By the way, "What are you gonna write?

"The only thing I wish he would've said there, if he felt it, and you'd have to ask him about that, but if you had to do it again, would you do it? You know, he's part of a decision-making process. And my answer is an emphatic yes because you can't let Iran have a nuclear weapon.

I think, historically, this will be a very good decision. Is it a good decision for today and tomorrow? Maybe not.

But you know, I have to go with what's right for our country. If they had a nuclear weapon during my term, I would be excoriated far worse than what's happened. So--Ross Douthat: All right.

Let's-- let's--President Donald Trump: I've stopped--Ross Douthat: Come--President Donald Trump: But Ross, I've stopped them from having a nuclear weapon. That's a big thing.The president argued that even with the Iran war, the U.S. economy in his second term has been very strong.Ross Douthat: But in poll after poll, people say they're unhappy with this economy in a way they weren't in the first term.

Cost of living, inflation, and so on. Is that all just the Iran war?President Donald Trump: Well, it's not really the Iran war because the numbers are phenomenal. I think it was bad messaging, maybe by me, but I would talk about it all the time.

So I don't know, how much can I talk about it? Look, the press doesn't cover-- positive news for Republicans. They don't cover certainly positive news for me.

So I have to do it myself. I have to get it out there. We have historically good numbers.

We have the highest stock market in history.Ross Douthat: But why don't Americans feel it, that--President Donald Trump: They don't--Ross Douthat: Why-- why don't they-- 'cause they're--President Donald Trump: Because I think--Ross Douthat: Obviously, like, you and the press, you and the media, you and our business have been in tension throughout your career.President Donald Trump: Correct.Ross Douthat: But you still won elections, right?President Donald Trump: Yeah.Ross Douthat: So why couldn't you win this time--President Donald Trump: I think it was bad messaging.Ross Douthat: What was the bad message?President Donald Trump: We couldn't get the word across.

Whether it was the message or the record, the Republican collapse will give Democrats in Congress new powers over budgets, hearings, and subpoenas.Ross Douthat: You came out after the midterms. You congratulated the Democrats.President Donald Trump: Correct.Ross Douthat: You said that you were open to working with them.President Donald Trump: True.Ross Douthat: What is one thing you would like to work with a Democratic majority on--President Donald Trump: I'd love to do something on immigration.Ross Douthat: What?President Donald Trump: Because-- well, soRoss Douthat: Do you think immigration hurt you in the midterms?

President Donald Trump: I think--Ross Douthat: Do you think the crackdown hurt you--President Donald Trump: I think it both helped and hurt. I think I got an A+ for closing up the border. I get very high marks for getting the bad ones out.

But I get hurt because we also took people that had good jobs, that-- that created one violation, or breaking of the law, and that was that they came into the country illegally. Now, there is a large part of the country that think that they should be put out. And there's a large part of the country that think that they should be allowed to stay if they're good people working in a landscaping company, or workin' in a hotel, or doing something, right?

And in some cases, paying taxes. And there's a large group of people who think that they should be allowed to stay. Ross Douthat: So you think your deportation policy--President Donald Trump: I think it was--Ross Douthat: Went too far--President Donald Trump: Too tough.Ross Douthat: It was too tough?President Donald Trump: I think it might be too tough, yeah.Ross Douthat: What would--President Donald Trump: And-- and I think--Ross Douthat: What does a deal look likePresident Donald Trump: I think ultimately--Ross Douthat: With the Democrats?President Donald Trump: That hurt me.

Well, the deal would be we would work something out. And I think it's something-- I think that's something that's actually doable.Ross Douthat: Doable to create--President Donald Trump: When you go into--Ross Douthat: Some kinda-- some kind of legal status--President Donald Trump: Yeah, Ross, when you go in--Ross Douthat: For the landscapers and the--President Donald Trump: Yeah.

When you go into a hotel and you have a woman that's worked there as-- you know, as a maid, as a cleaner, as a this, as a that, as a waitress, a lotta good things, great jobs, and all of a sudden, they're being taken outta the country, it's tough. It's a tough thing. But there's a group of people that I would say on the sort of pretty far right that would like everybody taken out.Ross Douthat: Do some of them--President Donald Trump: Then there's a group of people on the--Ross Douthat: Do-- do any of those people work in your administration?

Are they in--President Donald Trump: Yes.Ross Douthat: The building with us right now?President Donald Trump: Yeah, no, no. Well, there're a lotta those people. Then there's also people that are more modified on that.

In other words, get the killers out. Get all the-- the rough ones out. Get the drug dealers out.

But let the people that are here, and in some cases here for ten and 15 years, work a deal for them.Ross Douthat: You think the Democratic party right now has people in it who would be interested in this kind of deal?President Donald Trump: I think so, yeah. People have already called me.Ross Douthat: So I'll say I saw James Talarico, the new Democratic senator--President Donald Trump: Said very nice things, yeah--Ross Douthat: From Texas, I saw him on Fox News.

And he said immigration was one of the things he wanted--President Donald Trump: Others--Ross Douthat: To work with you on--President Donald Trump: Others too. South Carolina said. Numerous--Ross Douthat: You did-- you did--President Donald Trump: Numerous people that won--Ross Douthat: In the course--President Donald Trump: Said that.Ross Douthat: Of the campaign, you did occasionally call him Talafreako.President Donald Trump: Yeah, I did.Ross Douthat: Do you think you could work with the Democrats without insulting them--President Donald Trump: Yeah, I do--Ross Douthat: Consistently?President Donald Trump: I could.Ross Douthat: You think so--President Donald Trump: I also call-- I also--Ross Douthat: But you--President Donald Trump: Call many of them Dumocrats Ross Douthat: You did that just--President Donald Trump: 'Cause âRoss Douthat: The other day.

If-- if it took six months of not insulting the Democrats to get a deal done, do you think you could do it?President Donald Trump: Very easily.Ross Douthat: Okay. That'll be interestingâPresident Donald Trump: But you have to understand--Ross Douthat: To watch. Do you think you could--President Donald Trump: I'm here-- I'm here--Ross Douthat: Do it if they're--President Donald Trump: To help the country.Ross Douthat: Do you think-- think you could do it if they're investigating you?

If they're running investigations into your administration, can you work with them?President Donald Trump: Well, I did it for four years. You know, I-- they-- what they did with me was-- there's never been weaponization. They impeached me twice.

And there are those that say that worked out to my advantage. I mean, you know, 'causeRoss Douthat: Do you think they'll impeach you again?President Donald Trump: I can't imagine it, you know? They d-- hey, look, what have I done?

I've had the best two years in the history of the presidency. All this winning, according to the president, doesn't preclude some change of White House personnel.Ross Douthat: In a previous lifetime, you were rather famous for saying, "You're fired" quite often. President Donald Trump: YeahRoss Douthat: After a big midterm defeat like this, do you expect to fire anyone from your teamâPresident Donald Trump: I do.

Yeah.Ross Douthat: You do?President Donald Trump: Little bit.Ross Douthat: Little bit?President Donald Trump: I love my Cabinet. I think they're good. But I'll do-- be doin' maybe a few changes.

The first change came an hour after our conversation with the president. Susie Wiles, the president's chief of staff, was replaced by Deputy Chief of Staff Stephen Miller, the architect of the president's mass deportation policy. It's a move that seems to conflict with the president's professed desire to work with Democrats on immigration.We asked the president about another administration official whose job security is the subject of speculation.Ross Douthat: We saw Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth in the hall.

He was meeting with you just before now. His name has come up a few times--President Donald Trump: It has.Ross Douthat: As someone people have called for his resignation.President Donald Trump: They do.Ross Douthat: Do you have confidence in him?President Donald Trump: I do. Look, we've won two wars.

We've won Venezuela and taken out billions and billions and billions of dollars already. And we will be taking out many billions of dollars and get along very well. And-- you could call it a territory, you could call it whatever you want.

We won that war in less than one hour.Ross Douthat: And you credit Hegseth--President Donald Trump: And nobody was killed.Ross Douthat: You credit Pete Hegseth for that--President Donald Trump: No. But he was a part of it. This past week, Hegseth released a long video message defending his own tenure and the prosecution of the Iran war â a war the president claims is essentially finished.Ross Douthat: So you're not gonna escalate the war now that the midterms are overPresident Donald Trump: Well, I'm not looking to.

I don't think there's any reason to. I don't think there's any reason to. Look-- Ross Douthat: They still have nuclear material--President Donald Trump: They have--Ross Douthat: Right?President Donald Trump: They have nothing.

It's buried under thousands of tons of rock. Ross Douthat: So what's the deal in the end with them--President Donald Trump: The deal--Ross Douthat: That gets--President Donald Trump: The--Ross Douthat: That gets the Strait open--President Donald Trump: The deal--Ross Douthat: 'Cause it's important-- it's important to stress--President Donald Trump: No, no, the d--Ross Douthat: 'Cause--President Donald Trump: The strait is open.

We have ships--Ross Douthat: But--President Donald Trump: Going--Ross Douthat: But the ships--President Donald Trump: Through--Ross Douthat: That are going through are being babysat by a large U.S. military presence. So how do we make a deal--President Donald Trump: Not a very--Ross Douthat: That gets that--President Donald Trump: Not very expensive--Ross Douthat: Presence out of there?President Donald Trump: Not very expensive.Ross Douthat: We can just leave--President Donald Trump: And--Ross Douthat: Them there--President Donald Trump: At the end of--Ross Douthat: Indefinitely?President Donald Trump: This whole thing, those countries that we've protected are going to pay us back any and all costs that we've had for the war 'cause without us, they wouldn't exist.

Without us, Israel would not exist. Let me tell youRoss Douthat: Israel âPresident Donald Trump: Israel--Ross Douthat: Tell me-- tell me about--President Donald Trump: Israel would not exist except for Donald Trump because we went in with those beautiful B2 Bombers more than a year ago, and we hit the three sites at-- at the time.Ross Douthat: But on Israel, do you have regrets about the decision to help the Israelis do decapitation strikes on Iran because that changed the Iranian regime, and it seems like it made them escalate.

You could've just kept hitting the--President Donald Trump: Well--Ross Douthat: The nuclear facilities, right--President Donald Trump: Yeah, you could've done that, but-- we had people that w-- would have gone further. We decapitated their nuclear arsenal. Look, I deal with these people.

I deal with a lotta people, and that's what I've done my whole life. I make deals. And obviously, I make good deals 'cause I beca-- I made a lotta money and I became president.

But-- you know, it's-- that's a deal too.One place where the president's dealmaking has thus far fallen short is the war between Russia and Ukraine. Our interview came just days before Ukrainian, Russian, and American delegations were scheduled to meet in Abu Dhabi for the first time since February.Ross Douthat: You came into office promising to make peace in Ukraine.President Donald Trump: Yeah.Ross Douthat: There is still a war going on.

What's the biggest obstacle to peace?President Donald Trump: It was the hatred between Zelenskyy and Putin. If I had been president that war would've never started. Zero chance.

But it did start. So I inherited that war. I believe we're very close to making a deal--Ross Douthat: Who-- who do you trust more, President Putin or President Zelenskyy--President Donald Trump: Well, I'd rather not say, but I get along with both.

I believe that that war is going to end, and it's gonna end soon. And the only reason it's gonna end is because of me. There is tremendous hatred between President Putin and President Zelenskyy.

And-- you know, I--Ross Douthat: Isn't it more understandable coming from President Zelenskyy, given that his country was actually invaded?President Donald Trump: Well, it is. But when they had their first meeting there was great disrespect shown to Russia. So I'm not gonna say anything--Ross Douthat: I mean, but balancing out--President Donald Trump: Well-- well--Ross Douthat: Invading, disrespecting--President Donald Trump: Let's-- let's put it this way: the war never happened during my four years, and it was never going to happen, even though it was the apple of President Putin's eye.Ross Douthat: Do you think he is stringing you along?President Donald Trump: Oh, I don't think so.Ross Douthat: 'Cause you've been saying over and over you're gonna make peace.

And it just seems like he's the obstacle in the end--President Donald Trump: Well, there's been nobody that's been tougher on Russia than me. Look at our trade. Look what I've done to them on trade with the sanctions and everything else.

Ross Douthat: You've gone back and forth. You-- at some points you have done lots of things, big things in support of Ukraine. But just recently you lifted diesel sanctions on Russia.

Like, you've done various things to take pressure off Russia--President Donald Trump: I didn't lift diesel sanctions. I made it possible for Russia to give not us, but to the world-- thousands and thousands of barrels of oil, of diesel, which it needed. Didn't-- do any big favor.

Ross Douthat: But you expect it to all work out with a free and independent Ukraine--President Donald Trump: I think we're gonna have it done, and I think it's gonna happen and they're gonna end up with a little bit different shape Ukraine. President Donald Trump has been the dominant figure in American politics for a decade.

But now his time is running out. In the next two years, Mr. Trump will need to decide whether to endorse a successor.

He'll have to deal with accusations of corruption, a major concern for midterm voters, over wealth he piled up during his time in office. He will make consequential decisions about artificial intelligence, amid fears that AI threatens the future of the human race. And all of this, in the shadow of the 80-year-old president's own mortality.Ross Douthat: In two years someone else is gonna be the Republican nominee for president.President Donald Trump: Correct.Ross Douthat: I assume you're going to endorse someone for that.President Donald Trump: Probably.

Not necessarily--Ross Douthat: Not necessarily? What would make you--President Donald Trump: I've got so--Ross Douthat: What are you thinking about when you decide whether or not to endorse someone--President Donald Trump: I don't know, we have a tremendous bench. I mean, I have so many people that I have great relationships with.

And-- you know, not necessarily--Ross Douthat: Who do you-- who-- who would be on the list besides the vice president?President Donald Trump: Well, I think Marco's great. I think--Ross Douthat: Is he staying, by the way, as Secretary of State--President Donald Trump: I think so. I mean, he certainly loves it and he's doing great.

He's doing a fantastic job. The ones they think about, but there are many others and I'd rather not mention their names. There's some senators that are excellent.

I know 'em all, I like 'em a lot. So I may or may not get involved. I don't know.

Maybe I'm better off not getting involved.Ross Douthat: Do you think you can have MAGA without you as the leader?President Donald Trump: I think so. Because MAGA is basically common sense, you know? MAGA's strong borders, good military.

We have created wealth at a level that our country has never seen before--Ross Douthat: Including for yourself. There's a Forbes story that said that your net worth, maybe it's changed with the stock market recently, but your net worth went up by $3 billion since you--President Donald Trump: Well, so did everyone--Ross Douthat: --since you returned to--President Donald Trump: Okay, you ready?

So here's--Ross Douthat: Everyone's-- my net worth did not go up by $3 billion for--President Donald Trump: Well, you should've had stock--Ross Douthat: --for the record. I-- I should've-- I should've--President Donald Trump: You should've had stock.Ross Douthat: I should've had stock.President Donald Trump: Excuse me.

So I devote--Ross Douthat: How did-- how--President Donald Trump: --I devote--Ross Douthat: --how did-- how did it go up by $3 billion--President Donald Trump: Well, let me explain. I devote almost no time to my net worth. I don't care.

I make-- I have a lotta money, and far more than I ever thought I'd have. And I guess it's gone up. I don't even know.

I have a son who's a very straight, good guy. He watches over money. I don't even talk to him about it.

He watches. He gives-- they gave my money, I have a lotta cash, have-- had a lotta cash long before I came in here. I don't take a salary, you know?

Do you know I'm the only, supposedly, I don't know if that's right--Ross Douthat: It's very generous of you to the American taxpayer, but--President Donald Trump: --I am the only president-- that didn't take-- every other president took their salary. I'm sup--Ross Douthat: But this is-- all right, here's-- here's what I wanna understand.

So your son manages or helps manage a cryptocurrency company called World Liberty Financial. You are--President Donald Trump: Which-- which son are we talking about? Which--Ross Douthat: --a co-- you are a co-owner of that company.President Donald Trump: That's correct, yeah--Ross Douthat: Right?

That's correct, right? This company is also partially owned by investors connected to the government of the United Arab Emirates. I think if I told you that story and it was about the Biden family, if I said Joe Biden is the part owner of a company and it has all of these investments from the Middle East, you would say, "That sounds corrupt," right--President Donald Trump: Well, he-- he did have a lotta different--Ross Douthat: Sure, but-- but you--President Donald Trump: But here's the difference--Ross Douthat: --but-- but-- but why is it-- why is it different--President Donald Trump: Here's-- well, here's--Ross Douthat: --for you?President Donald Trump: --I'm gonna tell you why.

Because I know nothing about it.Ross Douthat: But why do you--President Donald Trump: I made a lot of money before--Ross Douthat: But then why do you need the money? Why not just divest? Walk away--President Donald Trump: Well, I-- I do.

Look, most of--Ross Douthat: But no, you didn't.President Donald Trump: --my money-- most of my money is in g-- is given to the biggest firms on Wall Street to invest. and they're index funds. So it came out that I trade-- traded, like, 40,000 stocks. So among the stocks would be, like, they'd have a tiny, little amount.

It's billions of dollars--Ross Douthat: Right, no, I-- I--President Donald Trump: It's billions, just so you understand--Ross Douthat: --I under-- I understand that. But companies that are--President Donald Trump: I have no idea--Ross Douthat: --invested in by people in foreign countries--President Donald Trump: I-- I-- I would like to--Ross Douthat: --it seems like you could just walk away from that and then, you know, and then you would not be accused--President Donald Trump: Well, I have--Ross Douthat: --of corruption, right?President Donald Trump: --I have, but you have sons where they go around and they build buildings.

That's what they do. That's what I did long before I became president. I did it better than anybody.

I was very good at real estate. I made a lotta money. But- but I have a company.

article_content_zh:
上周二，唐纳德·特朗普总统领导的共和党遭遇了非同寻常的中期选举失败——不仅失去了众议院和参议院，还失去了从德克萨斯州到堪萨斯州再到南卡罗来纳州的红色州的全州办公室，这些民主党几十年来都没有赢得过胜利。过去，这位总统曾因涉嫌舞弊和推翻 2020 年选举的努力而遭遇失败。

但当我们周五在白宫会见他自中期选举以来的第一次坐下来采访时，我们发现他有着令人惊讶的反思情绪，并且似乎接受了失败。我们的谈话内容广泛，涵盖：移民和腐败、伊朗和人工智能、他的潜在继任者和他自己的死亡。

但我们从选举结果开始。 罗斯·杜塔特：两年前，你们赢得了一场重大的、有些人可能会说是历史性的胜利。刚刚，共和党在中期选举中遭受了一场巨大的、有人可能会说是历史性的失败。请对刚刚发生的事情进行政治分析。 唐纳德·特朗普总统：嗯，第一，我没有参加投票。

但我为一些人努力竞选。而且——我想如果我参加了投票，情况会大不相同，因为你看到了受欢迎程度和喜爱程度。有爱。

我们举行了大规模集会。然而，你必须将这些选民转移给他们不喜欢的候选人。但除此之外还有一些事情。

他们不喜欢战争。他们不喜欢汽油价格上涨，因为我把汽油价格降到了最低水平，而且令人难以置信的是，以色列非常不喜欢。罗斯·杜塔特：让我们一一讨论。唐纳德·特朗普总统：继续。罗斯·杜塔特：从候选人开始，对吧？

你说很难将你自己的吸引力转移给候选人唐纳德·特朗普总统：是的。 罗斯·杜塔特：但在很多情况下，你选择了候选人。你支持肯·帕克斯顿——唐纳德·特朗普总统：嗯，我——罗斯·杜塔特：——在德克萨斯州。唐纳德·特朗普总统：我——罗斯·杜塔特：他度过了一段艰难的时光。唐纳德·特朗普总统：当然。罗斯·杜塔特：你支持达林·格雷厄姆——唐纳德·特朗普总统：但是——但是科宁——罗斯·杜塔特：——在南卡罗来纳州。唐纳德·特朗普总统：——科宁也会输。

亲爱的，我这样做是为了纪念一个叫林赛的人，他是我的朋友。而她也奋力抗争。她奋力抗争。

她确实做到了。罗斯·杜塔特：她失去了一个非常共和党的州。 唐纳德·特朗普总统：哦——罗斯·杜塔特：对一个非常自由的挑战者——唐纳德·特朗普总统：我赢了——我以迄今为止历史上最高的票数赢得了南卡罗来纳州。我以迄今为止历史上最高的票数赢得了德克萨斯州。

我赢得了佛罗里达州，顺便说一句，我确实支持了佛罗里达州。他将成为——一位伟大的州长和一位伟大的参议员。我对他们俩都表示赞同。

而且，如果我没有支持他们，他们就不会赢。 Ross Douthat：为什么它不能转移？你——你在路上，你说——唐纳德·特朗普总统：它没有转移——罗斯·杜塔特：你说，“像我在选票上一样投票。”唐纳德·特朗普总统：是的。它没有--Ross Douthat：人们没有吗？

或者——或者他们做到了？他们投票是因为生你的气吗——唐纳德·特朗普总统：不，他们——罗斯·杜塔特：关于——唐纳德·特朗普总统：我认为他们没有投票，真的。我认为在某些情况下，他们不喜欢候选人。

你知道，这就是他们的特权。罗斯·杜塔特：几天前，你们的副总统 JD 万斯在社交媒体上发帖说，“我们失败的原因是战争”，指的是伊朗。他在那篇文章中说了一些话——唐纳德·特朗普总统：我不反对——罗斯·杜塔特：关于以色列。

是的。那么你同意他的分析吗？唐纳德·特朗普总统：我不反对罗斯·杜塔特：你知道他会写那篇文章吗？唐纳德·特朗普总统：他问我怎么想。我说，“你写你的东西——”我说——罗斯·杜塔特：“写你的——”唐纳德·特朗普总统：你写你想要的——”罗斯·杜塔特：“写你的感受”？唐纳德·特朗普总统：顺便说一句，“你要写什么？

title: How Sequoia's Alfred Lin and Pat Grady erased Roelof Botha's legacy, halving GPs and unwinding his fund; sources say he joined SpaceX's board behind their backs (Financial Times)

content_snippet: Closures of London office and permanent capital fund mark latest efforts to streamline Silicon Valley VC firm
summary_en: Sequoia partners Alfred Lin and Pat Grady dismantled Roelof Botha's legacy by closing the London office and unwinding the permanent capital fund. This restructuring followed reports that Botha joined the SpaceX board without internal disclosure, effectively sidelining him.
title_zh: 红杉资本内部大清洗：罗洛夫被边缘化

title: Here’s the full text of Jensen Huang’s memo to Nvidia
title_en: Here’s the full text of Jensen Huang’s memo to Nvidia
author: The Verge AI
article_content:
Posts from this topic will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

In the memo Nvidia’s CEO acknowledges having an affair with a suspected Chinese spy.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

On Sunday, Nvidia announced it was launching an investigation into CEO Jensen Huang’s relationship with Alice Huang, an AI executive and agent of the Chinese government. In addition to the Board of Directors announcing the investigation, Huang sent a memo to Nvidia employees acknowledging the affair. You can read the full text below.

I owe my family and all of you an apology.

I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry.

Throughout my life, my family has given me love and support. They deserve my honesty and loyalty. Instead, I let them down and damaged the life we built together. I take full responsibility for what I did and the hurt I caused, and I accept the criticism that comes with it.

To my wife and family: I love you. I know an apology cannot undo what I have done. I hope our family will heal and that, over time, I can earn back your trust.

To my colleagues at NVIDIA, including those I have worked alongside for decades, and to our board, partners, and shareholders around the world: you deserve better from me. Leading NVIDIA is the privilege of my life. My responsibility is to serve you and be worthy of your trust. I have fallen short of that responsibility. I am fully committed to NVIDIA and will work to earn back your confidence.

Regarding the national security concerns raised in news reports, NVIDIA’s Board of Directors has initiated an independent investigation. I support the investigation and will cooperate fully. I love our country and our company. I am committed to protecting NVIDIA and supporting America’s national security. I am proud and grateful to be an American.

My family bears no responsibility for my choices. I do. Please give them privacy.
