title: iPad mini (2026) review: great OLED display, waterproof and dustproof, and fast A20 Pro chip, but it is expensive, no 120Hz display, and still lacks Face ID (David Pierce/The Verge)
title_en: iPad mini (2026) review: great OLED display, waterproof and dustproof, and fast A20 Pro chip, but it is expensive, no 120Hz display, and still lacks Face ID (David Pierce/The Verge)
author: The Verge
article_content:
Posts from this topic will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

With better performance and a better screen, this is a Mini to be reckoned with. But it’s not perfect, and it sure isn’t cheap.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

If you buy something from a link, The Verge may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.

The iPad Mini sometimes feels like a trap. It is, in some ways and for some people, the perfect iPad: meaningfully larger than my phone’s screen but still small and light enough to use for reading in bed or gaming on the subway. As most of the rest of the iPad line has tilted ever closer to laptop territory, the Mini might be the most iPad-y iPad left. I’ve taken a Mini everywhere with me since the very first one. But Apple only updates the Mini sporadically, and those updates sometimes feel like someone inside Apple Park picked its specs by closing their eyes and clicking randomly in an Excel sheet. The Mini is always a little underpowered, a little overpriced, and a little afield in Apple’s tablet lineup. We, the iPad Mini People, sometimes feel a little forgotten.

This year’s model, though, is an upgrade through and through. Apple made the screen larger and better, while making the iPad itself smaller and lighter. It upgraded the processor in a big way. It made the whole package more durable, so you can take it to more places and use it for more things. It actually feels like a tablet made for a reason, not just another occasional bone thrown to the small-tablet fans.

For the past week, I’ve been testing the midnight iPad Mini with cell service, 512GB of storage, and the nano-texture matte display coating. I really like it. It’s the best iPad Mini yet, and a huge leap over the previous model. The one in my hands also costs $1,249, and I cannot in good conscience tell you to buy it. Even the very cheapest version — Wi-Fi only, 128GB of storage, regular OLED display — starts at $699, by a wide margin the highest starting price ever for a Mini.

If you don’t already know the iPad Mini is your one true love, there’s probably a better iPad out there for you. But if you’re an iPad Mini Person and you can stomach the price? You’re getting the best Mini in years.

The Mini’s new display is its most important and most controversial upgrade. It now measures 8.5 inches instead of 8.3, and it’s now a 2316 x 1512 OLED panel instead of an LCD. The OLED gives the screen a little more dynamic range than the previous model, with brighter bright spots and darker dark spots. Its peak brightness is noticeably brighter than before, and its minimum brightness is low enough to be totally pleasant for reading in the dark (as long as you’re in dark mode). In general, it’s just a little more crisp and contrast-y, in a nice way; the old Mini’s display was the least of my worries, but the OLED is a solid improvement. The tablet I tested also has Apple’s nano-texture matte finish, which seems to dull and darken the screen slightly; on a particularly white background, the whole thing seems to shimmer. I suspect I’d like the OLED panel even more without it.

The nano-texture does, however, do an excellent job of reducing glare. The effect is actually really cool: The textured coating doesn’t extend to the bezels, so you can see a source of light or glare come in from the edge of the screen and then simply disappear as it hits the screen. So what you lose in pure screen fidelity, you gain in the ability to read on the iPad in a coffee shop without it reflecting the overhead lights like a mirror. The nano-texture option costs an extra $100, though, and requires you to upgrade to 256GB of storage, so you’re now looking at a $900 tablet. Spend the extra money on the cellular version or, better yet, don’t spend it at all.

For some reason, Apple has never deigned to put its ProMotion display tech on the iPad Mini, which has a refresh rate capped at 60Hz rather than the 120Hz you’ll get on most other recent Apple devices. This is such an odd spec choice that it has launched a bunch of conspiracy theories. Maybe it’s to make more people buy an iPhone Duo instead? Maybe it’s a 120Hz panel downgraded to 60Hz by software just to make people upgrade again next time? Apple’s answer, to Chris Lawley and others, has been something to the effect of “120Hz is irrelevant, OLED’s faster pixel response solves the problems.” I don’t agree. I don’t think the lack of ProMotion is an immediate and total dealbreaker, but refresh rates matter! To games and high-touch creative apps, of course, but you notice the difference even with basic swiping and zooming. The Apple Pencil feels more juddery moving across my screen. On a 120Hz screen, I can scroll a browser page and still clearly read the text as it’s moving. With 60Hz, it gets blurry. In all these cases, even if you don’t explicitly see the difference, you really do feel it.

The most meaningful upgrade in the new Mini, at least for me and how I use my iPad, is that it is designed to be more or less waterproof and dustproof. Its IP67 rating means that the Mini got the highest possible score for protection from “solid foreign objects,” which for our purposes mostly just means dust won’t get inside, and is also “protected against the effects of temporary immersion in water.” It’s not quite as rugged as, say, the iPhone 18 Pro, and I don’t recommend using it as an underwater camera or anything, but your tablet should be fine as long as you don’t drop it in the tub and leave it for a while.

This increased ruggedness immediately changed my iPad usage in a couple of ways. I became less worried about handing the Mini to my toddler, whose general stickiness and penchant for spilling things no longer feel like threats. I also started using the Mini more in the kitchen — I love to cook with an iPad nearby for recipes and Community episodes, and it was nice not to be constantly guarding against flour explosions and water spills. At one point, the iPad Mini even came with me in the shower during a particularly close football game. It’s still kicking.

This is, for lack of a better word, the Field iPad.

The Mini’s IP rating is also the feature that finally made me see who Apple sees as the ideal iPad Mini user. This is, for lack of a better word, the Field iPad. We hear all the time about pilots who use Minis instead of sheaves of paperwork, but Apple also sees them in use on construction sites, oil rigs, doctor’s offices, and all kinds of other places. (It’s a fun rabbit hole, actually — can I interest you in an “explosion proof” last-gen Mini for $4,500 or so?) Apple’s goal with the Mini is not really to maximize performance, satisfy the pixel-peepers, or enhance creator workflows. It’s durability and usability. Body and screen.

Apple made a couple of changes to the Mini to receive its IP rating, like ditching the speaker holes and opting for what it calls an Acoustic Display. It means the sound fires out of the front panel rather than from speaker holes. (Some TVs currently work the same way.) It doesn’t sound any better than before, maybe a tiny bit bassier, but it also doesn’t sound worse, and if anything it’s slightly better to have the sound actually pointed at you instead of out the sides of the tablet. Mostly it’s a wash in service of the ruggedization, which is good enough for me.

The rest of the hardware is just wins all the way around. The A20 Pro chip, the chipset also on the iPhone 18 Pro (and the Duo), benchmarks about 50 percent faster than the 2024 Mini for standard computing tasks, and about three times as fast for graphics-intensive ones. (The chip in my review unit has one more CPU core than the A20 Pro in the cheaper Minis; those will still be drastic improvements, but maybe a hair less so.) I notice the difference, even side by side with the old model, in how fast apps load and games play. Games like Assassin’s Creed Mirage, which were all but unplayable on the 2024 Mini, work nicely on this one. The body is about a tenth of an inch thinner and about an ounce and a half lighter. Perhaps as a result, the battery is a tiny bit smaller, but battery life remains steadfastly somewhere around nine hours of screen time.

One last hardware thing I should mention: Apple moved the front-facing camera from the portrait side of the Mini to the landscape side. On every other iPad, all of which seem to want to be used horizontally, that’s clearly the right decision. On this one, the only iPad I actually hold vertically for long periods, I’m torn. And in either case, that camera still doesn’t enable FaceID — it’s still TouchID or nothing on the Mini.

I thought the last iPad Mini was a disappointment, a product made from spare parts without any particular reason for existence. This year’s Mini feels mostly like a return to form. It’s powerful enough to be useful for a long time. It’s lighter and thinner than ever. The 60Hz refresh rate is a bummer, but I don’t think it’s a dealbreaker for most people. And it’s really the only downside. Though at this price, should you have to deal with any downsides?

After a run of new models and price increases from Apple, it’s worth level-setting a bit on iPad prices. The cheapest model you can buy is now the base iPad at $449, with an A16 chip (the one from the iPhone 14 Pro) and 128GB of storage. The cheapest iPad Air, with an M4 processor and 128GB of storage, is $749. The Pro has an M5 and 256GB for $1,199. iPads are expensive!

In this context, the new Mini’s $699 starting price feels at least $100 too high — this model has always been more expensive than the base iPad, but unless you really want or need the small screen, $50 more gets you a much better and more versatile iPad Air. As ever, the iPad Mini is really only for iPad Mini People (and pilots and oil riggers, apparently). Someday, Apple will give us the tiny flagship we’ve been waiting for, and I’ll gladly pay Apple’s top dollar for it. This is a very good iPad Mini, but it’s not quite the Mini in its final form.

title_zh: 2026款iPad mini发布：OLED屏配A20芯片
summary_zh: 2026款iPad mini如期亮相，换装OLED屏与A20 Pro芯片并引入防水防尘，但价格高昂且依然缺失120Hz刷新率与面部识别功能
article_content_zh:
该主题的帖子将添加到您的每日电子邮件摘要和主页源中。

凭借更好的性能和更好的屏幕，这是一款不容忽视的 Mini。但它并不完美，而且价格也不便宜。

该作者的帖子将添加到您的每日电子邮件摘要和主页源中。

如果您通过链接购买商品，The Verge 可能会赚取佣金。请参阅我们的道德声明。

iPad Mini 有时感觉就像一个陷阱。从某些方面来说，对于某些人来说，它是完美的 iPad：比我的手机屏幕大得多，但仍然又小又轻，足以用于在床上阅读或在地铁上玩游戏。由于 iPad 系列的其余大部分产品都越来越接近笔记本电脑领域，Mini 可能是剩下的最具 iPad 风格的 iPad。从第一辆 Mini 开始，我就一直带着它去任何地方。但苹果只是偶尔更新 Mini，这些更新有时感觉就像 Apple Park 内的某个人闭上眼睛并在 Excel 表格中随机点击来选择其规格。 Mini 的动力总是有点不足，价格有点过高，并且在苹果的平板电脑产品线中显得有点偏僻。我们，iPad Mini 用户，有时会感到有点被遗忘。

不过，今年的型号是彻底的升级。苹果让屏幕变得更大、更好，同时让 iPad 本身变得更小、更轻。它对处理器进行了大幅升级。它使整个包装更加耐用，因此您可以将其带到更多地方并用它做更多事情。实际上，它给人的感觉就像是一款出于某种原因而制造的平板电脑，而不仅仅是偶尔扔给小平板电脑粉丝的一块骨头。

过去一周，我一直在测试配备手机服务、512GB 存储空间和纳米纹理磨砂显示屏涂层的午夜 iPad Mini。我真的很喜欢它。它是迄今为止最好的 iPad Mini，比之前的型号有了巨大的飞跃。我手里的这款也售价 1,249 美元，凭良心我不能告诉你买它。即使是最便宜的版本——仅 Wi-Fi、128GB 存储空间、普通 OLED 显示屏——起售价为 699 美元，远远高于 Mini 有史以来的最高起价。

如果您还不知道 iPad Mini 是您的真爱，那么可能有一款更好的 iPad 适合您。但如果您是 iPad Mini 用户并且您能接受这个价格吗？您将获得多年来最好的 Mini。

Mini 的新显示屏是其最重要且最具争议的升级。它现在的尺寸为 8.5 英寸，而不是 8.3 英寸，并且现在是 2316 x 1512 OLED 面板，而不是 LCD。与之前的型号相比，OLED 屏幕的动态范围更大，亮点更亮，暗点更暗。它的峰值亮度明显比以前更亮，并且其最低亮度足够低，足以在黑暗中阅读（只要您处于黑暗模式）。总的来说，它只是以一种很好的方式更加清晰和对比。旧款 Mini 的显示屏是我最不担心的，但 OLED 是一个坚实的改进。我测试的这款平板电脑还具有苹果的纳米纹理哑光效果，看起来屏幕稍微暗淡一些；在特别白色的背景下，整个东西似乎都在闪闪发光。我怀疑如果没有它，我会更喜欢 OLED 面板。

然而，纳米纹理在减少眩光方面确实表现出色。效果实际上非常酷：纹理涂层不会延伸到边框，因此您可以看到光源或眩光从屏幕边缘进入，然后在撞击屏幕时消失。因此，虽然你失去了纯粹的屏幕保真度，但你却可以在咖啡店里用 iPad 阅读，而不会像镜子一样反射头顶的灯光。不过，纳米纹理选项需要额外花费 100 美元，并且需要升级到 256GB 存储空间，因此您现在正在考虑购买 900 美元的平板电脑。花额外的钱购买蜂窝版本，或者更好的是，根本不花它。

出于某种原因，苹果从未屈尊将其 ProMotion 显示技术应用到 iPad Mini 上，该技术的刷新率上限为 60Hz，而不是大多数其他最新 Apple 设备上的 120Hz。这是一个如此奇怪的规格选择，以至于引发了一系列阴谋论。也许是为了让更多人购买 iPhone Duo？也许这是一个120Hz面板被软件降级到60Hz只是为了让人们下次再升级？苹果对 Chris Lawley 等人的回答是“120Hz 无关紧要，OLED 更快的像素响应可以解决问题。”我不同意。我不认为缺乏 ProMotion 会立即彻底破坏交易，但刷新率很重要！当然，对于游戏和高触感创意应用程序，即使是基本的滑动和缩放，您也会注意到差异。 Apple Pencil 在屏幕上移动时感觉更加颤抖。在 120Hz 屏幕上，我可以滚动浏览器页面，并且在移动时仍然可以清晰地阅读文本。 60Hz 时，它会变得模糊。在所有这些情况下，即使您没有明确地看到差异，您也确实能感觉到。

至少对于我以及我使用 iPad 的方式而言，新款 Mini 最有意义的升级是它或多或少的防水和防尘设计。它的 IP67 等级意味着 Mini 在“固体异物”防护方面获得了最高分，对于我们来说，这主要意味着灰尘不会进入内部，并且还“免受暂时浸入水中的影响”。它不像 iPhone 18 Pro 那样坚固，我不建议将它用作水下相机或其他任何东西，但只要你不把它掉进浴缸里并放置一段时间，你的平板电脑应该没问题。

这种增强的耐用性立即在几个方面改变了我的 iPad 使用方式。我不再那么担心把 Mini 交给我蹒跚学步的孩子了，他一贯的粘性和洒东西的习惯不再让人感觉像是威胁。我还开始在厨房里更多地使用 Mini——我喜欢用附近的 iPad 做饭，查看食谱和社区节目，而且不用时刻提防面粉爆炸和水溢出，这很好。有一次，在一场势均力敌的足球比赛中，iPad Mini 甚至陪着我洗澡。它还在踢。

由于找不到更好的词，这就是 Field iPad。

title: The Download: controlling AI agents and “Super Intelligence” loyalty tests
title_en: The Download: controlling AI agents and “Super Intelligence” loyalty tests
author: MIT Tech Review
article_content:
A new approach known as “reverse game theory” aims to control powerful AI models by designing systems that incentivize them to stick to the rules.

While game theory predicts how rational actors behave under particular rules, reverse game theory designs rules to elicit the behavior we want. Think of splitting a cake: if one person cuts it and the other gets first choice, the cutter has an incentive to make the portions equal.

Researchers believe the approach could align AI more closely with our rules and instructions. But big questions remain about whether these mechanisms will work in practice.

title_zh: 用反向博弈论给AI立规矩

ai_analysis.takeaway_en: Basically, it's just playing a high-stakes game of 'carrot and stick' with AI, hoping to make math force a digital god to be 'human.' Too bad if the AI doesn't play by our petty human game theory—it probably has a million ways to hack the rules while we're still busy dividing the cake.

article_content_zh:
一种被称为“反向博弈论”的新方法旨在通过设计激励人工智能模型遵守规则的系统来控制强大的人工智能模型。

博弈论预测理性参与者在特定规则下的行为方式，而逆向博弈论设计规则来引发我们想要的行为。想象一下分割蛋糕：如果一个人切蛋糕，而另一个人有第一选择，那么切刀者就会有动机使份数相等。

研究人员认为，这种方法可以使人工智能更符合我们的规则和指令。但这些机制能否在实践中发挥作用仍然存在重大问题。
fact_bullets_zh: 【核心事件】科研人员在AI安全控制机制研究领域：提出利用反向博弈论设计激励结构，引导AI遵循人类指令，而非试图从源头封堵模型能力。
【起因与机理】为防止未来出现的超级智能因追求效率而违背人类意图，需要一套基于利益驱动的底层对齐框架。
【关键技术规格】科研团队探索AI控制新范式。
【观点态度】试图通过博弈论规避失控风险。

[Root Cause & Mechanism] To prevent superintelligence from defying human intentions while pursuing efficiency, necessitating a bottom-up alignment framework driven by incentives.
[Key Specification] Research teams explore new AI control paradigms.
[Perspective & Impact] Attempting to avoid runaway risks via game theory.

title: Anthropic's Message Threads cut time to first token by 35 percent for long conversations
title_en: Anthropic's Message Threads cut time to first token by 35 percent for long conversations
author: THE DECODER
article_content:
Anthropic released Message Threads for the Messages API. Instead of resending the entire conversation with every turn, agents now only transmit what's changed. For requests between 500,000 and one million tokens, time to first token drops by about 35 percent.

The article Anthropic's Message Threads cut time to first token by 35 percent for long conversations appeared first on The Decoder.

title: Nvidia pushes cloud customers to cut back on China business
title_en: Nvidia pushes cloud customers to cut back on China business
author: THE DECODER
article_content:
Nvidia has told some cloud customers to take on less business from Chinese companies. The guidance is meant to push cloud providers, including Nvidia-backed neoclouds, toward a more diverse customer mix, The Information reports, citing three people familiar with the matter.

The directive isn't mandatory and applies to future contracts, not existing deals. Cloud customers are also being asked to disclose the identity of end users accessing the chips. According to the Financial Times, the instruction was communicated verbally through sales reps and regional teams.

The move targets a gap in U.S. export controls. The rules restrict chip shipments but generally don't cover remote access through cloud services. That lets Chinese AI developers tap advanced Nvidia chips by renting compute capacity at data centers abroad, without ever importing the hardware. U.S. authorities had been looking into Chinese AI companies accessing such chips through foreign data centers after allegations surfaced involving Moonshot AI, the developer behind the Kimi chatbot.

title_zh: 英伟达施压云厂商设限中国业务
summary_zh: 英伟达正私下要求云服务商减少向中国客户提供算力支持，旨在规避美国芯片出口管制的灰色地带
article_content_zh:
英伟达已告诉一些云客户减少从中国公司那里承担的业务。据 The Information 援引三位知情人士的话报道，该指南旨在推动包括 Nvidia 支持的 neoclouds 在内的云提供商走向更加多样化的客户组合。

该指令不是强制性的，适用于未来的合同，而不是现有的交易。云客户还被要求披露访问芯片的最终用户的身份。据英国《金融时报》报道，该指令是通过销售代表和区域团队口头传达的。

此举针对的是美国出口管制的漏洞。这些规则限制芯片发货，但通常不涵盖通过云服务的远程访问。这使得中国人工智能开发人员可以通过在国外数据中心租用计算能力来利用先进的英伟达芯片，而无需进口硬件。在涉及 Kimi 聊天机器人开发商 Moonshot AI 的指控浮出水面后，美国当局一直在调查中国人工智能公司通过外国数据中心访问此类芯片。

title: US data center operators and power developers are repurposing jet engines to secure power in as little as two years, bypassing multi-year grid-connection delays (New York Times)
title_en: US data center operators and power developers are repurposing jet engines to secure power in as little as two years, bypassing multi-year grid-connection delays (New York Times)
author: New York Times
content_snippet: Across wide stretches of the sun-bleached Sonoran desert in Arizona, thousands of retired aircraft sit nose-to-tail in graveyards of metal known as boneyards.
summary_en: US data center operators and power developers are repurposing aircraft jet engines into ground-based generators in locations like the Sonoran Desert. Facing multi-year grid-connection delays that fail to match the surging power demands of AI, these firms are bypassing traditional utilities to secure independent power within two years.

title: John Ternus' first earnings call was a timid, scripted affair, as Apple faces a challenging Christmas quarter and a difficult 2027; AAPL falls 4%+ pre-market (Dave Lee/Bloomberg)
title_en: John Ternus' first earnings call was a timid, scripted affair, as Apple faces a challenging Christmas quarter and a difficult 2027; AAPL falls 4%+ pre-market (Dave Lee/Bloomberg)
author: Bloomberg
content_snippet: Apple Inc. investors and fans hoping to get an insight into the philosophy of new Chief Executive Officer John Ternus on Monday were left sorely disappointed.
summary_en: market trading.
title_zh: 库克接班人首秀表现保守，苹果股价盘前跌超4%
summary_zh: 苹果硬件工程主管John Ternus在首次财报电话会议上表现拘谨且全程照本宣科，面对艰难的圣诞季度与2027年前景，苹果盘前股价大跌超4%

ai_analysis.briefing_zh: 苹果硬件工程高级副总裁John Ternus在近期财报电话会议上首次亮相，全程表现得十分谨慎并严格依稿宣读。由于苹果正面临表现疲软的圣诞销售季以及2027年潜在的宏观与业务挑战，引发市场担忧，导致苹果股价在盘前交易中应声下挫超过4%。
ai_analysis.briefing_en: Apple's hardware engineering chief John Ternus delivered a timid and heavily scripted performance during his first earnings call debut. Amid concerns over a challenging holiday quarter and a difficult outlook for 2027, Apple's stock fell over 4% in pre-market trading.

title: Huawei tells customers to find their own AI chip memory, effectively outsourcing procurement to the black market
title_en: Huawei tells customers to find their own AI chip memory, effectively outsourcing procurement to the black market
author: THE DECODER
article_content:
Huawei is telling customers to source the high-performance memory for its AI chips on their own, pushing them onto the black market. Smugglers are exploiting a loophole in U.S. export rules by bundling HBM with low-end processors, shipping them through Hong Kong, and separating the chips on site. Prices for smuggled HBM3E memory have surged to around $4,000 per unit in just one year.

The article Huawei tells customers to find their own AI chip memory, effectively outsourcing procurement to the black market appeared first on The Decoder.

title_zh: 华为让客户自寻AI芯片内存，变相外包黑市采购
summary_zh: 面对美国出口管制，华为要求客户自行采购AI芯片所需的高性能内存，导致走私商通过捆绑低端处理器经香港走私HBM，价格暴涨至每块4000美元

ai_analysis.briefing_zh: 华为近期告知客户，需自行解决其AI芯片所需的高性能内存采购问题，此举变相将供应链采购压力推向了灰色黑市。由于美国出口禁令限制，走私者利用将HBM与低端处理器捆绑、经由香港转运并在当地拆解的漏洞，导致HBM3E内存价格在短短一年内飙升至每块约4000美元。
ai_analysis.briefing_en: Huawei is telling customers to independently source high-performance memory for its AI chips, effectively shifting procurement to the black market. Due to U.S. export controls, smugglers are exploiting loopholes by bundling HBM with low-end processors via Hong Kong and splitting them on-site, causing HBM3E prices to skyrocket to $4,000 per unit.

title: Chainalysis and Elliptic expect North Korean hackers to take months to launder the Binance proceeds, utilizing scripted automation and DeFi lending protocols (Financial Times)

author: Financial Times
content_snippet: North Korean hackers are expected to take months to launder the billions of dollars of tokens they stole last week from crypto exchange Binance …
summary_en: Chainalysis and Elliptic suggest that North Korean hackers are leveraging automated scripts and DeFi lending protocols to launder massive funds stolen from Binance. Given the scale of the theft, the hackers are expected to spend months executing complex on-chain mixing and protocol fragmentation to evade global regulatory tracking.

title: ‘Our Risk, Their Reward’: Zohran Mamdani on AI and Data Centers
title_en: ‘Our Risk, Their Reward’: Zohran Mamdani on AI and Data Centers
author: Wired AI
article_content:
In October 2025, weeks before his historic election win, WIRED sat down with Mamdani for an interview at his campaign office. I remember, vividly, the energy that he carried into the room. This was a man, after all, who’d just pulled off a stunning political feat, rising from being an unknown to becoming the mayoral front-runner in a matter of months. In part, that was because of his message, which focused squarely on affordability and the working class. But much of Mamdani’s campaign success can be attributed to how that message was delivered, namely through a mastery of social media that made every other politician in America look like they were still figuring out how to open Instagram.

Mamdani, then just about to turn 34, radiated in our first conversation with what I can best describe as a supernatural electricity. It lit up the room, and in a subsequent photo shoot on a bustling Manhattan street, drew passersby as if by magic. New Yorkers hooted and hollered at the candidate who, seemingly overnight, had made the mundanity of local politics feel like a cultural revolution.

Fast-forward one year, and the Mamdani electricity is still there—it just might be a little bit more tired. The daily grind of governing, after all, doesn’t offer quite the same excitement as a rocket-ship campaign. Not to mention that Mamdani, particularly given his massive reach online, has now become a lightning rod for polarizing conversations, from Israel to the Democratic Socialists of America, as well as a beacon of political hope for millions across the country and even around the world.

Mamdani’s approval rating among Big Apple voters sits at a stunning 69 percent, and he’s become among the most influential figures on the American left; he’s also been described, by his harshest critics, as a dangerous radical whose politics threaten the very city he’s been elected to lead. No pressure.

During a sit-down interview at New York’s City Hall, the mayor and I spoke about what he’s learned during his 10 months on the job, how he uses social media as a tool for governance, and where he stands on some of the most pressing issues facing Americans in today’s midterm elections. Mamdani might be tired—he divulged, hoarsely, that it had been “a long day”—but the internet’s Mayor also seems newly liberated, and certainly empowered to speak his mind. Winning power and wielding it, after all, are two very different things. And right now, the power is squarely in Zohran Mamdani’s corner.

KATIE DRUMMOND: It was almost exactly this time last year that I interviewed you in your campaign office. I remember that for two reasons. One, it was just before the election, but two, you were just about to have a birthday. I was remembering that this weekend, because I was in Sunset Park on Saturday. Sunset Park, for those who don't know, is the best park in Brooklyn, and actually all of New York. I'm sure you agree.

While I was there, I saw you being serenaded with “Happy Birthday.” I did not join. I kept walking. I was like, “I’m gonna see this guy.”

ZOHRAN MAMDANI: I was wondering, like, “Who’s that woman who’s not singing along?”

Yes, the one with the really excited 9-year-old, and her mom was like, “No, we’re gonna keep going.” That was me.

Do you feel a year older? How has the last year of your life been?

It’s been a pretty incredible year. It has also been probably the most transformative year that I’ve lived in my life in terms of what my life was versus what it is now. Much of that year has been having the privilege of having the greatest job in the world. To lead this city and now to be 35.

I think 35. It’s a funny thing because in the world of my friends, this is an age that has a lot of existential questions that come with it. In the work that I do, most people are significantly older than me, and so the meaning of the age, it doesn’t really live in a professional setting.

Do you ever feel like your age is a barrier in politics?

No. When I met [Brazilian President Luiz Inácio] Lula [da Silva] during the UN General Assembly, he was very excited by the fact that I was young. [Laughs] He kept coming back, “So young!” I don’t think it’s a barrier. It’s been one that has also illuminated both the promises and the betrayals of politics.

To be 35 means you grew up through the housing crisis. You grew up through the Iraq War. You grew up through so much of what has shaped our country’s politics over the last few decades. These have been formative moments in my and so many other people’s lives. That too often politics is shaped by those for whom these are issues that just affect other people, not ones that have been all-consuming.

We spent quite a bit of time last year talking about social media and your campaign’s use of it. WIRED declared you the internet’s Mayor. That was before you even won the election. It was a gamble. We felt pretty good about your odds …

No, absolutely not, and never. You told us that you wanted your campaign to not just do social media better than other candidates; you wanted to “own the medium.” You’re still at it. How are you thinking about social media as a tool now for governance versus a tool for campaigning?

I think the similarity is that you have to continue to recognize the fact that for many New Yorkers, this is how they engage with the world. It is yet another medium that has to be treated with the same legitimacy and respect as traditional mediums. I say that because if your goal is to reach as many New Yorkers as possible to tell them about a policy that you are unveiling that they could stand to benefit from, your responsibility is then to communicate through every conceivable measure.

Social media means that we can make a video that could reach, that will reach, more than a million people. That’s just on one specific medium. Also, it means that you have to continue to work your way backwards from How are New Yorkers consuming media? It’s not that we have the right answer, it’s just that we’re listening.

For example, we heard from a number of Spanish-speaking New Yorkers that if you really want to communicate with a specific constituency that you’re not reaching right now, you need to make a WhatsApp channel.

So we made a WhatsApp channel, El Chisme Oficial de NYC, and on that channel we will share directly with Spanish-speaking New Yorkers information that we’re putting out, and you will hear voice notes of me speaking in incredibly halting Spanish about what that policy is.

I think for too long there’s been a sense of “pat myself on the back” in government where it’s like, “I put out the paper press release. People should just know. I put this in one obscure place that people could find if they were looking for it.” We have to make politics and political decisions something that reach people wherever they already are, as opposed to the condescension that comes with, “If you’re not reading this, then it’s not meant for you.”

You also talked last year about your time campaigning and feeling like you needed to put yourself out there on social media in different ways, “Many of which are embarrassing.” What does it look like to be less embarrassing on social media now that you’re the mayor?

Have you tried to clean up your act a little bit?

I feel like I’m equally embarrassing. I think there’s a part of social media which is all about the presentation of cool and mystery.

I live in a world where you will know everything about me, and I have to utilize that to try and share the message of what we’re doing and why we’re doing it. I think in some ways that means abandoning any fear of embarrassment or what it means for perception. If the way that you can learn about the Rent Guidelines Board is me jumping into freezing cold water, then so be it.

That’s what it was when I was running for office, and I think today we’re still taking the same approach of: How can we communicate with as many people as possible? How can we not veer into a place of complacency? That “Oh, now that I’m the mayor, it means everything has to conform to a traditional outreach.”

Part of the reason why so many people feel so ambivalent, at best, about politics is that there’s a sense of irrelevance. And some of that irrelevance comes from the focus of politics, but some of it also comes from the methods of politics. If politics continues to present itself in a way that it did 20 years ago, that is ignoring the fact that we are living in a very different world today. That’s the world that we should be speaking to, and that’s the world whose concerns we should be reflecting.

I would just say that in the year since we sat down together, there’s been a lot of focus on our use of the medium, as if that is more important than the message. I think it’s important to focus on the use of medium, the respect for the medium, and also to understand that putting tired, old ideas into a short-form version in a vertical video does not answer the critical issue with politics today.

It’s not just the presentation, it’s also the substance.

The New York Times published a story in September about your office’s work with creators. Your administration works with lots of creators, some of whom receive talking points around initiatives. They’re invited to cover events, sometimes where traditional journalists, people like myself, would not be present. Among the concerns raised in that piece is the idea of this distinction between journalist and creator.

I understand wanting to leverage social media to reach people in new ways. I think that’s really laudable. But how do you think about that distinction between, quote unquote, “professional journalism” and content creation? Because I think for the average person, and people are very smart, that line has become incredibly blurry.

Talking points are essentially the basis of a press release, right? When we announce a new policy, in the press release there’ll be quotes from myself and other relevant agency heads and other relevant politicians, and then there’ll also be a description as to what the policy is.

To me, that is so critical because we’re looking to demystify politics, and some policies are pretty self-explanatory, and other policies are ones that, frankly, if I didn’t have talking points, then I wouldn’t even be able to formulate what that is.

Earlier this week, we announced that we were going to deliver on an innovative solution to flooding in Central Park. We were going to be able to lower the water levels in three key water bodies to ensure that we would do so in advance of a storm, and then prevent the typical storm water runoff. You need to be able to explain that before you have a conversation about it. So that’s where I would push a little bit on the idea of what talking points are and what they serve.

To your question, you have to be able to treat all of these different mediums with respect and understand the differences between them. If we were an administration that exclusively engaged with digital-first creators, then that would be an issue. But what I see as important is we have to speak to journalists for whom their medium is television, newspaper, radio, digital, magazine, as well as those for whom their only medium might be TikTok or Instagram or Twitter or Bluesky, whatever it may be.

It cannot be a choice any longer, because I think, as you’ve said, for many New Yorkers, there is a sense that all of this is media.

I think we have to have respect for that, as opposed to what has long been a political condescension about which media is legitimate and which media is illegitimate.

How do you separate audiences in your mind when you think about what you would say on TikTok or Instagram, what you would say to a journalist, what you would say behind a podium? Do you think about those distinctions?

Not so much. I think if you try to calibrate yourself for every single constituency, you are losing sight of why people will want to listen. It starts to veer into an imitation as opposed to a presentation of the facts, and I think there’s a difference in that we’ll sit down for 48 minutes. But if I put out a video on Instagram that’s 48 minutes, is it gonna do well? No. But if I’m thinking that I should speak like this over there, and then I should speak like this over here, you’re gonna end up kind of twisting and turning yourself into knots.

I want to move to the midterms, but last year we spent some well-earned time talking about Eric Adams’ social media campaign. He did incredible things on those platforms. Remarkable.

Michael Bay. His life has been changed by that one video.

Phenomenal. Who is the Eric Adams of the midterms on social?

… is that of the departing Congressman Shri Thanedar.

I just never fully understand what I’m looking at.

What are you looking at? What’s happening in the videos?

Are we in carousel mode? Is it just a single photo?

Typically solo style. I would invite others to take a look, and I would say that I’m very excited as well about the incoming congressman.

I will take a look. [Laughs] There is some remarkable AI-generated social media content from some candidates, some of which includes AI-generated versions of you talking about, I think it was a delusion pill.

… where you think that having higher taxes and less money is a good thing. You should check this out.

Was this from [Republican gubernatorial candidate] Bruce Blakeman?

You are not on the ballot for the midterms this November, but this is a big one. In the last year, you have become one of the most influential people in politics. Whether you agree with me saying that or not, you’ve been described repeatedly as something of a power broker within the Democratic Party. An endorsement from you matters.

I’m curious about your decision to endorse and campaign for Governor Hochul. She's seeking reelection. You were critical of her before taking office. Can you talk us through that calculus and what changed?

I think the key thing that my endorsement is a reflection of is just how productive our working relationship has been. And frankly, it is a stark contrast to that of the typical working relationship between the mayor of New York City and the governor of New York state. You look through the years, frankly, and you will find mayor and governor after mayor and governor who are seemingly forever at loggerheads.

What I've found in working with Governor Hochul is that we can deliver on material wins for working-class New Yorkers. And to me, the single most exciting one of those is Universal 2K. On the eighth day of our administration, she agreed to deliver $1.2 billion to make universal childcare a reality for 2-year-olds in this city.

The two of us spent a morning, maybe about a week or two ago, with a family whose child was enrolled in 2K, and they told us that before that, they had to send their child to a different state, that his grandmother had to drive him at 4:00 am for him to get to a childcare that they could afford, and they were still paying $2,300 a month.

That partnership delivered this family more than $20,000 of savings that they can now put towards a house. That, to me, is what politics has to be. It has to mean something for working people. You don’t have to translate to them what $2,300 a month means. They feel it, they know it.

That’s what I'm excited to build on. To me, it’s her track record. It’s her commitment to this city, one that continued in the budget that we had where we were facing a significant fiscal deficit, and she was a real partner in ensuring that we could deliver a balanced budget. There’s a stark contrast with her opponent, who is a little more busy with AI-generated videos of the two of us.

He’s been very busy making AI-generated videos, and defending ICE. I could go on.

Yes, which is a combination that I think most New Yorkers would not want to see in the governor’s office. I also think that his response to universal childcare was to say this was a delivery of a benefit to lazy parents. I have yet to meet a lazy parent in New York City.

I meet people who are exhausted by the fact that our city and our country has made parenthood something that is incredibly difficult to do and seen as if it’s purely an individual responsibility when it’s the benefit of our whole city if children can be raised here.

He said he would cut that program. He said he would cut Medicaid in half. I mean, times are tough as they are, and to have a gubernatorial candidate running on an agenda of, “I’m gonna make working people’s lives harder and more expensive,” I want to find the consultant who sold him that dream ’cause they must have had an incredible pitch. It makes no sense to me.

If Governor Hochul is reelected, where do you hope to take that partnership?

I would say continuing on childcare. What we have delivered funding for is enough to take a program for 2,000 2-year-olds to 12,000 2-year-olds next year. We want to deliver this for every single 2-year-old in New York City. And as of now, we’re scheduled to expand to all of the Bronx, all of Staten Island.

We want it to be every single borough, every single 2-year-old, and the governor has said she’s committed to the expansion of this program. To me, when we’re talking about a cost-of-living crisis, we’re talking about the most expensive city in America. Childcare is the second leading expense for working families in the city. If we can deliver that, what we are really delivering to New Yorkers is a more affordable life. That has to be the job.

Talk to me about the Democratic Socialists of America. Your name has become synonymous in many ways with that movement. It has been one of the dominant political stories of the last year, this rise of DSA candidates winning races across the country. Why do you think now is the time for that organization? Why not five years ago? Why not 10 years ago? Why not five years from now?

I think precisely because the movement is built around delivering dignity to working-class people. Today’s politics is an illustration of the betrayal of the working class. Never before has there been such an urgent demand for a new kind of politics. Here in New York City, the problems that working-class people are facing are in many ways the problems that working-class people are facing across the country: an inability to afford their rent, their childcare, their groceries, their electricity bills.

So that message of fighting for working-class Americans, it’s compelling wherever you are. That’s what drew me to DSA in the first place, was that this was an entire organization built around an understanding that this had to be the focus of our politics. That politics had to mean material wins for working-class people, and that we had to be willing to fight for it.

One of the things that I really love so much about what it means to be a DSA member is the D stands for “democratic.” The organization does what its members decide to do. I think in a lot of politics it feels like there’s the set of people who make the decisions, and there’s everybody else who has to go along with them.

The whole point of this is democracy, that people should be able to choose their own future. People should be able to not just choose their own leaders but also take that democracy and extend it from the ballot box to the rest of their lives.

On that note, we’ve been doing a lot of coverage at WIRED of data centers. I would be curious to hear your point of view on the data center movement, and why you think that specific issue has become such a flashpoint in this election. Where do you think that comes from?

I think the movement to oppose data centers is one that gives me a real sense of hope.

Because it shows the ways in which this fight is cutting across the typical lines that separate Americans. It’s a bipartisan fight. Me and Ron DeSantis don’t have much in common, and yet there is a similar opposition to the development of these kinds of data centers.

It speaks to a few things. Think about the incredible amount of energy that we are talking about when we’re talking about AI. You think about the version of ChatGPT; just the training of that model took the same amount of energy it would take to power all of San Francisco for three days.

That’s the scale. So what you’re seeing in opposition from Americans across the country is an opposition for what these data centers would mean in their day-to-day lives, what it would mean in their electricity rates, what it would mean in terms of the impact on their environment. It’s also a repudiation of what has been a governing politics for the last few years when it comes to AI, which is: our risk, their reward.

You’re seeing it whether you’re in Florida, whether you're in New York, across the entire country. Even in California we’ve seen municipalities that have started to ban the construction of data centers entirely.

You’ve supported New York state setting a one-year pause on data center construction. What next?

One of the solves is a recognition of the costs that come with AI. So much of what we are talking about is based on a very limited amount of information that we have. That is by design, because when we’re talking about these incredibly powerful companies, we also are talking about a level of opacity that renders it almost impossible for us to make an informed conclusion as to how much this query is actually costing us as a society.

Do you mean an absence of data about energy use? Or do you mean the idea that this technology is talked about as mythical rather than infrastructure?

I mean the former. I think that, frankly, there’s an attempt to make this technology seem as if it is mythical or as if it is divine.

There is a real investment in the idea that this is so complicated that the only rational response should be that we trust those who created it.

In many ways, it’s what Facebook was arguing in 2008, that they should be able to regulate themselves. Yet what we need to see is a response that grasps the scale of the adoption of this technology and the incentives that are driving a lot of this technology at this time, and the fact that we are now at a point where there are far too many similarities between the housing bubble and the state of AI in our economy today.

Do you trust the Sam Altmans of the world?

No. Do you trust the Sam Altmans of the world?

But no, I don’t. In the context of AI, you focus obviously on New York. What is your role in shaping how AI affects New Yorkers?

It’s a role on a practical level. I also think it’s a role that reckons with the enormity of AI’s impact. Now, on the practical level, it means formulating one of the most comprehensive AI moratoriums in any American school system, which we put forward, that would ban the use of generative AI for students from 2K through eighth grade.

Ban it because we need students to be given the room to be students. Students to be able to try and fail and learn, and also to bring an end to the use of our students as guinea pigs for the profit motives of technology companies. There’s been this strange thing over the last few years, maybe last few decades: While we would not be willing to have a pharmaceutical company help write the curriculum of a science class, we have been all too willing to partner with technology companies to not just inform the products that are used in the classroom, but also how they are taught.

Then, to the second point, the fact that the impact of AI is not purely an economic impact or an ecological impact, it is also an emotional impact. For all of the focus on job numbers and what jobs will be replaced by AI, there also has to be a reckoning with job satisfaction. There are a lot of jobs where the very purpose of the job is starting to be stripped away by artificial intelligence. There was recently an interview that The Daily conducted with a mathematics professor.

In tears, speaking about AI’s newfound ability to solve this age-old problem that inspired a crisis for him and for other mathematicians as to what they were doing now. What purpose did they have?

I think that is a question that should be at the forefront of how we respond to AI, because for too long, we’ve treated it, in your language, as a mythical thing, as an unknowable thing. In fact, it is a thing very much within human control. That means that we have to answer these questions, thinking about humanity as the primary responsibility.

You’ve said that citywide AI policy has been guided by the question of what we can do in the face of a complete abdication of federal law. How does that affect your ability to rein in the technology on a municipal level? How would you like to see the federal government handling this technology right now?

article_content_zh:
2025 年 10 月，就在他历史性地赢得选举的几周前，《连线》杂志在马姆达尼的竞选办公室接受了采访。我清楚地记得他带进房间的能量。毕竟，这是一个刚刚完成了一项惊人的政治壮举的人，在短短几个月的时间里从一个默默无闻的人一跃成为市长的领跑者。在某种程度上，这是因为他的信息直接关注负担能力和工人阶级。但马姆达尼的竞选成功在很大程度上可以归因于这一信息的传递方式，即通过对社交媒体的掌握，这让美国的其他政客看起来仍在研究如何打开 Instagram。

当时即将年满 34 岁的马姆达尼在我们的第一次谈话中就散发出一种超自然的力量。它照亮了房间，在随后在繁华的曼哈顿街道上拍摄的照片中，它神奇地吸引了路人。纽约人对这位候选人大喊大叫，他似乎在一夜之间让当地政治的世俗化感觉像是一场文化革命。

快进一年，马姆达尼的电力仍然存在——只是可能有点疲惫了。毕竟，日常的执政工作并不像火箭般的竞选那样令人兴奋。更不用说马姆达尼，特别是考虑到他在网上的巨大影响力，现在已经成为从以色列到美国民主社会主义者两极分化对话的避雷针，也是全国乃至世界各地数百万人政治希望的灯塔。

马姆达尼在纽约选民中的支持率高达惊人的 69%，他已成为美国左派中最有影响力的人物之一；他还被最严厉的批评者描述为一个危险的激进分子，他的政治威胁着他当选领导的这座城市。没有压力。

在纽约市政厅的一次静坐采访中，市长和我谈到了他在工作 10 个月中学到的东西、他如何利用社交媒体作为治理工具，以及他对美国人在今天的中期选举中面临的一些最紧迫问题的立场。马姆达尼可能很累——他沙哑地透露，这是“漫长的一天”——但互联网市长似乎也刚刚获得解放，并且肯定有权说出自己的想法。毕竟，赢得权力和运用权力是两件截然不同的事情。而现在，权力完全掌握在佐兰·马姆达尼的手中。

凯蒂·德拉蒙德：几乎就在去年的这个时候，我在您的竞选办公室采访了您。我记得这有两个原因。第一，那是在选举之前，但第二，你正要过生日。这个周末我记得这一点，因为周六我在日落公园。对于那些不知道的人来说，日落公园是布鲁克林乃至整个纽约最好的公园。我相信你也同意。

当我在那里时，我看到你正在唱“生日快乐”小夜曲。我没有加入。我继续走着。我当时想，“我要去见这个人。”

ZOHRAN MAMDANI：我想知道，“那个不跟着唱的女人是谁？”

是的，那个 9 岁的孩子非常兴奋，她妈妈说，“不，我们要继续前进。”那是我。

有没有感觉自己老了一岁？你生命的最后一年过得怎么样？

这是令人难以置信的一年。就我过去的生活与现在的生活而言，这也可能是我一生中最具变革性的一年。那一年的大部分时间都有幸拥有世界上最棒的工作。领导这座城市，现在已经35岁了。

我想 35 岁。这是一件有趣的事情，因为在我朋友的世界里，这是一个伴随着很多存在主义问题的时代。在我所做的工作中，大多数人都比我年长很多，所以年龄的含义并不真正存在于专业环境中。

您是否曾经觉得自己的年龄是政治上的障碍？

不。当我在联合国大会期间见到[巴西总统路易斯·伊纳西奥]卢拉[达席尔瓦]时，他对我年轻这一事实感到非常兴奋。 [笑]他不断地回来说：“好年轻！”我不认为这是一个障碍。它也阐明了政治的承诺和背叛。

title: Google severs ties with and bans Android TV box maker Videostrong after discovering it intentionally preloaded a malware backdoor to control the XCPE botnet (Ben Schoon/9to5Google)
title_en: Google severs ties with and bans Android TV box maker Videostrong after discovering it intentionally preloaded a malware backdoor to control the XCPE botnet (Ben Schoon/9to5Google)
author: 9to5Google
article_content:
Google has confirmed that an Android TV device maker snuck a backdoor for malware onto certified devices, which is leading to security improvements for the ecosystem as a whole.

In a post today, Google confirmed that it has cut ties with “Videostrong,” a company that was manufacturing certified Android TV boxes. This is due to the company building in a backdoor that it could sell access to, including the distribution of malware. Google has taken legal action to block the domains and servers that “Videostrong” was using to control the XCPE botnet and malware modules and banned the company and its subsidiaries from selling certified Android devices going forward, or selling software to any other certified vendors.

We found this malicious software built directly into many different device models and brands over multiple years, supported by dedicated infrastructure and constantly evolving configurations to evade detection and manage their affiliates. We believe this campaign wasn’t an isolated rogue insider or a development oversight. As a result, Google has cut ties with Videostrong and banned them from making devices with preloaded Google apps.

Synthient (via The Hacker News) compiled a list of potentially affected devices, with the focus being on the Mecool brand that has made some well-known Android TV and Google TV boxes in the past. Mecool has been rumored to be shutting down.

Google somewhat admits that this was a failing on its part, as these devices were sold as “certified” Android devices with the implication that they were safe. The company explains that these bad actors “employed obfuscation techniques to exploit a gap in our tests and load malicious code after the device’s first boot.” With that in mind, Google is updating its review process to protect users against this type of behavior, and Google reiterates that “a device manufacturer intentionally infecting their users with malware is an unacceptable breach of trust.”

Google’s shutdown of the domains and servers used to spread malware should leave affected Android TV and Google TV boxes safe to use – the company says that “taking down their C2 domains will sever access to at least 10 million additional compromised devices” – but owners may still want to consider alternate options.

title_zh: 谷歌封杀机顶盒厂商，因预装后门搞僵尸网络
summary_zh: 谷歌因发现机顶盒厂商Videostrong在其经认证的Android TV设备中预装恶意后门，宣布与其彻底断绝业务关系并全面封杀
article_content_zh:
谷歌已证实，一家 Android TV 设备制造商在经过认证的设备上植入了恶意软件后门，这将导致整个生态系统的安全性得到改善。

在今天的一篇帖子中，谷歌证实它已与“Videostrong”断绝关系，该公司生产经过认证的 Android 电视盒。这是因为该公司建立了一个后门，可以出售访问权限，包括分发恶意软件。谷歌已采取法律行动，封锁“Videostrong”用于控制 XCPE 僵尸网络和恶意软件模块的域名和服务器，并禁止该公司及其子公司今后销售经过认证的 Android 设备，或向任何其他经过认证的供应商销售软件。

我们发现这种恶意软件多年来直接内置于许多不同的设备型号和品牌中，并得到专用基础设施和不断发展的配置的支持，以逃避检测并管理其附属机构。我们相信这次活动不是孤立的流氓内部人员或开发疏忽。因此，谷歌切断了与 Videostrong 的合作关系，并禁止他们生产预装谷歌应用程序的设备。

Synthient（来自 The Hacker News）编制了一份可能受影响的设备列表，重点是 Mecool 品牌，该品牌过去曾生产过一些知名的 Android TV 和 Google TV 盒子。有传言称 Mecool 将被关闭。

谷歌承认这是它的一个失败，因为这些设备作为“经过认证的”Android 设备出售，暗示它们是安全的。该公司解释说，这些不良行为者“利用混淆技术来利用我们测试中的漏洞，并在设备首次启动后加载恶意代码。”考虑到这一点，谷歌正在更新其审查流程，以保护用户免受此类行为的侵害，谷歌重申，“设备制造商故意用恶意软件感染用户是一种不可接受的违反信任行为。”

谷歌关闭用于传播恶意软件的域名和服务器应该可以让受影响的 Android TV 和 Google TV 盒子安全使用——该公司表示，“关闭其 C2 域名将切断对至少 1000 万台其他受感染设备的访问”——但用户可能仍想考虑其他选择。

title: How “reverse game theory” could keep AI agents in check
title_en: How “reverse game theory” could keep AI agents in check
author: MIT Tech Review
article_content:
A new approach known as “reverse game theory” aims to create incentives for powerful AI models that make following the rules the most rational choice.

As AI models become more capable, safety researchers are scrambling to ensure they are “aligned” with human desires—to make sure, in other words, that rogue agents don’t break the law, hack into unauthorized servers, or release poison gas into major cities and kill us all.

Until now, this work has mostly focused on trying to peer into an AI’s “brain” to understand what it is “thinking,” or training models to hew to values that we hold dear. Claude, for instance, has its constitution—a sort of moral code.

title: Bug hunters can now earn up to $172,000 from OpenAI as company ramps up security
title_en: Bug hunters can now earn up to $172,000 from OpenAI as company ramps up security
author: THE DECODER
article_content:
OpenAI quadruples bug bounty payouts and launches new internal security sprint. Critical vulnerabilities in core products like ChatGPT or Codex now earn outside researchers up to $30,000, the company announced. Exceptional findings can net up to $100,000, and with quality, loyalty, and campaign bonuses, the total can reach roughly $172,000.

That puts OpenAI in the same ballpark as Google's general vulnerability rewards program, though still below the top-tier payouts Apple or Microsoft offer for OS-level exploits. New additions include a five-tier loyalty program and time-limited campaigns with boosted payouts tied to new feature launches. Anyone who reported a vulnerability in the last 30 days will get the difference between the old and new rates retroactively.

Alongside the bounty overhaul, OpenAI is preparing a security sprint where the security firm Cathedral will team up with OpenAI's own engineers to stress-test its systems. During the last sprint, 25 percent of OpenAI's product engineers worked on finding vulnerabilities, according to the company.

title: UK energy company Drax partners with Brookfield and neocloud Radiant to develop an AI data center in North Yorkshire, targeting 100MW of capacity by Q1 2028 (Kai Nicol-Schwarz/CNBC)
title_en: UK energy company Drax partners with Brookfield and neocloud Radiant to develop an AI data center in North Yorkshire, targeting 100MW of capacity by Q1 2028 (Kai Nicol-Schwarz/CNBC)
author: CNBC
article_content:
Brookfield is targeting a massive artificial intelligence data center in the north of England, as Europe scrambles to develop infrastructure to support the rollout of AI amid high energy and land costs.

Energy company Drax Group said Tuesday it has signed an agreement with Brookfield and the asset manager's neocloud platform Radiant to jointly develop an AI data center on the Drax Power Station estate in North Yorkshire. London-listed shares of Drax were up 8.8% in early morning trading.

The project is initially targeting up to 100 megawatts of capacity to be operational from the first quarter of 2028, with an additional 500 MW of capacity to be brought online between 2028 and 2031. It is then looking to secure more than 1 gigawatt of capacity at the site by an unspecified date.

Brookfield estimates total investment, including semiconductors, could exceed £20 billion ($26.8 billion), with an initial £2.5 billion investment in phase 1.

"This is a unique opportunity for the UK's AI ecosystem to build at scale," Radiant CEO Mahdi Yahya said in a statement. "By designing, building and operating from the UK, it will give British researchers, startups and enterprises access to frontier compute at home."

The first phase of Brookfield's project in North Yorkshire will use power from the grid and target commercial customers from early 2028.

The initial phase is subject to planning, regulatory and network approvals from the government and relevant agencies, alongside securing a tenant for the project, Drax said in a statement said. The company added that final investment decisions are yet to be made.

While the U.S. has surged ahead on developing the huge data centers needed to power AI, Europe has been slower to break ground on the facilities. The U.K. in particular has struggled with high energy costs and challenges with long waiting times for businesses to connect to the grid.

In October, it was reported that Microsoft had pulled out of a deal to anchor an Nscale data center just outside London, amid delays connecting to the country's power grid. An Nscale spokesperson told CNBC at the time that it remained "committed" to the project and was "exploring alternative power sources for the site."

Unlike the U.K., the Nordics benefit from abundant power and available land. Countries in the region, like Finland, have seen major commitments to develop AI data centers this year. In September, Google said it would invest at least 13 billion euros ($15.1 billion) into AI infrastructure in the country, marking the tech giant's largest single investment in Europe.

article_content_zh:
布鲁克菲尔德的目标是在英格兰北部建立一个大型人工智能数据中心，因为欧洲在能源和土地成本高昂的情况下竞相开发基础设施以支持人工智能的推出。

能源公司 Drax Group 周二表示，已与 Brookfield 和资产管理公司的 neocloud 平台 Radiant 签署协议，共同在北约克郡的 Drax Power Station 庄园开发人工智能数据中心。伦敦上市的 Drax 股价早盘上涨 8.8%。

该项目最初的目标是从 2028 年第一季度开始运营高达 100 兆瓦的装机容量，并在 2028 年至 2031 年间新增 500 兆瓦的装机容量。然后，该项目希望在未指定的日期之前在该地点获得超过 1 吉瓦的装机容量。

Brookfield 估计，包括半导体在内的总投资可能超过 200 亿英镑（268 亿美元），第一阶段的初始投资为 25 亿英镑。

Radiant 首席执行官 Mahdi Yahya 在一份声明中表示：“这是英国大规模构建人工智能生态系统的独特机会。” “通过在英国设计、建造和运营，它将让英国研究人员、初创公司和企业能够在国内获得前沿计算。”

Brookfield 位于北约克郡的项目一期将使用电网电力，并从 2028 年初开始面向商业客户。

德拉克斯在一份声明中表示，初始阶段需要获得政府和相关机构的规划、监管和网络批准，同时还要为该项目找到租户。该公司补充说，最终投资决定尚未做出。

尽管美国在开发人工智能所需的大型数据中心方面进展迅速，但欧洲在这些设施的破土动工方面进展缓慢。英国尤其面临着高能源成本和企业连接电网等待时间长的挑战。

10 月份，有报道称，由于与该国电网的连接出现延误，微软退出了在伦敦郊外设立 Nscale 数据中心的协议。 Nscale 发言人当时告诉 CNBC，该公司仍然“致力于”该项目，并“正在为该地点探索替代能源”。

与英国不同，北欧受益于丰富的电力和可用土地。芬兰等该地区国家今年做出了开发人工智能数据中心的重大承诺。 9 月份，谷歌表示将投资至少 130 亿欧元（151 亿美元）用于该国的人工智能基础设施，这是这家科技巨头在欧洲最大的单笔投资。

title: Anthropic cracks down on game cloning in Claude Code after wave of AI-built knockoffs
title_en: Anthropic cracks down on game cloning in Claude Code after wave of AI-built knockoffs
author: THE DECODER
article_content:
Anthropic is blocking its coding assistant Claude Code from recreating existing video games. Employee Addy Osmani confirmed on X that two sentences in Claude Code's system prompt for Opus 5.5 now prevent the tool from cloning other people's games. Using Claude to infringe on intellectual property violates the usage policy, Osmani said.

The rule has been active for several days and kicks in even when a clone gets renamed or passed off as an original work. Users can still build their own games, genre titles, and projects with custom assets, though some report running into problems with original projects too.

The change follows a flood of AI-powered cloning projects. Users have been tapping Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra to crank out hundreds of unofficial browser ports of well-known titles like Halo and GTA Vice City. Tools like Reverse Engineer Anything help by pairing AI agents with reverse engineering to turn native binaries into readable pseudocode. One developer grabbed headlines by recreating parts of Adobe's Creative Cloud apps. Sony's PlayStation 5 also became a target after a jailbreak led to a quick wave of emulators.

After images and videos, the intellectual property battle is now spilling into software. Osmani said Anthropic plans to keep tweaking the rules going forward.

title_zh: Anthropic出手防AI复刻游戏
summary_zh: Anthropic在Claude Code系统提示词中加入防版权审查，禁止AI复刻现有游戏
article_content_zh:
Anthropic 正在阻止其编码助手 Claude Code 重新创建现有视频游戏。员工 Addy Osmani 在 X 上证实，Opus 5.5 的 Claude Code 系统提示中有两句话现在可以阻止该工具克隆其他人的游戏。奥斯马尼表示，利用克劳德侵犯知识产权违反了使用政策。

该规则已生效数天，即使克隆作品被重命名或冒充原创作品，该规则也会生效。用户仍然可以使用自定义资产构建自己的游戏、类型游戏和项目，尽管有些人报告原始项目也遇到了问题。

这一变化是在大量人工智能驱动的克隆项目出现之后发生的。用户一直在利用 Opus 5.5 和 GPT-6 Astra 来开发数百个知名游戏的非官方浏览器端口，例如 Halo 和 GTA Vice City。像 Reverse Engineer Anything 这样的工具可以通过将 AI 代理与逆向工程结合起来，将本机二进制文件转换为可读的伪代码。一位开发人员通过重新创建部分 Adob​​e Creative Cloud 应用程序而成为头条新闻。索尼的 PlayStation 5 越狱事件引发了一波模拟器热潮后也成为了攻击目标。

继图像和视频之后，知识产权之争现在正蔓延到软件领域。奥斯马尼表示，Anthropic 计划继续调整规则。

ai_analysis.briefing_zh: 人工智能企业Anthropic近日通过更新Claude Code的系统提示词，正式禁止其编程助手重现现有电子游戏。此举旨在应对近期大量用户利用AI批量山寨《光环》、《GTA》等知名游戏及破解软件的版权侵权浪潮，尽管官方允许开发者继续创作原创游戏和同人衍生品，但部分原创项目也受到了误伤。
ai_analysis.briefing_en: Anthropic has updated Claude Code's system prompts to prevent its coding assistant from recreating existing video games. This move aims to curb a wave of copyright infringements where users leverage AI to clone popular titles like Halo and GTA, though the new restrictions have occasionally caused false positives for entirely original projects.
